Adapted from Kameron Decker Harris’s Fall 2026 lecture notes “Sets 0” to “Sets 3”, which are typed transcriptions of Scott Wehrwein’s Spring 2025 handwritten lecture notes. These come from those notes:

roster notation, and that order and repetition do not matter in a set;
the table of sets of numbers;
set-builder notation with a test and with an expression;
cardinality, and the pattern of the example of a set whose elements are sets;
countably infinite sets, and the diagonal argument that the real numbers are not countable;
subsets, strict subsets and power sets;
tuples and Cartesian products, including products of three sets;
union, intersection, difference, complement and the universal set (with its example of the even integers), with their other notations;
Venn diagrams.

The exercises are new.




1 Sets and their elements







Exercise 1 (Days that begin with T) Let \(W\) be the set of days of the week whose English names begin with the letter T. List the elements of \(W\).










SolutionSolution






Solution 1. \(W = {\mathopen{}\left\{\text{Tuesday}, \text{Thursday}\right\}\mathclose{}}\).











Definition 1 (Set) A set (Wikipedia contributors 2026n) is a collection of distinct objects, called its elements. We write \(a \in A\) when \(a\) is an element of the set \(A\), and \(a \notin A\) when it is not. Two sets are equal when they have exactly the same elements.











Remark 1 (Naive and formal set theory). Definition 1 is the informal (“naive”) notion of a set, which is all these notes need. Formal set theory states axioms for sets instead (Wikipedia contributors 2026n). For example, the last sentence of Definition 1, that two sets are equal when they have exactly the same elements, is one of those axioms, the axiom of extensionality.











Example 1 (Sets of die rolls) The possible results of rolling a six-sided die form the set \({\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\), with \(3 \in {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\) and \(7 \notin {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\). The sets \({\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3\right\}\mathclose{}}\) and \({\mathopen{}\left\{3, 2, 1\right\}\mathclose{}}\) are equal, because they have the same elements; the order in which the elements are listed does not matter.











Definition 2 (Roster notation) Writing a set (Definition 1) by listing its elements between braces, as in \({\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3\right\}\mathclose{}}\), is called roster notation (Wikipedia contributors 2026n). An ellipsis, “\(\ldots\)”, can stand for elements that follow a clear pattern, as in \({\mathopen{}\left\{10, 20, 30, \ldots, 90\right\}\mathclose{}}\).











Example 2 (Order and repetition do not matter) The sets \({\mathopen{}\left\{3, 1, 2\right\}\mathclose{}}\), \({\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3\right\}\mathclose{}}\) and \({\mathopen{}\left\{1, 1, 2, 3, 3\right\}\mathclose{}}\) are equal, because each has exactly the elements \(1\), \(2\) and \(3\) (Definition 1). A roster can list any objects, not only numbers: \({\mathopen{}\left\{\text{red}, \text{green}, \text{blue}\right\}\mathclose{}}\) is a set with three elements.











Definition 3 (Natural numbers (our convention)) In these notes, the natural numbers (Wikipedia contributors 2026j) are the positive integers (Definition: Positive integers):
\[\mathbb{N}\stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3, \ldots\right\}\mathclose{}\]










NoteOther conventions for the natural numbers



Other sources may define \(\mathbb{N}\) differently, so check each source’s definition before reading its formulas:

Many sources include \(0\) in \(\mathbb{N}\). The international standard ISO 80000-2 defines \(\mathbb{N}\) to include \(0\), continuing the earlier standard ISO 31-11 (1978).
Other sources start \(\mathbb{N}\) at \(1\), as these notes do.
To remove the ambiguity, some sources write \(\mathbb{N}_1\) or \(\mathbb{Z}^+\) for \(\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3, \ldots\right\}\mathclose{}\), and \(\mathbb{N}_0\) or \(\mathbb{Z}^{0+}\) for \(\mathopen{}\left\{0, 1, 2, \ldots\right\}\mathclose{}\).
The words vary too. “Positive integers” (\(\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3, \ldots\right\}\mathclose{}\)) and “non-negative integers” (\(\mathopen{}\left\{0, 1, 2, \ldots\right\}\mathclose{}\)) are unambiguous. “Whole numbers” usually includes \(0\), but can also mean all of the integers, negative ones included. “Counting numbers” usually starts at \(1\), but some sources include \(0\).
Some older texts write \(J\) for the natural numbers.

When a formula’s meaning depends on whether \(0\) is included, we write the set out explicitly, for example \(\mathopen{}\left\{0, 1, 2, \ldots\right\}\mathclose{}\) or \(\mathopen{}\left\{1, \ldots, n\right\}\mathclose{}\).
Source: Wikipedia, “Natural number”, “Terminology and notation” and “Zero as natural number”, which cites ISO 80000-2:2019 and the textbooks using each notation.









Definition 4 (Real numbers) A real number (Wikipedia contributors 2026m) is a number that can be written as a decimal expansion: an integer part, followed by a decimal point and a finite or infinite list of decimal places after it. Equivalently, the real numbers are the points on the number line. The set of real numbers is written \(\mathbb{R}\).











Remark 2 (A working definition). Definition 4 is a working definition, not a construction: it does not say what an infinite decimal expansion is, or how to add or multiply two of them. Rudin (1976, Appendix to Chapter 1) constructs the real numbers rigorously. Some real numbers have two decimal expansions: for example, \(0.999\ldots\) and \(1.000\ldots\) are the same real number, \(1\).

2 Set-builder notation







Exercise 2 (Natural numbers with small cubes) List the natural numbers (Definition 3) \(n\) with \(n^3 < 100\).










SolutionSolution






Solution 2. \(1\), \(2\), \(3\) and \(4\), whose cubes are \(1\), \(8\), \(27\) and \(64\). Every other natural number \(n\) has \(n \ge 5\), so \(n^3 \ge 125\), which is not less than \(100\).











Definition 5 (Set-builder notation) For a set \(A\) and a statement \(P(x)\) about an element \(x\), set-builder notation (Wikipedia contributors 2026o) \({\mathopen{}\left\{x \in A : P(x)\right\}\mathclose{}}\) denotes the set of elements \(x\) of \(A\) for which \(P(x)\) is true.











Example 3 (Even die rolls in set-builder notation) \({\mathopen{}\left\{x \in {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\right\}\mathclose{}} : x \text{ is even}\right\}\mathclose{}} = {\mathopen{}\left\{2, 4, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\) is the set of even rolls, and \({\mathopen{}\left\{x \in \mathbb{R}: x > 0\right\}\mathclose{}}\) is the set of positive real numbers.











Definition 6 (Empty set) The empty set (Wikipedia contributors 2026f), denoted \(\emptyset\), is the set that has no elements.











Remark 4 (Other notation for the empty set). Other sources write \({\mathopen{}\left\{\right\}\mathclose{}}\) for \(\emptyset\) (Wikipedia contributors 2026f). Some sources call it the null set, but in measure theory a “null set” usually means a set of measure zero, which need not be empty. For example, the interval \([0, 0] = {\mathopen{}\left\{0\right\}\mathclose{}}\) has length \(0 - 0 = 0\), so it is a null set in that sense, but it is not empty, because \(0 \in {\mathopen{}\left\{0\right\}\mathclose{}}\).











Example 4 (Impossible die rolls) No roll of a six-sided die is greater than 6, so \({\mathopen{}\left\{x \in {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\right\}\mathclose{}} : x > 6\right\}\mathclose{}} = \emptyset\).











Definition 7 (Set-builder notation with an expression) For a set \(A\) and an expression \(f(x)\) that has a value for each element \(x\) of \(A\), the notation \({\mathopen{}\left\{f(x) : x \in A\right\}\mathclose{}}\) denotes the set of the values \(f(x)\) for \(x \in A\) (Wikipedia contributors 2026o). That is, an object \(y\) is an element of \({\mathopen{}\left\{f(x) : x \in A\right\}\mathclose{}}\) when \(y = f(x)\) for some \(x \in A\).











Example 5 (Two ways to build a set)  

The numbers of Exercise 2 form the set \({\mathopen{}\left\{n \in \mathbb{N}: n^3 < 100\right\}\mathclose{}} = {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3, 4\right\}\mathclose{}}\) (Definition 5).
Their cubes form the set \({\mathopen{}\left\{n^3 : n \in {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3, 4\right\}\mathclose{}}\right\}\mathclose{}} = {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 8, 27, 64\right\}\mathclose{}}\) (Definition 7).
\({\mathopen{}\left\{2^k : k \in \mathbb{N}\right\}\mathclose{}} = {\mathopen{}\left\{2, 4, 8, 16, \ldots\right\}\mathclose{}}\), the powers of \(2\) after \(2^0\).
\({\mathopen{}\left\{(-1)^k : k \in \mathbb{N}\right\}\mathclose{}} = {\mathopen{}\left\{-1, 1\right\}\mathclose{}}\): many values of \(k\) give the same value, and each value is one element of the set.







3 Cardinality







Exercise 3 (Letters in a word) How many different letters does the word MISSISSIPPI use?










SolutionSolution






Solution 3. Four: M, I, S and P. The set of its letters is \({\mathopen{}\left\{\text{M}, \text{I}, \text{S}, \text{P}\right\}\mathclose{}}\), and listing a letter again, as the word does, does not add an element (Example 2).











Definition 8 (Finite set) A set \(A\) is finite (Wikipedia contributors 2026g) if it is empty, or if, for some natural number \(n\), its elements can be listed as a finite sequence (Definition: Finite sequence) \(a_1, \ldots, a_n\) in which each element of \(A\) appears exactly once.











Definition 9 (Cardinality) For a finite set \(A\) (Definition 8), the number \(n\) in such a list is the cardinality (Wikipedia contributors 2026b) of \(A\), its number of elements, written \(\mathopen{}\left|A\right|\mathclose{}\); the empty set has cardinality \(\mathopen{}\left|\emptyset\right|\mathclose{} = 0\).











Remark 5 (Two meanings of \(\mathopen{}\left|\cdot\right|\mathclose{}\)). Applied to a set, the bars \(\mathopen{}\left|A\right|\mathclose{}\) mean the cardinality of \(A\). Applied to a number, \(\mathopen{}\left|x\right|\mathclose{}\) means its absolute value, or its modulus when \(x\) is complex. For example, \(\mathopen{}\left|{\mathopen{}\left\{-3\right\}\mathclose{}}\right|\mathclose{} = 1\), but \(\mathopen{}\left|-3\right|\mathclose{} = 3\).











Definition 10 (Infinite set) A set that is not finite (Definition 8) is infinite (Wikipedia contributors 2026h).











Example 6 (Finite and infinite sets)  

\({\mathopen{}\left\{2, 4, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\) is finite, with \(\mathopen{}\left|{\mathopen{}\left\{2, 4, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\right|\mathclose{} = 3\).
\({\mathopen{}\left\{1, 1, 2\right\}\mathclose{}} = {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2\right\}\mathclose{}}\), so \(\mathopen{}\left|{\mathopen{}\left\{1, 1, 2\right\}\mathclose{}}\right|\mathclose{} = 2\): a repeated listing does not count twice.
\(\emptyset\) is finite, with \(\mathopen{}\left|\emptyset\right|\mathclose{} = 0\).
The natural numbers \(\mathbb{N}= {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3, \ldots\right\}\mathclose{}}\) are infinite: for any \(n\), a list \(a_1, \ldots, a_n\) of natural numbers misses the natural number \(a_1 + \cdots + a_n + 1\), which is larger than every number in the list.












Remark 6 (Sets can be elements of sets). The elements of a set can themselves be sets. For example, \(S = {\mathopen{}\left\{{\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2\right\}\mathclose{}}, 3, {\mathopen{}\left\{3\right\}\mathclose{}}\right\}\mathclose{}}\) has three elements: the set \({\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2\right\}\mathclose{}}\), the number \(3\), and the set \({\mathopen{}\left\{3\right\}\mathclose{}}\). So \({\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2\right\}\mathclose{}} \in S\), but \(1 \notin S\), because \(1\) is an element of an element of \(S\), not an element of \(S\). And \(3 \ne {\mathopen{}\left\{3\right\}\mathclose{}}\): one is a number, and the other is a set with one element. So \(\mathopen{}\left|S\right|\mathclose{} = 3\) (Definition 9).











Definition 11 (Countable set) A set is countable (Wikipedia contributors 2026e) if it is finite (Definition 8), or if its elements can be listed as a sequence (Definition: Sequence) \(a_1, a_2, a_3, \ldots\) in which every element appears.











Definition 12 (Countably infinite set) A set is countably infinite if it is countable and not finite.











Example 7 (Countable and uncountable sets)  

\({\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\) is countable, because it is finite.
The non-negative integers \({\mathopen{}\left\{0, 1, 2, \ldots\right\}\mathclose{}}\) are countably infinite: the sequence \(0, 1, 2, \ldots\) lists them.
The integers are countably infinite too: the sequence \(0, 1, -1, 2, -2, 3, -3, \ldots\) lists every one of them.












Remark 7 (Numbers with only one decimal expansion). These notes use one more fact about the real numbers without proving it. A real number has two decimal expansions only if one of them ends in repeating \(9\)s and the other in repeating \(0\)s, as \(0.999\ldots\) and \(1.000\ldots\) do (Remark 2). So a number whose decimal places are all \(4\)s and \(5\)s, such as \(0.545454\ldots\), has only one decimal expansion.











Theorem 1 (The real numbers are not countable) The set of real numbers \(\mathbb{R}\) (Definition 4) is not countable (Definition 11) (Wikipedia contributors 2026a).










ProofProof






Proof. Suppose, for contradiction (Definition: Proof by contradiction), that \(\mathbb{R}\) is countable. \(\mathbb{R}\) is not finite, because it contains the natural numbers, and a list of every real number would include a list of every natural number, which cannot be finite (Example 6). So the elements of \(\mathbb{R}\) can be listed as a sequence \(r_1, r_2, r_3, \ldots\) in which every real number appears. Write each \(r_n\) as a decimal expansion, choosing one if \(r_n\) has two. Let \(d\) be the number between \(0\) and \(1\) whose \(n\)th decimal place is

\(5\), if the \(n\)th decimal place of \(r_n\) is not \(5\);
\(4\), if the \(n\)th decimal place of \(r_n\) is \(5\).

Then \(d\) is a real number, so \(d = r_m\) for some \(m\). The decimal places of \(d\) are all \(4\)s and \(5\)s, so \(d\) has only one decimal expansion (Remark 7), and the expansion chosen for \(r_m\) must be that one. But the two expansions differ in the \(m\)th decimal place, by the choice of \(d\). That is a contradiction, so \(\mathbb{R}\) is not countable.











Example 8 (The diagonal number for a list) Suppose a list of real numbers starts
\[
\begin{aligned}
r_1 &= 0.\mathbf{7}071\ldots \\
r_2 &= 3.1\mathbf{4}15\ldots \\
r_3 &= -2.71\mathbf{8}2\ldots \\
r_4 &= 0.555\mathbf{5}\ldots
\end{aligned}
\]
The bold digits are the \(n\)th decimal places of the \(r_n\): \(7\), \(4\), \(8\) and \(5\). The proof of Theorem 1 builds \(d = 0.5554\ldots\), which differs from \(r_1\) in the first decimal place, from \(r_2\) in the second, from \(r_3\) in the third, and from \(r_4\) in the fourth. However the list continues, \(d\) is not on it.






4 Subsets and power sets







Exercise 4 (An element that is also a subset) Let \(B = {\mathopen{}\left\{1, {\mathopen{}\left\{1\right\}\mathclose{}}\right\}\mathclose{}}\). A set \(A\) is a subset of \(B\) when every element of \(A\) is an element of \(B\). Find a set that is both an element of \(B\) and a subset of \(B\).










SolutionSolution






Solution 4. The set \({\mathopen{}\left\{1\right\}\mathclose{}}\) works. It is listed in \(B\), so it is an element of \(B\). And \(1\), the one element of \({\mathopen{}\left\{1\right\}\mathclose{}}\), is also listed in \(B\), so every element of \({\mathopen{}\left\{1\right\}\mathclose{}}\) is an element of \(B\).











Definition 13 (Subset) A set \(A\) is a subset (Wikipedia contributors 2026p) of a set \(B\), written \(A \subseteq B\), if every element of \(A\) is an element of \(B\).











Example 9 (Even die rolls) The even die rolls form a subset of the possible rolls: \({\mathopen{}\left\{2, 4, 6\right\}\mathclose{}} \subseteq {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\), because each of \(2\), \(4\), and \(6\) is a possible roll. The set \({\mathopen{}\left\{2, 4, 7\right\}\mathclose{}}\) is not a subset of \({\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\), because \(7\) is not a possible roll.











Definition 14 (Strict subset (proper subset)) A set \(A\) is a strict subset (also called a proper subset) of a set \(B\), written \(A \subsetneq B\), if \(A\) is a subset of \(B\) and \(A \neq B\).











Remark 8 (The symbol \(\subset\)). Sources disagree about the symbol \(\subset\): some use it for “subset” (\(\subseteq\)), and others for “strict subset” (\(\subsetneq\)) (Wikipedia contributors 2026p). For example, \({\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2\right\}\mathclose{}} \subset {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2\right\}\mathclose{}}\) is true in the first reading, because \({\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2\right\}\mathclose{}} \subseteq {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2\right\}\mathclose{}}\), and false in the second, because the two sets are equal. These notes avoid \(\subset\) and write \(\subseteq\) or \(\subsetneq\).











Example 10 (Strict subsets)  

\({\mathopen{}\left\{2, 4, 6\right\}\mathclose{}} \subsetneq {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\), because \({\mathopen{}\left\{2, 4, 6\right\}\mathclose{}} \subseteq {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\) (Example 9), and \(1\) is in the second set but not the first.
\(\mathbb{N}\subsetneq \mathbb{Z}\), because every natural number is an integer, and \(-1\) is an integer that is not a natural number.
\(\mathbb{Z} \subseteq \mathbb{Z}\), because every integer is an integer, but \(\mathbb{Z}\) is not a strict subset of itself.












Theorem 2 (The empty set is a subset of every set) For every set \(A\), \(\emptyset \subseteq A\).










ProofProof






Proof. By Definition 13, \(\emptyset \subseteq A\) fails only if some element of \(\emptyset\) is not in \(A\). The empty set has no elements, so no such element exists.











Theorem 3 (Every set is a subset of itself) For every set \(A\), \(A \subseteq A\).










ProofProof






Proof. Every element of \(A\) is an element of \(A\), which is Definition 13 with \(B = A\).











Definition 15 (Power set) The power set of a set \(A\), written \(\mathcal{P}(A)\), is the set of all subsets (Definition 13) of \(A\) (Wikipedia contributors 2026l):
\[
\mathcal{P}(A) \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}{\mathopen{}\left\{S : S \subseteq A\right\}\mathclose{}}.
\]











Example 11 (The subsets of a three-element set) \[
\mathcal{P}({\mathopen{}\left\{a, b, c\right\}\mathclose{}}) = {\mathopen{}\left\{\emptyset, {\mathopen{}\left\{a\right\}\mathclose{}}, {\mathopen{}\left\{b\right\}\mathclose{}}, {\mathopen{}\left\{c\right\}\mathclose{}}, {\mathopen{}\left\{a, b\right\}\mathclose{}}, {\mathopen{}\left\{a, c\right\}\mathclose{}}, {\mathopen{}\left\{b, c\right\}\mathclose{}}, {\mathopen{}\left\{a, b, c\right\}\mathclose{}}\right\}\mathclose{}}.
\]
Each element of \(\mathcal{P}({\mathopen{}\left\{a, b, c\right\}\mathclose{}})\) is a set. For example, \({\mathopen{}\left\{a\right\}\mathclose{}} \in \mathcal{P}({\mathopen{}\left\{a, b, c\right\}\mathclose{}})\), but \(a \notin \mathcal{P}({\mathopen{}\left\{a, b, c\right\}\mathclose{}})\). The list includes \(\emptyset\) (Theorem 2) and \({\mathopen{}\left\{a, b, c\right\}\mathclose{}}\) itself (Theorem 3).






5 Ordered pairs and Cartesian products







Exercise 5 (Sandwich orders) A sandwich shop makes sandwiches on rye or wheat bread, with a filling of ham, cheese or tomato. List every choice of one bread and one filling, writing each choice as (bread, filling).










SolutionSolution






Solution 5. (rye, ham), (rye, cheese), (rye, tomato), (wheat, ham), (wheat, cheese) and (wheat, tomato).











Definition 16 (Ordered pair) An ordered pair (Wikipedia contributors 2026k) \((a, b)\) is a pair of objects listed in order, with \(a\) first and \(b\) second; two ordered pairs are equal, \((a, b) = (c, d)\), when \(a = c\) and \(b = d\).











Definition 17 (Tuple) For a natural number \(n\), an \(n\)-tuple \((a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n)\) is a list of \(n\) objects in order (Wikipedia contributors 2026q). Two \(n\)-tuples are equal when their entries are equal in each position. A \(2\)-tuple is an ordered pair (Definition 16).











Example 12 (Tuples are not sets)  

\((1, 2) \ne (2, 1)\), because their first entries differ, but \({\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2\right\}\mathclose{}} = {\mathopen{}\left\{2, 1\right\}\mathclose{}}\), because order does not matter in a set (Definition 1).
\((4, 4, 1)\) is a \(3\)-tuple whose first two entries are equal, but \({\mathopen{}\left\{4, 4, 1\right\}\mathclose{}} = {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 4\right\}\mathclose{}}\) has two elements.












Definition 18 (Cartesian product) The Cartesian product (Wikipedia contributors 2026c) of sets \(A\) and \(B\), written \(A \times B\), is the set of ordered pairs whose first entry is in \(A\) and whose second entry is in \(B\):
\[A \times B \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}{\mathopen{}\left\{(a, b) : a \in A \text{ and } b \in B\right\}\mathclose{}}\]











Definition 19 (Cartesian product of several sets) For a natural number \(n\) and sets \(A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n\), the Cartesian product \(A_1 \times A_2 \times \cdots \times A_n\) is the set of \(n\)-tuples (Definition 17) whose \(i\)th entry is in \(A_i\) for each \(i\) (Wikipedia contributors 2026c):
\[
A_1 \times \cdots \times A_n \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}{\mathopen{}\left\{(a_1, \ldots, a_n) : a_i \in A_i \text{ for each } i\right\}\mathclose{}}.
\]
For \(n = 2\) this is Definition 18.











Example 13 (Cartesian products)  

The choices in Exercise 5 are the Cartesian product \({\mathopen{}\left\{\text{rye}, \text{wheat}\right\}\mathclose{}} \times {\mathopen{}\left\{\text{ham}, \text{cheese}, \text{tomato}\right\}\mathclose{}}\) (Definition 18).
\({\mathopen{}\left\{\text{ham}, \text{cheese}, \text{tomato}\right\}\mathclose{}} \times {\mathopen{}\left\{\text{rye}, \text{wheat}\right\}\mathclose{}}\) is a different set: it holds \((\text{ham}, \text{rye})\), which is not \((\text{rye}, \text{ham})\) (Example 12).
\(\mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{R}\) is the set of points \((x, y)\) in the plane.
Adding a choice of drink gives \(3\)-tuples (Definition 19), such as \((\text{rye}, \text{ham}, \text{tea}) \in {\mathopen{}\left\{\text{rye}, \text{wheat}\right\}\mathclose{}} \times {\mathopen{}\left\{\text{ham}, \text{cheese}, \text{tomato}\right\}\mathclose{}} \times {\mathopen{}\left\{\text{tea}, \text{juice}\right\}\mathclose{}}\).







6 Set operations







Exercise 6 (Two sets from their overlap) Find sets \(A\) and \(B\) whose common elements are exactly \(2\) and \(3\), and whose elements together are exactly \(1\), \(2\), \(3\) and \(4\).










SolutionSolution






Solution 6. \(A = {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3\right\}\mathclose{}}\) and \(B = {\mathopen{}\left\{2, 3, 4\right\}\mathclose{}}\) work: the elements in both are \(2\) and \(3\), and the elements in one or the other are \(1\), \(2\), \(3\) and \(4\). So do \(A = {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3, 4\right\}\mathclose{}}\) and \(B = {\mathopen{}\left\{2, 3\right\}\mathclose{}}\).











Definition 20 (Union) The union (Wikipedia contributors 2026r) of sets \(A\) and \(B\), written \(A \cup B\), is the set of elements that are in \(A\), in \(B\), or in both:
\[A \cup B \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}{\mathopen{}\left\{x : x \in A \text{ or } x \in B\right\}\mathclose{}}\]











Definition 21 (Intersection) The intersection (Wikipedia contributors 2026i) of sets \(A\) and \(B\), written \(A \cap B\), is the set of elements that are in both \(A\) and \(B\):
\[A \cap B \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}{\mathopen{}\left\{x : x \in A \text{ and } x \in B\right\}\mathclose{}}\]











Definition 22 (Set difference) The set difference (Wikipedia contributors 2026d) of sets \(A\) and \(B\), written \(A \setminus B\), is the set of elements of \(A\) that are not in \(B\):
\[A \setminus B \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}{\mathopen{}\left\{x \in A : x \notin B\right\}\mathclose{}}\]











Remark 9 (Other notation for the set difference). Some sources write \(A - B\) for \(A \setminus B\) (Wikipedia contributors 2026d).











Example 14 (Combining sets of die rolls) Let \(A = {\mathopen{}\left\{2, 4, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\) (the even rolls) and \(B = {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3\right\}\mathclose{}}\) (the rolls of at most 3). Then:

\(A \cup B = {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3, 4, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\), the rolls that are even or at most 3;
\(A \cap B = {\mathopen{}\left\{2\right\}\mathclose{}}\), the only roll that is both;
\(A \setminus B = {\mathopen{}\left\{4, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\), the even rolls greater than 3;
\({\mathopen{}\left\{2, 4, 6\right\}\mathclose{}} \cap {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 3, 5\right\}\mathclose{}} = \emptyset\): no roll is both even and odd.












Definition 23 (Complement) Let \(A\) be a subset of a set \(S\). The complement (Wikipedia contributors 2026d) of \(A\) in \(S\) is the set difference (Definition 22) \(S \setminus A\): the elements of \(S\) that are not in \(A\). When the set \(S\) is clear from context, the complement of \(A\) is written \(A^c\):
\[A^c \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}S \setminus A = {\mathopen{}\left\{x \in S : x \notin A\right\}\mathclose{}}\]











Remark 10 (The universal set, and other notation for the complement). The set \(S\) in Definition 23 is sometimes called the universal set. Which universal set to use depends on the context: for a set of even integers it might be \(\mathbb{Z}\), and for a set of letters it might be the 26 letters of the alphabet. Some sources write \(\overline{A}\) for \(A^c\) (Wikipedia contributors 2026d).











Example 15 (Complements of sets of die rolls) Let \(S = {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\) be the possible rolls of a die.

The complement of the even rolls \(A = {\mathopen{}\left\{2, 4, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\) is \(A^c = {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 3, 5\right\}\mathclose{}}\), the odd rolls.
The complement of \(S\) itself is \(S^c = \emptyset\), and the complement of \(\emptyset\) is \(\emptyset^c = S\).

The complement depends on \(S\): in \(S = {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\), the complement of \({\mathopen{}\left\{2, 4, 6\right\}\mathclose{}}\) is \({\mathopen{}\left\{1, 3, 5\right\}\mathclose{}}\), but in \(S = {\mathopen{}\left\{2, 4, 6, 8\right\}\mathclose{}}\), it is \({\mathopen{}\left\{8\right\}\mathclose{}}\).











Definition 24 (Venn diagram) A Venn diagram draws sets as overlapping circles inside a rectangle, which stands for the set \(S\) that the sets are subsets of, as in Definition 23. Each region of the picture stands for the elements that are in some of the sets and not in the others.











Example 16 (Letters of two words) Let \(L\) be the set of letters in the word LOGIC, and \(M\) the set of letters in the word MAGIC, inside the set \(S\) of the 26 letters of the alphabet. Figure 1 draws them.



Figure 1: The letters of LOGIC (\(L\)) and of MAGIC (\(M\)), with \(L \cap M\) shaded.







The shaded region, inside both circles, is \(L \cap M = {\mathopen{}\left\{\text{G}, \text{I}, \text{C}\right\}\mathclose{}}\).
The part of circle \(L\) outside circle \(M\) is \(L \setminus M = {\mathopen{}\left\{\text{L}, \text{O}\right\}\mathclose{}}\).
Everything inside either circle is \(L \cup M = {\mathopen{}\left\{\text{L}, \text{O}, \text{G}, \text{I}, \text{C}, \text{M}, \text{A}\right\}\mathclose{}}\).
Everything in the rectangle outside circle \(L\) is \(L^c\), the 21 letters not in LOGIC.

title: Recursion
text:
NoteSource





The topics of this chapter follow Kameron Decker Harris’s Fall 2026 lecture notes on recursion and recursive functions. These come from those notes:

the two parts of a recursive definition, a base case and a recursive rule;
the recursive definitions of the natural numbers and of the strings over an alphabet;
the three questions to ask when writing a recursive function: the base case, the recursive call and the combination;
the definition of a recursive algorithm.

Everything else is new: the exercises, the other examples, the Racket functions, the algorithm, the theorems and their proofs.




1 Recursive definitions







Exercise 1 (Double and subtract one) A sequence (Definition: Sequence) starts with \(a_0 = 2\), and each later term is twice the term before it, minus 1. Find \(a_1\), \(a_2\), \(a_3\), \(a_4\) and \(a_5\).










SolutionSolution






Solution 1. Each term comes from the one before it:
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_1 &= 2 \cdot 2 - 1 = 3,
\\ a_2 &= 2 \cdot 3 - 1 = 5,
\\ a_3 &= 2 \cdot 5 - 1 = 9,
\\ a_4 &= 2 \cdot 9 - 1 = 17,
\\ a_5 &= 2 \cdot 17 - 1 = 33.
\end{aligned}
\]
To find \(a_5\) this way, we had to find \(a_1\) through \(a_4\) first.











Definition 1 (Recursive definition) Let \(n_0\) be an integer (Definition: Integers). A recursive definition (Wikipedia contributors 2026f) of a function (Definition: Function (map, mapping, transformation)) \(f\) on the integers \(n \ge n_0\) has two parts:

Base case: the value of \(f\) is given directly at \(n_0\), and possibly at a few more of the smallest inputs.
Recursive rule: \(f(n)\) at every other input \(n\) is given in terms of the values of \(f\) at inputs that are smaller than \(n\) and at least \(n_0\).












Example 1 (The double-minus-one sequence, defined recursively) The sequence of Exercise 1 has a recursive definition (Definition 1) with \(n_0 = 0\). Its base case is
\[
a_0 = 2,
\]
and its recursive rule is
\[
a_n = 2 a_{n-1} - 1
\quad\text{for every integer } n \ge 1.
\]
The recursive rule gives \(a_n\) from the single value \(a_{n-1}\) just before it, so this is a recursively defined sequence (Definition: Recursively defined sequence) with \(m = 1\).











Definition 2 (Floor) The floor \(\mathopen{}\left\lfloor x\right\rfloor\mathclose{}\) of a real number (Definition: Real numbers) \(x\) (Wikipedia contributors 2026b) is the largest integer (Definition: Integers) that is at most \(x\).











Example 2 (Some floors) By Definition 2,

\(\mathopen{}\left\lfloor 3.7\right\rfloor\mathclose{} = 3\), since 3 is an integer at most 3.7 and 4 is not;
\(\mathopen{}\left\lfloor 5\right\rfloor\mathclose{} = 5\), since 5 is already an integer;
\(\mathopen{}\left\lfloor-1.5\right\rfloor\mathclose{} = -2\), since \(-2\) is at most \(-1.5\) and \(-1\) is not.

For a natural number (Definition: Natural numbers (our convention)) \(n\), the floor \(\mathopen{}\left\lfloor n / 10\right\rfloor\mathclose{}\) is \(n\) with its last decimal digit removed, such as \(\mathopen{}\left\lfloor 2026 / 10\right\rfloor\mathclose{} = \mathopen{}\left\lfloor 202.6\right\rfloor\mathclose{} = 202\).











Example 3 (Counting digits) Define a function \(d\) on the natural numbers (Definition: Natural numbers (our convention)) by
\[
d(n) =
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if } n \le 9,
\\ 1 + d\mathopen{}\left(\mathopen{}\left\lfloor n / 10\right\rfloor\mathclose{}\right)\mathclose{} & \text{if } n \ge 10,
\end{cases}
\]
where \(\mathopen{}\left\lfloor n / 10\right\rfloor\mathclose{}\) is the floor (Definition 2) of \(n / 10\), which is \(n\) with its last decimal digit removed. The first line is the base case and the second is the recursive rule (Definition 1). For \(n \ge 10\), the input \(\mathopen{}\left\lfloor n / 10\right\rfloor\mathclose{}\) is at least 1 and at most \(n / 10\), which is less than \(n\), so the recursive rule uses a smaller input, but usually not \(n - 1\). For example,
\[
\begin{aligned}
d(2026)
&= 1 + d(202)
\\&= 1 + 1 + d(20)
\\&= 1 + 1 + 1 + d(2)
\\&= 1 + 1 + 1 + 1
\\&= 4,
\end{aligned}
\]
and 2026 has 4 digits.






2 Recursively defined sets







Exercise 2 (Building a set of integers) A set (Definition: Set) \(S\) of integers is built by two rules:

\(1 \in S\);
if \(x \in S\), then \(x + 2 \in S\) and \(3x \in S\).

Every element of \(S\) comes from these two rules. Find every element of \(S\) that is less than 12.










SolutionSolution






Solution 2. Starting from 1 and adding 2 again and again gives \(1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11\), so all six are in \(S\). Tripling gives nothing new below 12: \(3 \cdot 1 = 3\) and \(3 \cdot 3 = 9\) are already in the list, and tripling 5 or more gives at least 15. Both rules turn an odd number into an odd number, so no even number is in \(S\). So the elements of \(S\) less than 12 are \(1, 3, 5, 7, 9\) and \(11\).











Definition 3 (Recursively defined set) A recursively defined set (Wikipedia contributors 2026f) is a set (Definition: Set) given by two parts, named as in Definition 1:

a base case, which names some elements of the set directly;
a recursive rule, which says how to build new elements of the set from elements already in it.

The set has no other elements: each of its elements comes from the base case by applying the recursive rule a finite number of times.











Example 4 (The natural numbers, defined recursively) The natural numbers (Definition: Natural numbers (our convention)) are a recursively defined set (Definition 3). The base case is \(1 \in \mathbb{N}\), and the recursive rule is that if \(n \in \mathbb{N}\), then \(n + 1 \in \mathbb{N}\). The base case gives 1, one application of the rule gives \(1 + 1 = 2\), a second gives \(2 + 1 = 3\), and so on. The non-negative integers (Definition: Non-negative integers) have the same recursive rule, with the base case \(0 \in \mathbb{N}_0\).











Definition 4 (Alphabet) An alphabet (Wikipedia contributors 2026a) is a finite, non-empty set (Definition: Set), whose elements are called its symbols. An alphabet is often written \(\Sigma\), the capital Greek letter sigma.











Example 5 (Three alphabets) Each of these sets is an alphabet (Definition 4):

\(\mathopen{}\left\{0, 1\right\}\mathclose{}\), the two binary digits;
\(\mathopen{}\left\{\mathtt{A}, \mathtt{C}, \mathtt{G}, \mathtt{T}\right\}\mathclose{}\), the four bases of DNA;
\(\mathopen{}\left\{\mathtt{a}, \mathtt{b}, \ldots, \mathtt{z}\right\}\mathclose{}\), the 26 lowercase letters of English.

The set of all integers is not an alphabet, because it is not finite.











Definition 5 (String) Let \(\Sigma\) be an alphabet (Definition 4). The set \(\Sigma^*\) of strings over \(\Sigma\) (Wikipedia contributors 2026g) is the recursively defined set (Definition 3) with

base case: the empty string \(\lambda\), which has no symbols, is in \(\Sigma^*\);
recursive rule: if \(w \in \Sigma^*\) and \(x \in \Sigma\), then \(w x \in \Sigma^*\), where \(w x\) is the string \(w\) followed by the symbol \(x\).

Racket and Python write the empty string "".











Example 6 (Building a string of DNA bases) Let \(\Sigma = \mathopen{}\left\{\mathtt{A}, \mathtt{C}, \mathtt{G}, \mathtt{T}\right\}\mathclose{}\). The string \(\mathtt{GAT}\) is in \(\Sigma^*\) (Definition 5), by three applications of the recursive rule:

\(\lambda \in \Sigma^*\) and \(\mathtt{G} \in \Sigma\), so \(\lambda \mathtt{G} = \mathtt{G}\) is in \(\Sigma^*\);
\(\mathtt{G} \in \Sigma^*\) and \(\mathtt{A} \in \Sigma\), so \(\mathtt{GA} \in \Sigma^*\);
\(\mathtt{GA} \in \Sigma^*\) and \(\mathtt{T} \in \Sigma\), so \(\mathtt{GAT} \in \Sigma^*\).

The string \(\mathtt{GAU}\) is not in \(\Sigma^*\), since the rule adds only symbols of \(\Sigma\), and \(\mathtt{U} \notin \Sigma\).











Definition 6 (Palindrome) A palindrome (Wikipedia contributors 2026d) is a string (Definition 5) that reads the same backward as forward: its \(i\)th symbol equals its \(i\)th symbol from the end, for every \(i\).











Example 7 (Some palindromes) Over the alphabet of lowercase letters, \(\mathtt{noon}\) and \(\mathtt{racecar}\) are palindromes (Definition 6), and so is \(\mathtt{abba}\), from Exercise: Completing a palindrome. The string \(\mathtt{recur}\) is not a palindrome: backward it reads \(\mathtt{rucer}\). The empty string and every string of one symbol are palindromes.






3 Recursion in Racket







Exercise 3 (Tracing a recursive Racket function) The Racket function binary takes a non-negative integer (Definition: Non-negative integers) n and returns a string:
(define (binary n)
  (if (< n 2)
      (number->string n)
      (string-append (binary (quotient n 2))
                     (number->string (remainder n 2)))))
Here

(if test a b) returns a when test is true and b when it is false;
(quotient n 2) is \(\mathopen{}\left\lfloor n / 2\right\rfloor\mathclose{}\), the floor (Definition 2) of \(n / 2\);
(remainder n 2) is the remainder, 0 or 1, left after dividing n by 2;
number->string turns a number into the string of its digits;
string-append joins two strings into one.

Run (binary 6) by hand: write down each call of binary that it makes, and the string that each call returns.










SolutionSolution






Solution 3. Since \(6 \ge 2\), (binary 6) calls (binary 3), because \(\mathopen{}\left\lfloor 6 / 2\right\rfloor\mathclose{} = 3\), and puts "0", the remainder of 6 divided by 2, after its result. Since \(3 \ge 2\), (binary 3) calls (binary 1) and puts "1" after its result. Since \(1 < 2\), (binary 1) returns "1" without calling binary again. Replacing each call with what it returns:
(binary 6)
= (string-append (binary 3) "0")
= (string-append (string-append (binary 1) "1") "0")
= (string-append (string-append "1" "1") "0")
= (string-append "11" "0")
= "110"
So (binary 1) returns "1", (binary 3) returns "11", and (binary 6) returns "110". That is 6 written in base 2, since \(1 \cdot 4 + 1 \cdot 2 + 0 \cdot 1 = 6\).











Remark 1 (Three questions for writing a recursive function). A Racket function that calls itself, such as binary in Exercise 3, answers three questions:

Base case. Which inputs does it answer directly? For binary, the inputs 0 and 1, whose base-2 form is the single digit "0" or "1".
Recursive call. Which smaller input does it call itself on? For binary, the input \(\mathopen{}\left\lfloor n / 2\right\rfloor\mathclose{}\), which is less than \(n\) when \(n \ge 2\).
Combination. How does it turn the result of the recursive call into its own answer? For binary, it puts the last base-2 digit of \(n\), the remainder of \(n\) divided by 2, after the result.

The base case is the branch of the if that does not call the function, and the recursive call and the combination make up the other branch.











Example 8 (Counting digits in Racket) The recursive definition of \(d\) in Example 3 becomes a Racket function line by line:
(define (digits n)
  (if (< n 10)
      1
      (+ 1 (digits (quotient n 10)))))
Following Remark 1:

the base case answers 1 for every input less than 10;
the recursive call is (digits (quotient n 10)), on \(\mathopen{}\left\lfloor n / 10\right\rfloor\mathclose{}\), which is less than \(n\);
the combination adds 1 to the result of the recursive call.

(digits 2026) calls (digits 202), (digits 20) and (digits 2) in turn, as in Example 3, and returns 4.






4 Lists







Exercise 4 (Building a list with cons) In Racket, empty is the list with no elements, and (cons x xs) is the list whose first element is x, followed by the elements of the list xs. For example, (cons 5 empty) is the one-element list '(5). Write the list '(7 2 9) using only cons, empty and numbers.










SolutionSolution






Solution 4. Build the list from its last element forward:

(cons 9 empty) is '(9);
(cons 2 (cons 9 empty)) is '(2 9);
(cons 7 (cons 2 (cons 9 empty))) is '(7 2 9).

So '(7 2 9) is (cons 7 (cons 2 (cons 9 empty))).











Definition 7 (List) Let \(A\) be a set (Definition: Set). The set of lists of elements of \(A\) (Wikipedia contributors 2026c) is the recursively defined set (Definition 3) with

base case: the empty list, written \(\mathtt{empty}\), is a list;
recursive rule: if \(x \in A\) and \(L\) is a list, then \(\operatorname{cons}(x, L)\) is a list, whose first element is \(x\) and whose rest is \(L\).

Racket writes the empty list as empty or '(), and \(\operatorname{cons}(x, L)\) as (cons x L), and (first L) and (rest L) return the two parts of a list that is not empty. Racket also has the older names car for first and cdr for rest. Python writes the empty list [].











Example 9 (Taking a list apart) Let L be the list '(7 2 9) (Definition 7), which Solution 4 builds as (cons 7 (cons 2 (cons 9 empty))). Then

(first L) is 7, and (rest L) is '(2 9);
(first (rest L)) is 2;
(rest (rest (rest L))) is empty.

(first empty) raises an error, since the empty list is not built by cons and has no first element.











Definition 8 (Length of a list) The length \(\operatorname{len}(L)\) of a list \(L\) (Definition 7) is defined recursively, following the two parts of the definition of a list:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{len}(\mathtt{empty}) &= 0,
\\ \operatorname{len}\mathopen{}\left(\operatorname{cons}(x, L)\right)\mathclose{} &= 1 + \operatorname{len}(L).
\end{aligned}
\]











Example 10 (The length of '(7 2 9)) In Racket, the definition of length (Definition 8) is
(define (len L)
  (if (empty? L)
      0
      (+ 1 (len (rest L)))))
where (empty? L) tests whether L is the empty list. Replacing each call with the recursive rule:
(len '(7 2 9))
= (+ 1 (len '(2 9)))
= (+ 1 (+ 1 (len '(9))))
= (+ 1 (+ 1 (+ 1 (len '()))))
= (+ 1 (+ 1 (+ 1 0)))
= 3
Racket’s built-in length gives the same values.











Definition 9 (Appending two lists) The append \(\operatorname{app}(L, M)\) of two lists \(L\) and \(M\) (Definition 7), the list of the elements of \(L\) followed by the elements of \(M\), is defined recursively on \(L\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{app}(\mathtt{empty}, M) &= M,
\\ \operatorname{app}\mathopen{}\left(\operatorname{cons}(x, L), M\right)\mathclose{} &= \operatorname{cons}\mathopen{}\left(x, \operatorname{app}(L, M)\right)\mathclose{}.
\end{aligned}
\]











Example 11 (Appending '(1 2) and '(3)) In Racket, the definition of append (Definition 9) is
(define (app L M)
  (if (empty? L)
      M
      (cons (first L) (app (rest L) M))))
The recursion takes L apart and leaves M alone:
(app '(1 2) '(3))
= (cons 1 (app '(2) '(3)))
= (cons 1 (cons 2 (app '() '(3))))
= (cons 1 (cons 2 '(3)))
= '(1 2 3)
Racket’s built-in append gives the same values.






5 Recursive algorithms







Exercise 5 (Is it a palindrome?) The algorithm pal, in the pseudocode of Remark: How to read the pseudocode in this chapter, tests whether a string is a palindrome (Definition 6):
procedure pal(s)        // s is a string s[1] s[2] ... s[n] of n symbols
    if n <= 1
        return true
    if s[1] != s[n]
        return false
    return pal(s[2..n-1])   // s without its first and last symbols
Here != means \(\ne\), and s[2..n-1] is the string of the symbols s[2] through s[n-1], which is the empty string when \(n = 2\), since the range 2..1 is empty. Run pal(level) by hand: write down each call of pal that it makes, and what each call returns.










SolutionSolution






Solution 5.

pal(v) returns true, so pal(eve) returns true, and so pal(level) returns true: \(\mathtt{level}\) is a palindrome.











Definition 10 (Recursive algorithm) An algorithm (Definition: Algorithm) is recursive (Wikipedia contributors 2026e) if it solves a problem by calling itself on smaller inputs of the same problem and using what those calls return. The inputs that it answers without calling itself are its base cases, as in Definition 1.











Example 12 (pal is recursive) The algorithm pal of Exercise 5 is recursive (Definition 10). On a string of \(n \ge 2\) symbols whose first and last symbols match, it calls itself on the string without those two symbols, which has \(n - 2\) symbols, and returns what that call returns.
It answers directly in two cases: when \(n \le 1\), since the empty string and a single symbol read the same backward, and when the first and last symbols differ. For example, pal(recur) finds that the first and last symbols are both r, and calls pal(ecu). That call finds e and u, which differ, and returns false, so pal(recur) returns false.






6 Proofs about recursive definitions







Exercise 6 (Guessing a formula) Compare each term \(a_0, a_1, \ldots, a_5\) of the sequence in Solution 1 with the power \(2^n\), and guess a formula for \(a_n\) that does not use the earlier terms.










SolutionSolution

Each term is one more than the power below it, so a good guess is \(a_n = 2^n + 1\). Six terms do not prove the guess for every \(n\).











Theorem 1 (A formula for the double-minus-one sequence) Let \(a_0, a_1, \ldots\) be the sequence with \(a_0 = 2\) and \(a_n = 2 a_{n-1} - 1\) for every integer \(n \ge 1\) (Example 1). Then \(a_n = 2^n + 1\) for every non-negative integer \(n\).










ProofProof






Proof. We use induction (Definition: Proof by induction), following Remark: The shape of a proof by induction with \(n_0 = 0\). Let \(P(n)\) be the equation \(a_n = 2^n + 1\).
Base case. \(a_0 = 2 = 2^0 + 1\).
Inductive step. Let \(k \ge 0\) be an integer, and suppose \(P(k)\): \(a_k = 2^k + 1\). The goal \(P(k + 1)\) is \(a_{k + 1} = 2^{k + 1} + 1\). Since \(k + 1 \ge 1\), the recursive rule gives \(a_{k + 1}\), and
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{k + 1}
&= 2 a_k - 1
&& \text{(recursive rule)}
\\&= 2 \mathopen{}\left(2^k + 1\right)\mathclose{} - 1
&& \text{(induction hypothesis)}
\\&= 2^{k + 1} + 2 - 1
\\&= 2^{k + 1} + 1.
\end{aligned}
\]
So \(P(k + 1)\) holds, and by induction \(a_n = 2^n + 1\) for every non-negative integer \(n\).











Definition 11 (Structural induction) Structural induction (Wikipedia contributors 2026h) is a way to prove that every element of a recursively defined set (Definition 3) has a property \(P\), in two steps:

Base case. Show that every element that the set’s base case names has \(P\).
Inductive step. Show that whenever the recursive rule builds a new element from elements that have \(P\), the new element has \(P\) too.












Example 13 (Every element of \(S\) is odd) Let \(S\) be the set of Exercise 2. It is a recursively defined set (Definition 3), with base case \(1 \in S\) and recursive rule that if \(x \in S\), then \(x + 2 \in S\) and \(3x \in S\). We use structural induction (Definition 11) to show that every element of \(S\) is a positive odd (Definition: Even integer) integer.
Base case. The base case names 1, and \(1 = 2 \cdot 0 + 1\) is positive and odd.
Inductive step. Let \(x \in S\) be a positive odd integer, so \(x = 2j + 1\) for some integer \(j \ge 0\). The recursive rule builds \(x + 2\) and \(3x\) from \(x\), and
\[
\begin{aligned}
x + 2 &= 2(j + 1) + 1,
\\ 3x &= 6j + 3 = 2(3j + 1) + 1,
\end{aligned}
\]
which are positive and odd, since \(j + 1\) and \(3j + 1\) are non-negative integers.
So every element of \(S\) is a positive odd integer. Every positive odd integer \(2j + 1\) is in \(S\) too, since it comes from 1 by adding 2 a total of \(j\) times. So \(S\) is the set of positive odd integers, as Solution 2 found for the elements less than 12.











Remark 2 (Why structural induction works). Every element of a recursively defined set (Definition 3) comes from the base case by applying the recursive rule some number \(k \ge 0\) of times. Let \(Q(k)\) be the claim that every element built with \(k\) applications of the rule has the property \(P\). Strong induction (Definition: Proof by strong induction) on \(k\) proves \(Q(k)\) for every \(k \ge 0\):

an element built with 0 applications is named by the base case, so it has \(P\) by the base case of Definition 11;
an element built with \(k \ge 1\) applications comes, by its last application, from elements built with fewer applications, which have \(P\) by the strong induction hypothesis, so it has \(P\) by the inductive step.

So every element of the set has \(P\).











Theorem 2 (Appending adds lengths) For all lists \(L\) and \(M\) (Definition 7),
\[
\operatorname{len}\mathopen{}\left(\operatorname{app}(L, M)\right)\mathclose{} = \operatorname{len}(L) + \operatorname{len}(M),
\]
where \(\operatorname{len}\) is the length (Definition 8) and \(\operatorname{app}\) is the append (Definition 9).










ProofProof






Proof. Let \(M\) be a list. We use structural induction (Definition 11) on \(L\), with \(P(L)\) the equation \(\operatorname{len}\mathopen{}\left(\operatorname{app}(L, M)\right)\mathclose{} = \operatorname{len}(L) + \operatorname{len}(M)\).
Base case. The base case of Definition 7 names only the empty list, and
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{len}\mathopen{}\left(\operatorname{app}(\mathtt{empty}, M)\right)\mathclose{}
&= \operatorname{len}(M)
&& \text{(definition of } \operatorname{app} \text{)}
\\&= 0 + \operatorname{len}(M)
\\&= \operatorname{len}(\mathtt{empty}) + \operatorname{len}(M).
&& \text{(definition of } \operatorname{len} \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
Inductive step. The recursive rule builds \(\operatorname{cons}(x, L)\) from an element \(x\) and a list \(L\). Suppose \(P(L)\). Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
& \operatorname{len}\mathopen{}\left(\operatorname{app}\mathopen{}\left(\operatorname{cons}(x, L), M\right)\mathclose{}\right)\mathclose{}
\\&= \operatorname{len}\mathopen{}\left(\operatorname{cons}\mathopen{}\left(x, \operatorname{app}(L, M)\right)\mathclose{}\right)\mathclose{}
&& \text{(definition of } \operatorname{app} \text{)}
\\&= 1 + \operatorname{len}\mathopen{}\left(\operatorname{app}(L, M)\right)\mathclose{}
&& \text{(definition of } \operatorname{len} \text{)}
\\&= 1 + \operatorname{len}(L) + \operatorname{len}(M)
&& \text{(induction hypothesis } P(L) \text{)}
\\&= \operatorname{len}\mathopen{}\left(\operatorname{cons}(x, L)\right)\mathclose{} + \operatorname{len}(M),
&& \text{(definition of } \operatorname{len} \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
which is \(P\mathopen{}\left(\operatorname{cons}(x, L)\right)\mathclose{}\). By structural induction, \(P(L)\) holds for every list \(L\). Since \(M\) was any list, the equation holds for all lists \(L\) and \(M\).











Theorem 3 (The function \(d\) counts digits) Let \(d\) be the function of Example 3. For every natural number \(n\),
\[
10^{d(n) - 1} \le n < 10^{d(n)},
\]
so \(n\) has exactly \(d(n)\) decimal digits.










ProofProof






Proof. A natural number \(n\) has \(m\) digits exactly when \(10^{m - 1} \le n < 10^m\), since \(10^{m - 1}\), which is 1 followed by \(m - 1\) zeros, is the smallest natural number with \(m\) digits, and \(10^m\), which is 1 followed by \(m\) zeros, is the smallest with \(m + 1\). So the inequalities say that \(n\) has \(d(n)\) digits.
The recursive rule uses \(d\mathopen{}\left(\mathopen{}\left\lfloor n / 10\right\rfloor\mathclose{}\right)\mathclose{}\), not \(d(n - 1)\), so we use strong induction (Definition: Proof by strong induction). Let \(n\) be a natural number, and suppose the inequalities hold for every natural number less than \(n\).
If \(n \le 9\), then \(d(n) = 1\), and \(10^0 = 1 \le n < 10 = 10^1\).
If \(n \ge 10\), let \(q = \mathopen{}\left\lfloor n / 10\right\rfloor\mathclose{}\). Then \(q \le n / 10 < q + 1\), so \(10q \le n < 10q + 10\). Also \(q \ge 1\), since \(n / 10 \ge 1\), and \(q < n\), so \(q\) is a natural number less than \(n\), and by the strong induction hypothesis
\[
10^{d(q) - 1} \le q < 10^{d(q)}.
\]
The recursive rule gives \(d(n) = 1 + d(q)\). For the lower bound,
\[
\begin{aligned}
n
&\ge 10 q
\\&\ge 10 \cdot 10^{d(q) - 1}
&& \text{(strong induction hypothesis)}
\\&= 10^{d(q)}
\\&= 10^{d(n) - 1}.
&& \text{(} d(n) = 1 + d(q) \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
For the upper bound, \(q\) and \(10^{d(q)}\) are integers with \(q < 10^{d(q)}\), so \(q + 1 \le 10^{d(q)}\), and
\[
\begin{aligned}
n
&< 10 (q + 1)
\\&\le 10 \cdot 10^{d(q)}
&& \text{(} q + 1 \le 10^{d(q)} \text{)}
\\&= 10^{d(q) + 1}
\\&= 10^{d(n)}.
&& \text{(} d(n) = 1 + d(q) \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
So the inequalities hold for \(n\), and by strong induction they hold for every natural number \(n\).

2.1 Evaluating compound propositions







Exercise 3 (Evaluate a compound proposition) Suppose \(P\) is true, \(Q\) is false, and \(R\) is false. Is \((\neg P \lor Q) \land \neg R\) true or false?










SolutionSolution






Solution 3. Substitute the truth values, then evaluate from the innermost parentheses outward:
\[
\begin{aligned}
(\neg P \lor Q) \land \neg R
&= (\neg \mathrm{T} \lor \mathrm{F}) \land \neg \mathrm{F} \\
&= (\mathrm{F} \lor \mathrm{F}) \land \mathrm{T} \\
&= \mathrm{F} \land \mathrm{T} \\
&= \mathrm{F}
\end{aligned}
\]
The proposition is false.











Exercise 4 (Evaluate another compound proposition) With the same truth values as Exercise 3 (\(P\) true, \(Q\) false, \(R\) false), is \(\neg (P \land Q) \lor R\) true or false?










SolutionSolution






Solution 4. \[
\begin{aligned}
\neg (P \land Q) \lor R
&= \neg (\mathrm{T} \land \mathrm{F}) \lor \mathrm{F} \\
&= \neg \mathrm{F} \lor \mathrm{F} \\
&= \mathrm{T} \lor \mathrm{F} \\
&= \mathrm{T}
\end{aligned}
\]
The proposition is true.

2.2 Truth tables







Exercise 5 (How many cases?) Exercise 4 found the truth value of \(\neg (P \land Q) \lor R\) for one choice of truth values of \(P\), \(Q\) and \(R\). How many different choices are there?










SolutionSolution






Solution 5. Each of \(P\), \(Q\) and \(R\) is either true or false, independently of the other two, so there are \(2 \times 2 \times 2 = 2^3 = 8\) choices. With \(n\) propositions there are \(2^n\).

title: Propositional Logic

3.1 The converse







Exercise 9 (Reverse an implication) For all real numbers \(x\) and \(y\), “if \(x = y\), then \(x^2 = y^2\)” is true. Is “if \(x^2 = y^2\), then \(x = y\)” also true for all real numbers \(x\) and \(y\)?










SolutionSolution






Solution 9. No. Take \(x = 1\) and \(y = -1\). Then \(x^2 = 1 = y^2\), so the premise is true, but \(x \ne y\), so the conclusion is false.
Swapping the premise and the conclusion of a true implication can give a false one.











Definition 9 (Converse) The converse (Wikipedia contributors 2026b) of the proposition “if \(P\), then \(Q\)” is the proposition “if \(Q\), then \(P\)”.

title: Propositional Logic
text:
3.2 Conditionals in English







Exercise 10 (“Only if”) Rewrite “I go to class only if I am healthy” in the form “if \(P\), then \(Q\)”.










SolutionSolution






Solution 10. “If I go to class, then I am healthy.”
The sentence says that going to class requires being healthy, so whenever I go to class, I am healthy. It does not say “if I am healthy, then I go to class”; that is its converse (Definition 9), and a healthy person may still skip class.
In general, “\(P\) only if \(Q\)” means \(P \Rightarrow Q\).











Remark 5 (English phrasings of \(P \Rightarrow Q\)). Each of these sentences means \(P \Rightarrow Q\):

If \(P\), then \(Q\).
\(Q\) if \(P\).
\(Q\) whenever \(P\).
\(Q\), provided that \(P\).
Whenever \(P\), then also \(Q\).
\(P\) is a sufficient condition for \(Q\).
For \(Q\), it is sufficient that \(P\).
\(Q\) is a necessary condition for \(P\).
For \(P\), it is necessary that \(Q\).
\(P\) only if \(Q\).

title: Loop Invariants
text:
NoteSource





The topics of this chapter follow Kameron Decker Harris’s Fall 2026 worksheet on loop invariants:

what a loop invariant is;
the three parts of a loop invariant proof: initialization, maintenance and termination;
proving that a loop stops;
choosing an invariant strong enough to give the result;
invariants for a loop inside another loop.

Everything else is new: the algorithms, the exercises, the examples, the theorems and their proofs.




1 Preconditions and postconditions







Exercise 1 (Tracing a square-root loop) The algorithm root takes a non-negative integer (Definition: Non-negative integers) \(n\):
procedure root(n)        // n is a non-negative integer
    r := 0
    while (r + 1) * (r + 1) <= n
        r := r + 1
    return r
Run root(20) by hand. Each time the condition after while is tested, write down the value of r and whether the condition is true, and say which number root(20) returns.










SolutionSolution






Solution 1.

\((r + 1)^2 \le 20\)?

The condition is false at the fifth test, so the loop stops there, and root(20) returns 4. The answer satisfies \(4^2 = 16 \le 20 < 25 = 5^2\): 4 is the largest integer whose square is at most 20.











Remark 1 (How to read the pseudocode in this chapter). The algorithms (Definition: Algorithm) in this chapter are written in pseudocode, not in a particular programming language:

x := e sets the variable x to the value of the expression e;
the indented lines under while are the body of the loop, and a while loop tests its condition before every pass through the body, running the body when the condition is true and stopping when it is false;
for i := a to b runs its body once for each of \(i = a, a + 1, \ldots, b\), and not at all if \(a > b\);
A[1..n] is an array of \(n\) entries A[1], …, A[n];
text after // is a comment, which the algorithm ignores.

In Solution 1, the body of root runs four times, and its condition is tested five times: once before each pass through the body, and once more when the loop stops.











Definition 1 (Precondition) A precondition of an algorithm (Definition: Algorithm) is a condition on its input that the algorithm assumes is true when it starts.











Definition 2 (Postcondition) A postcondition of an algorithm is a condition on its input and its output that is required to be true when the algorithm stops, provided that its precondition (Definition 1) was true when it started.











Example 1 (What root promises) For root from Exercise 1, the precondition (Definition 1) is

\(n\) is a non-negative integer,

and the postcondition (Definition 2) is

the returned value \(r\) is a non-negative integer with \(r^2 \le n < (r + 1)^2\).

For a non-negative integer \(r\), the two inequalities \(r^2 \le n < (r + 1)^2\) say that \(r \le \sqrt{n} < r + 1\), so the postcondition says that \(r = \mathopen{}\left\lfloor\sqrt{n}\right\rfloor\mathclose{}\), the largest integer whose square is at most \(n\). Solution 1 checks it for \(n = 20\), where \(r = 4\).











Definition 3 (Correct algorithm) An algorithm is correct for a given precondition (Definition 1) and postcondition (Definition 2) if, for every input that satisfies the precondition, the algorithm stops, and the postcondition is true when it stops.











Example 2 (A version of root that is not correct) Change r := 0 in root to r := 1, and keep the rest. On the input \(n = 0\), which satisfies the precondition of Example 1, the condition \((1 + 1)^2 \le 0\) is false at the first test, so the loop body never runs and the algorithm returns \(r = 1\). But \(1^2 = 1 > 0\), so the postcondition \(r^2 \le n\) is false. One input is enough to show that this version is not correct (Definition 3), even though it returns the right value for every \(n \ge 1\).
To show that an algorithm is correct, we need an argument that covers every input at once.






2 Loop invariants







Exercise 2 (One pass through the body of root) In root (Exercise 1), suppose that at some test of the condition after while, r is an integer with \(r^2 \le n\), and the condition \((r + 1)^2 \le n\) is true. Show that \(r^2 \le n\) is true again at the next test.










SolutionSolution






Solution 2. Since the condition is true, the body runs once and replaces r with \(r' = r + 1\), and then the condition is tested again. At that next test,
\[
\begin{aligned}
(r')^2
&= (r + 1)^2
\\&\le n,
&& \text{(the condition was true)}
\end{aligned}
\]
so \(r^2 \le n\) is true again, for the new value of r.











Definition 4 (Guard of a loop) The guard of a while loop is the condition written after while: the loop tests it before each pass through the body, runs the body when it is true, and stops when it is false.











Example 3 (The guard of a for loop) The guard (Definition 4) of root (Exercise 1) is \((r + 1)^2 \le n\).
A for loop is a while loop written more briefly. The loop on the left does the same thing as the loop on the right, provided the body changes neither i nor b:
for i := a to b              i := a
    body                     while i <= b
                                 body
                                 i := i + 1
So the guard of for i := a to b is \(i \le b\), and the loop stops at the first test where \(i = b + 1\), or at once if \(a > b\).











Definition 5 (Loop invariant) A loop invariant of a loop is a statement about the loop’s variables that is true every time the loop’s guard (Definition 4) is tested, before the first pass through the body and after each pass, for every input that satisfies the algorithm’s precondition (Definition 1).











Example 4 (A statement that holds at every test of root) In the run of root(20) in Solution 1, r takes the values 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 at the five tests of the guard. The statement “\(r^2 \le n\)” is true at all five tests, as a loop invariant (Definition 5) must be, and Solution 2 shows, for every \(n\), that a pass through the body never turns it from true to false. The statement “\(r < 4\)”, by contrast, is true at the first four tests but false at the fifth, so it is not a loop invariant of root.











Theorem 1 (The loop invariant theorem) Let \(I\) be a statement about the variables of a while loop whose guard (Definition 4) is \(G\). Suppose that

\(I\) is true at the first test of the guard, and
whenever \(I\) and \(G\) are both true at a test of the guard, \(I\) is true at the next test.

Then \(I\) is a loop invariant (Definition 5) of the loop. In particular, if the loop stops, then \(I\) is true and \(G\) is false when it stops.










ProofProof






Proof. We use induction (Definition: Proof by induction) on the number of passes through the body. For each non-negative integer \(k\), let \(P(k)\) be the claim

if the body runs at least \(k\) times, then \(I\) is true at the test of the guard that follows the first \(k\) passes.

The test that follows the first \(0\) passes is the first test.
Base case. \(P(0)\) is hypothesis 1.
Inductive step. Let \(k \ge 1\), suppose \(P(k - 1)\) holds, and suppose the body runs at least \(k\) times. Then it runs at least \(k - 1\) times, so by \(P(k - 1)\), \(I\) is true at the test that follows the first \(k - 1\) passes. The \(k\)th pass comes right after that test, and the body runs only when the guard is true, so \(G\) is also true at that test. By hypothesis 2, \(I\) is true at the next test, which is the test that follows the first \(k\) passes. So \(P(k)\) holds.
By induction, \(P(k)\) holds for every \(k \ge 0\). Every test of the guard follows the first \(k\) passes for some \(k \ge 0\), so \(I\) is true at every test, and \(I\) is a loop invariant. The loop stops only at a test where \(G\) is false, and \(I\) is true at that test too.











Remark 2 (The three parts of a loop invariant proof). A proof that an algorithm with one loop is correct (Definition 3) usually names a statement \(I\) and shows three things.
Initialization. Assuming the precondition, \(I\) is true at the first test of the guard.
Maintenance. If \(I\) and the guard are both true at a test, then \(I\) is true at the next test.
Termination. The loop stops, and when it stops, \(I\) together with the guard being false implies the postcondition.
Initialization and maintenance are the two hypotheses of Theorem 1, and they play the roles of the base case and the inductive step of a proof by induction (Definition: Proof by induction). The theorem then says that \(I\) is a loop invariant, so the proof does not have to repeat the induction each time. Termination is the part an induction proof does not have: the theorem says what is true if the loop stops, not that it does.











Example 5 (root is correct) We show that root (Exercise 1) is correct (Definition 3) for the precondition and postcondition of Example 1. Let \(n\) be a non-negative integer, and let \(I\) be the statement

r is a non-negative integer and \(r^2 \le n\).

Initialization. At the first test, \(r = 0\), which is a non-negative integer, and \(r^2 = 0 \le n\), since \(n \ge 0\).
Maintenance. Suppose \(I\) and the guard \((r + 1)^2 \le n\) are true at a test. The body replaces r with \(r + 1\), which is again a non-negative integer, and Solution 2 shows that \((r + 1)^2 \le n\). So \(I\) is true at the next test.
Termination. By Theorem 1, \(I\) is true at every test. A non-negative integer \(r\) satisfies \(r \le r^2\) (if \(r = 0\), both sides are \(0\), and if \(r \ge 1\), then \(r^2 = r \cdot r \ge r \cdot 1\)), so \(r \le r^2 \le n\) at every test. Each pass through the body increases r by 1, starting from 0, so if the body runs at least \(k\) times, then \(r = k\) at the test after the first \(k\) passes, and so \(k \le n\). So the body runs at most \(n\) times, and the loop stops. When it stops, \(I\) is true and the guard is false, so
\[
r^2 \le n
\quad\text{and}\quad
n < (r + 1)^2,
\]
and root returns this \(r\), a non-negative integer. That is the postcondition.






3 Termination







Exercise 3 (A loop that halves) The algorithm halvings takes a natural number (Definition: Natural numbers (our convention)) \(n\) and counts how many times \(n\) can be halved, rounding down, before it reaches 1:
procedure halvings(n)    // n is a natural number
    k := n
    c := 0
    while k >= 2
        k := floor(k / 2)
        c := c + 1
    return c
Here floor(x) is the largest integer that is at most x. Explain why the loop stops for every natural number \(n\).










SolutionSolution






Solution 3. First, k is a natural number at every test of the guard. At the first test \(k = n\), a natural number. If \(k\) is a natural number and the guard \(k \ge 2\) is true, then \(k / 2 \ge 1\), so the new value \(\mathopen{}\left\lfloor k / 2\right\rfloor\mathclose{}\) is an integer that is at least 1. So, by Theorem 1, “k is a natural number” is a loop invariant.
Second, each pass through the body makes k smaller: the new value is \(\mathopen{}\left\lfloor k / 2\right\rfloor\mathclose{} \le k / 2 < k\), since \(k > 0\). Both values are integers, so k decreases by at least 1.
So, if the body runs at least \(j\) times, then at the test after the first \(j\) passes, \(1 \le k \le n - j\), and so \(j \le n - 1\). The body runs at most \(n - 1\) times, and the loop stops.











Definition 6 (Loop variant) A loop variant of a loop is an integer-valued expression in the loop’s variables that is at least 0 at every test of the loop’s guard (Definition 4), and that is smaller after each pass through the body than it was before that pass, for every input that satisfies the algorithm’s precondition (Definition 1).











Example 6 (Loop variants of halvings and root) Solution 3 shows that k is a loop variant (Definition 6) of halvings: it is an integer that is at least 1, and so at least 0, at every test, and each pass through the body makes it smaller. A loop can have more than one loop variant: k - 1 is another one, since it is at least 0 at every test and decreases by the same amount as k.
The termination part of Example 5 is an argument about the loop variant \(n - r\) of root. It is an integer, it is at least 0 at every test because \(r \le n\) there, and each pass through the body increases r by 1, so it decreases \(n - r\) by 1.











Theorem 2 (A loop with a variant stops) If a loop has a loop variant (Definition 6) whose value at the first test of the guard is \(v_0\), then the body runs at most \(v_0\) times, and so the loop stops.










ProofProof






Proof. Write \(v\) for the loop variant. For each non-negative integer \(k\), let \(P(k)\) be the claim

if the body runs at least \(k\) times, then \(v \le v_0 - k\) at the test that follows the first \(k\) passes.

We prove \(P(k)\) for every \(k \ge 0\) by induction (Definition: Proof by induction).
Base case. The test that follows the first \(0\) passes is the first test, where \(v = v_0\).
Inductive step. Let \(k \ge 1\), suppose \(P(k - 1)\) holds, and suppose the body runs at least \(k\) times. By \(P(k - 1)\), \(v \le v_0 - (k - 1)\) at the test that follows the first \(k - 1\) passes. The \(k\)th pass makes the integer \(v\) smaller, so it lowers \(v\) by at least 1, and \(v \le v_0 - k\) at the next test. So \(P(k)\) holds.
Now suppose the body runs at least \(k\) times. By \(P(k)\), \(v \le v_0 - k\) at the test that follows the first \(k\) passes, and \(v \ge 0\) at every test, so \(0 \le v_0 - k\), that is, \(k \le v_0\). So the body cannot run \(v_0 + 1\) times.











Example 7 (A countdown timer) The algorithm countdown counts down a timer that starts at \(x\) minutes and 0 seconds, one second per pass:
procedure countdown(x)   // x is a non-negative integer
    y := 0               // x is the minutes, y the seconds
    while x > 0 or y > 0
        if y > 0
            y := y - 1
        else
            x := x - 1
            y := 59
Neither x nor y is a loop variant (Definition 6): x stays the same while y counts down, and y jumps from 0 to 59 when x goes down. The total number of seconds left, \(60x + y\), is one.
To see this, first let \(I\) be the statement “x and y are integers with \(x \ge 0\) and \(0 \le y \le 59\)”. At the first test, \(x \ge 0\) and \(y = 0\), so \(I\) is true. Suppose \(I\) and the guard are true at a test. If \(y > 0\), the body replaces y with \(y - 1\), which is between 0 and 58, and leaves x alone. Otherwise \(y = 0\), so the guard says \(x > 0\), and the body replaces x with \(x - 1 \ge 0\) and y with 59. Either way \(I\) is true at the next test, so by Theorem 1, \(I\) is a loop invariant.
So \(60x + y \ge 0\) at every test. Each pass through the body lowers \(60x + y\) by exactly 1: if \(y > 0\), the new value is \(60x + (y - 1)\), and if \(y = 0\), the new value is
\[
\begin{aligned}
60(x - 1) + 59
&= 60x - 1
\\&= (60x + y) - 1.
&& \text{(since } y = 0 \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
So \(60x + y\) is a loop variant. Write \(x_0\) for the input value of x. The variant starts at \(60 x_0\), so by Theorem 2 the body runs at most \(60 x_0\) times, and the loop stops. When it stops, the guard is false, so \(x \le 0\) and \(y \le 0\), and \(I\) gives \(x \ge 0\) and \(y \ge 0\), so \(x = 0\) and \(y = 0\), where \(60x + y = 0\). The variant went down by exactly 1 each time, so the body ran exactly \(60 x_0\) times, once for each second.











Remark 3 (A loop nobody knows how to stop). The process of Example: A proposition whose truth value nobody knows is the loop
while n != 1
    if n is even
        n := n / 2
    else
        n := 3 * n + 1
on a positive integer \(n\). Nobody knows whether it stops for every positive integer \(n\): that is the Collatz conjecture (Wikipedia contributors 2026). So nobody has found a loop variant (Definition 6) for it, since Theorem 2 would then prove that it always stops. Termination is a separate claim from what an invariant gives, and it can be the hard part.






4 Choosing a strong enough invariant







Exercise 4 (The two ends of a reversal) The algorithm reverse reverses an array A[1..n], where \(n \ge 0\), by swapping its outermost entries and moving inward:
procedure reverse(A, n)  // A[1..n] is an array, n >= 0
    i := 1
    j := n
    while i < j
        swap A[i] and A[j]
        i := i + 1
        j := j - 1
Show that \(i + j = n + 1\) is a loop invariant (Definition 5) of its loop.










SolutionSolution






Solution 4. We check the two hypotheses of Theorem 1.
Initialization. At the first test, \(i = 1\) and \(j = n\), so \(i + j = n + 1\).
Maintenance. Suppose \(i + j = n + 1\) and the guard \(i < j\) are true at a test. The swap does not change i or j, and the body then replaces i with \(i + 1\) and j with \(j - 1\). At the next test,
\[
\begin{aligned}
(i + 1) + (j - 1)
&= i + j
\\&= n + 1.
\end{aligned}
\]
So, by Theorem 1, \(i + j = n + 1\) is a loop invariant.











Remark 4 (A true invariant can be too weak). The postcondition (Definition 2) of reverse is about the entries of A: writing B[1..n] for the array as it was before the loop, it says that \(A[k] = B[n + 1 - k]\) for every \(k\) with \(1 \le k \le n\). The loop invariant \(i + j = n + 1\) of Solution 4 is true, but it says nothing about A, so no amount of reasoning from it, and from the guard being false, can reach this postcondition.
The invariant, together with the guard being false, has to imply the postcondition. Here the guard mentions only i and j, so the invariant itself has to say something about the entries of A. A good way to find one is to ask what the loop has finished so far, and what it has not touched yet, at a test partway through the loop.











Example 8 (reverse is correct) Let B[1..n] be the array A as it was before the loop of Exercise 4. At a test partway through, the loop has swapped the entries outside positions \(i\) to \(j\), and has not touched the entries from \(i\) to \(j\). So let \(I\) be the statement made of these three parts:

(a) \(i + j = n + 1\) and \(i \le j + 1\);
(b) \(A[k] = B[n + 1 - k]\) for every \(k\) with \(1 \le k < i\) or \(j < k \le n\);
(c) \(A[k] = B[k]\) for every \(k\) with \(i \le k \le j\).

Initialization. At the first test, \(i = 1\) and \(j = n\). Part (a) holds because \(1 + n = n + 1\) and \(1 \le n + 1\), since \(n \ge 0\). No \(k\) between 1 and \(n\) has \(k < 1\) or \(k > n\), so (b) says nothing. Nothing has changed yet, so \(A[k] = B[k]\) for every \(k\), and (c) holds.
Maintenance. Suppose \(I\) and the guard \(i < j\) are true at a test. By (c), \(A[i] = B[i]\) and \(A[j] = B[j]\) before the swap. By (a), \(j = n + 1 - i\) and \(i = n + 1 - j\). So after the swap,
\[
A[i] = B[j] = B[n + 1 - i]
\quad\text{and}\quad
A[j] = B[i] = B[n + 1 - j],
\]
and no other entry changes. The body then replaces i with \(i' = i + 1\) and j with \(j' = j - 1\).

Part (a): \(i' + j' = i + j = n + 1\), as in Solution 4. Since \(i\) and \(j\) are integers and \(i < j\), we have \(i + 1 \le j\), so \(i' \le j = j' + 1\).
Part (b): a \(k\) with \(k < i'\) has \(k < i\), where the swap did not change \(A[k]\) and (b) already held, or \(k = i\), just shown. A \(k\) with \(k > j'\) has \(k > j\) or \(k = j\), in the same way.
Part (c): a \(k\) with \(i' \le k \le j'\) has \(i < k < j\), so the swap did not change \(A[k]\), and \(A[k] = B[k]\) by (c).

So \(I\) is true at the next test.
Termination. By Theorem 1, \(I\) is true at every test. By (a), \(i \le j + 1\), so \(j - i + 1 \ge 0\) at every test, and each pass lowers \(j - i + 1\) by 2. So \(j - i + 1\) is a loop variant (Definition 6), and by Theorem 2 the loop stops. When it stops, the guard is false, so \(i \ge j\), and with (a), \(i = j\) or \(i = j + 1\). Now let \(1 \le k \le n\).

If \(k < i\) or \(k > j\), then \(A[k] = B[n + 1 - k]\) by (b).
Otherwise \(i \le k \le j\), which can only happen when \(i = j = k\). Then (a) gives \(2k = n + 1\), so \(k = n + 1 - k\), and (c) gives \(A[k] = B[k] = B[n + 1 - k]\).

So \(A[k] = B[n + 1 - k]\) for every \(k\), which is the postcondition of Remark 4. The middle entry of an array of odd length is the one that never moves.






5 Nested loops







Exercise 5 (Looking for a repeated entry) The algorithm has_repeat decides whether some value appears twice in an array A[1..n], where \(n \ge 1\), by comparing every pair of positions:
procedure has_repeat(A, n)   // A[1..n] is an array, n >= 1
    found := false
    for i := 1 to n - 1
        for j := i + 1 to n
            if A[i] = A[j]
                found := true
    return found
Run has_repeat on the array \(A = (3, 1, 4, 1)\), with \(n = 4\). List the pairs \((i, j)\) that the inner loop compares, in order, and give the first pair at which found becomes true.










SolutionSolution

The inner loop compares the six pairs in the table, in that order. found first becomes true at \((2, 4)\), since \(A[2] = A[4] = 1\), and it stays true, so has_repeat returns true.











Remark 5 (Proving a nested loop correct). A loop inside another loop gets its own loop invariant (Definition 5). The proof usually goes from the inside out:

prove the inner loop’s invariant, using the outer loop’s invariant at the test where the inner loop starts;
read off what the inner loop has done when it stops;
use that in the maintenance step of the outer loop’s invariant.

Each for loop is a while loop (Example 3), so each invariant is a statement about the tests of that loop’s guard.











Example 9 (has_repeat is correct) In has_repeat (Exercise 5), call a pair of positions \((p, q)\) a match if \(1 \le p < q \le n\) and \(A[p] = A[q]\). The postcondition is that has_repeat returns true if A has a match, and false if it has none. The algorithm never changes A. We follow Remark 5.
The inner loop. Fix a pass of the outer loop with index \(i\), where \(1 \le i \le n - 1\), and suppose that, when the inner loop starts,

found is true exactly when there is a match \((p, q)\) with \(p < i\),

which is the outer loop’s invariant \(K\), proved in the next part. Let \(J\) be the statement

\(i + 1 \le j \le n + 1\), and found is true exactly when there is a match \((p, q)\) with \(p < i\), or with \(p = i\) and \(q < j\).


Initialization: at the first test, \(j = i + 1 \le n\). No \(q\) has \(i < q < i + 1\), so \(J\) says the same as the supposition above.
Maintenance: suppose \(J\) and the guard \(j \le n\) are true at a test. A match with \(p < i\), or with \(p = i\) and \(q < j + 1\), is either one of the matches that \(J\) describes or the pair \((i, j)\). If \(A[i] = A[j]\), the body sets found to true, and \((i, j)\) is such a match. If not, found does not change, and \((i, j)\) is not a match. Either way, after j becomes \(j + 1 \le n + 1\), \(J\) is true at the next test.
Termination: by Theorem 1, \(J\) is a loop invariant, so \(n + 1 - j \ge 0\) at every test, and each pass lowers \(n + 1 - j\) by 1. So \(n + 1 - j\) is a loop variant (Definition 6), and the inner loop stops (Theorem 2). It stops when \(j \le n\) is false, so, with \(j \le n + 1\), \(j = n + 1\). Every match has \(q \le n < n + 1\), so, when the inner loop stops,

found is true exactly when there is a match \((p, q)\) with \(p < i\) or \(p = i\), that is, with \(p < i + 1\).


The outer loop. Let \(K\) be the statement

\(1 \le i \le n\), and found is true exactly when there is a match \((p, q)\) with \(p < i\).


Initialization: at the first test, \(i = 1 \le n\), since \(n \ge 1\), found is false, and no match has \(p < 1\).
Maintenance: suppose \(K\) and the guard \(i \le n - 1\) are true at a test. Then the inner loop runs, and when it stops, found is true exactly when there is a match with \(p < i + 1\). After i becomes \(i + 1 \le n\), \(K\) is true at the next test.
Termination: by Theorem 1, \(K\) is a loop invariant, so \(n - i \ge 0\) at every test, and each pass lowers \(n - i\) by 1. So \(n - i\) is a loop variant, and the outer loop stops. It stops when \(i \le n - 1\) is false, so, with \(i \le n\), \(i = n\). Every match has \(p < q \le n\), so \(p < n\). So, when the outer loop stops, found is true exactly when A has a match, and the algorithm returns found.
