Adapted from Kameron Decker Harris’s Fall 2026 lecture notes “Proving Non-Conditional Statements, Disproof”, which are typed transcriptions of Scott Wehrwein’s Spring 2025 handwritten lecture notes. These come from those notes:

the outline of an “if and only if” proof;
the outline of an existence proof that names an element;
proving that several propositions are equivalent with a cycle of conditionals;
the constructive example of half of a positive number;
the non-constructive example of an irrational power of an irrational number;
disproving a proposition by proving its negation.

The exercises are new.




1 Proving if and only if







Exercise 1 (A sum of squares equal to zero) Let \(x\) and \(y\) be real numbers. Prove: \(x^2 + y^2 = 0\) if and only if \(x = 0\) and \(y = 0\) (Definition: If and only if).
Hint: prove the two directions one at a time.










SolutionSolution






Solution 1. If \(x = 0\) and \(y = 0\), then \(x^2 + y^2 = 0\). Suppose \(x = 0\) and \(y = 0\). Then \(x^2 + y^2 = 0^2 + 0^2 = 0\).
If \(x^2 + y^2 = 0\), then \(x = 0\) and \(y = 0\). Suppose \(x^2 + y^2 = 0\). A square of a real number is never negative, so \(y^2 \ge 0\), and
\[
\begin{aligned}
x^2
&= -y^2
&& \text{(subtract } y^2 \text{ from both sides of } x^2 + y^2 = 0 \text{)}
\\&\le 0.
&& \text{(} y^2 \ge 0 \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
Also \(x^2 \ge 0\), so \(x^2 = 0\), and so \(x = 0\). The same steps with \(x\) and \(y\) swapped give \(y = 0\).











Theorem 1 (A biconditional is two conditionals) For propositions \(P\) and \(Q\),
\[
(P \Leftrightarrow Q) \equiv \mathopen{}\left((P \Rightarrow Q) \land (Q \Rightarrow P)\right)\mathclose{}.
\]










ProofProof






Proof. The fifth and last columns of this truth table (Definition: Truth table) match in every row (Definition: If and only if, Definition: Implies, Definition: And):

So the two propositions are logically equivalent (Definition: Logical equivalence).











Example 1 (Proving both directions) Claim: let \(n\) be an integer. Then \(n\) is even if and only if \(n + 2\) is even.
By Theorem 1, it is enough to prove two conditionals.

If \(n\) is even, then \(n = 2k\) for some integer \(k\) (Definition: Even integer), so \(n + 2 = 2k + 2 = 2(k + 1)\), and \(k + 1\) is an integer (Remark: Facts about integers used without proof). So \(n + 2\) is even.
If \(n + 2\) is even, then \(n + 2 = 2m\) for some integer \(m\), so \(n = 2m - 2 = 2(m - 1)\), and \(m - 1\) is an integer. So \(n\) is even.












Remark 1 (The shape of an “if and only if” proof). A proof of “\(P\) if and only if \(Q\)” has two parts:

(\(\Rightarrow\)) Suppose \(P\).
\(\vdots\)
Therefore \(Q\).

(\(\Leftarrow\)) Suppose \(Q\).
\(\vdots\)
Therefore \(P\).

Each part is a proof of a conditional, so each can be a direct proof (Definition: Direct proof), a proof by contrapositive (Definition: Proof by contrapositive), or a proof by contradiction (Definition: Proof by contradiction), and the two parts need not use the same method.











Theorem 2 (A cycle of conditionals) Let \(P_1, P_2, \ldots, P_k\) be propositions. If \(P_1 \Rightarrow P_2\), \(P_2 \Rightarrow P_3\), \(\ldots\), \(P_{k-1} \Rightarrow P_k\) and \(P_k \Rightarrow P_1\) are all true, then \(P_1, \ldots, P_k\) all have the same truth value.










ProofProof






Proof. Suppose one of the propositions, \(P_i\), is true. By modus ponens (Theorem: Common rules of inference), \(P_i \Rightarrow P_{i+1}\) makes \(P_{i+1}\) true, then \(P_{i+1} \Rightarrow P_{i+2}\) makes \(P_{i+2}\) true, and so on around the cycle, with \(P_k \Rightarrow P_1\) leading from \(P_k\) back to \(P_1\), until every proposition in the list is true. So either all of \(P_1, \ldots, P_k\) are true, or none of them is true, and then all of them are false.











Example 2 (Three ways to say “odd”) Let \(n\) be an integer, and consider

\(P_1\): \(n\) is odd;
\(P_2\): \(n + 1\) is even;
\(P_3\): \(n - 1\) is even.

By Theorem 2, three conditionals show that all three have the same truth value.

\(P_1 \Rightarrow P_2\): if \(n = 2k + 1\) (Definition: Odd integer), then \(n + 1 = 2k + 2 = 2(k + 1)\).
\(P_2 \Rightarrow P_3\): if \(n + 1 = 2m\), then \(n - 1 = 2m - 2 = 2(m - 1)\).
\(P_3 \Rightarrow P_1\): if \(n - 1 = 2j\), then \(n = 2j + 1\).

In each step the new multiplier, \(k + 1\), \(m - 1\) or \(j\), is an integer (Remark: Facts about integers used without proof). Proving all six conditionals between pairs would have taken twice as many steps.






2 Proving existence







Exercise 2 (A solution in integers) Show that there are integers \(x\) and \(y\) with \(5x + 3y = 1\).










SolutionSolution






Solution 2. Take \(x = 2\) and \(y = -3\). Then \(5x + 3y = 5 \cdot 2 + 3 \cdot(-3) = 10 - 9 = 1\). So integers with \(5x + 3y = 1\) exist (Definition: Existential quantifier). Other pairs work too, such as \(x = -1\) and \(y = 2\).











Definition 1 (Constructive proof) A constructive proof of a proposition \(\exists x \in S,\ P(x)\) (Definition: Existential quantifier) names a particular element of \(S\) and shows that \(P\) is true of it (Wikipedia contributors 2026). A proposition with several existential quantifiers, such as “there are integers \(m\) and \(n\) with \(m + n = 1\)”, gets a constructive proof that names one element for each quantifier.











Example 3 (Half of a positive number) Claim: for every positive real number \(x\), there is a positive real number \(y\) with \(y < x\).
Let \(x\) be a positive real number. We give a constructive proof of “there is a positive real number \(y\) with \(y < x\)” for this \(x\): take \(y = \frac{x}{2}\). Then \(y > 0\), because \(x > 0\), and
\[
\begin{aligned}
x - y
&= x - \frac{x}{2}
&& \text{(substitute } y = \tfrac{x}{2} \text{)}
\\&= \frac{x}{2}
&& \text{(arithmetic)}
\\&> 0,
&& \text{(} x > 0 \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
so \(y < x\). The element named, \(\frac{x}{2}\), depends on \(x\), which a “for every \(x\), there is a \(y\)” statement allows.
The solution to Exercise 2 is also a constructive proof: it names the integers \(2\) and \(-3\).











Definition 2 (Non-constructive proof) A non-constructive proof of a proposition \(\exists x \in S,\ P(x)\) shows that it is true without naming any element \(x\) of \(S\) for which \(P(x)\) is true (Wikipedia contributors 2026).











Example 4 (An irrational power of an irrational number) Claim: there are irrational numbers \(x\) and \(y\) (Definition: Irrational numbers) for which \(x^y\) is rational (Definition: Rational numbers).
The number \(\sqrt{2}\) is irrational (Theorem: \(\sqrt{2}\) is irrational). Consider \(\sqrt{2}^{\sqrt{2}}\), and take two cases (Definition: Proof by cases).
Case 1: \(\sqrt{2}^{\sqrt{2}}\) is rational. Then \(x = \sqrt{2}\) and \(y = \sqrt{2}\) work.
Case 2: \(\sqrt{2}^{\sqrt{2}}\) is irrational. Then take \(x = \sqrt{2}^{\sqrt{2}}\) and \(y = \sqrt{2}\), both irrational, and
\[
\begin{aligned}
x^y
&= \mathopen{}\left(\sqrt{2}^{\sqrt{2}}\right)\mathclose{}^{\sqrt{2}}
&& \text{(substitute } x \text{ and } y \text{)}
\\&= \sqrt{2}^{\sqrt{2} \cdot\sqrt{2}}
&& \text{(a power of a power multiplies the exponents)}
\\&= \sqrt{2}^{2}
&& \text{(} \sqrt{2} \cdot\sqrt{2} = 2 \text{)}
\\&= 2,
\end{aligned}
\]
which is rational, since \(2 = \frac{2}{1}\).
Every number is rational or irrational, so one of the cases holds, and the claim is true. The proof does not say which case holds, so it does not name a pair \(x, y\) that works.






3 Disproof







Exercise 3 (Prove or disprove) Prove or disprove: for every real number \(x\), if \(x^2 > 1\), then \(x > 1\).










SolutionSolution






Solution 3. The proposition is false. Take \(x = -2\). Then \(x^2 = 4 > 1\), but \(x > 1\) is false. So \(x = -2\) makes “if \(x^2 > 1\), then \(x > 1\)” false (Definition: Implies), and so it is a counterexample (Definition: Counterexample) to the proposition.











Definition 3 (Disproof) A disproof of a proposition \(P\) is a proof (Definition: Proof) of its negation, \(\neg P\) (Definition: Not).











Example 5 (No integer squares to two) Claim to disprove: there is an integer \(n\) with \(n^2 = 2\).
By Theorem: Negating a quantifier, its negation is “for every integer \(n\), \(n^2 \ne 2\)”. We prove the negation by cases (Definition: Proof by cases). Let \(n\) be an integer.

If \(n\) is \(-1\), \(0\) or \(1\), then \(n^2\) is \(1\), \(0\) or \(1\), which is not \(2\).
Otherwise \(n \le -2\) or \(n \ge 2\), so \(\mathopen{}\left|n\right|\mathclose{} \ge 2\), and \(n^2 = \mathopen{}\left|n\right|\mathclose{}^2 \ge 2^2 = 4\), so \(n^2 \ne 2\).












Exercise 4 (An equation with a solution) Prove or disprove: there are integers \(m\) and \(n\) with \(6m + 4n = 2\).










SolutionSolution






Solution 4. The proposition is true. Take \(m = 1\) and \(n = -1\). Then \(6m + 4n = 6 - 4 = 2\).











Exercise 5 (An equation without a solution) Prove or disprove: there are integers \(m\) and \(n\) with \(6m + 4n = 3\).










SolutionSolution






Solution 5. The proposition is false. Applying Theorem: Negating a quantifier to each of its two quantifiers in turn, its negation is “for all integers \(m\) and \(n\), \(6m + 4n \ne 3\)”, and we prove that. Let \(m\) and \(n\) be integers. Then \(6m + 4n = 2(3m + 2n)\), and \(3m + 2n\) is an integer (Remark: Facts about integers used without proof), so \(6m + 4n\) is even (Definition: Even integer). But \(3 = 2 \cdot 1 + 1\) is odd (Definition: Odd integer), and no integer is both even and odd (Remark: Facts about integers used without proof), so \(6m + 4n \ne 3\).

The rules of inference, the definition of “divides”, the observation that a definition’s “if” means “if and only if”, the template for a direct proof, and the ideas of proof by cases and “without loss of generality” come from those notes; the exercises are new.
The definitions of logical entailment, the integers, even and odd integers, and proof are included from the mathematics prerequisites notes, so they read the same in both places.




1 Rules of inference







Exercise 1 (Which conclusions are safe?) Let \(P\) be “the tests pass”, \(Q\) be “the build is deployed” and \(R\) be “the build is rolled back”. Each argument below lists some propositions, then “so”, then one more proposition. For each argument, decide whether the proposition after “so” must be true whenever all of the propositions before it are true.

\(P \Rightarrow Q\) and \(P\), so \(Q\).
\(P \Rightarrow Q\) and \(Q\), so \(P\).
\(P \Rightarrow Q\) and \(\neg Q\), so \(\neg P\).
\(P \lor R\) and \(\neg R\), so \(P\).











SolutionSolution






Solution 1. 

Yes. \(P \Rightarrow Q\) is false when \(P\) is true and \(Q\) is false (Definition: Implies), so if \(P \Rightarrow Q\) and \(P\) are both true, \(Q\) is true.
No. If the tests fail but someone deploys the build by hand, \(P\) is false and \(Q\) is true. Then \(P \Rightarrow Q\) and \(Q\) are both true, and \(P\) is false.
Yes. \(\neg Q\) is true, so \(Q\) is false (Definition: Not). If \(P\) were true, \(P \Rightarrow Q\) would be false, so \(P\) is false and \(\neg P\) is true.
Yes. \(\neg R\) is true, so \(R\) is false (Definition: Not). \(P \lor R\) is true only if \(P\) or \(R\) is true (Definition: Or), so \(P\) is true.












Definition 1 (Argument) An argument is a list of propositions (Definition: Proposition (statement)), called its premises, together with one more proposition, called its conclusion. An argument is written with “so” or \(\therefore\) before its conclusion.











Remark 1 (Two uses of “premise” and “conclusion”). The premise and conclusion of a conditional \(P \Rightarrow Q\) (Remark: Names for the parts, and other notation) are its parts \(P\) and \(Q\). The premises and conclusion of an argument (Definition 1) are whole propositions: in argument 1 of Exercise 1, the premises are \(P \Rightarrow Q\) and \(P\), and the conclusion is \(Q\).











Definition 2 (Logical entailment (logical consequence, deductive consequence)) Propositions or predicates \(P_1, \ldots, P_n\) (Definition: Proposition (statement), Definition: Predicate) logically entail (Wikipedia contributors 2026b) a proposition or predicate \(Q\) when every choice of values for their variables that makes all of \(P_1, \ldots, P_n\) true also makes \(Q\) true. Then \(Q\) is a logical consequence, or deductive consequence, of \(P_1, \ldots, P_n\).











Example 1 (Entailment in the deployment arguments) In Exercise 1, the premises of arguments 1, 3 and 4 (Definition 1) logically entail their conclusions (Definition 2). The premises of argument 2 do not: the values \(P\) false and \(Q\) true make both premises true and the conclusion false.











Definition 3 (Rule of inference) A rule of inference is a pattern of argument (Definition 1), written in terms of propositions \(P, Q, \ldots\), whose premises logically entail its conclusion (Definition 2) whatever propositions are put in place of \(P, Q, \ldots\). It is written with its premises above a line and its conclusion below: \[
\frac{P_1, \ldots, P_n}{Q}.
\]











Example 2 (Modus ponens) Argument 1 of Exercise 1 follows the pattern \[
\frac{P \Rightarrow Q, \quad P}{Q},
\] called modus ponens. It is a rule of inference (Definition 3): by Solution 1, its premises entail its conclusion for any propositions \(P\) and \(Q\), not only for tests and builds.











Theorem 1 (Common rules of inference) For propositions \(P\) and \(Q\), each of the following is a rule of inference (Definition 3):

modus ponens: \[
\frac{P \Rightarrow Q, \quad P}{Q}
\]
modus tollens: \[
\frac{P \Rightarrow Q, \quad \neg Q}{\neg P}
\]
disjunctive syllogism: \[
\frac{P \lor Q, \quad \neg P}{Q}
\]
simplification: \[
\frac{P \land Q}{P}
\]
conjunction: \[
\frac{P, \quad Q}{P \land Q}
\]
addition: \[
\frac{P}{P \lor Q}
\]











ProofProof






Proof. For each rule, suppose every premise is true, and show that the conclusion is true.

\(P \Rightarrow Q\) is false when \(P\) is true and \(Q\) is false (Definition: Implies). \(P\) is true and \(P \Rightarrow Q\) is true, so \(Q\) is not false.
\(\neg Q\) is true, so \(Q\) is false (Definition: Not). If \(P\) were true, \(P \Rightarrow Q\) would be false, so \(P\) is false and \(\neg P\) is true.
\(\neg P\) is true, so \(P\) is false. \(P \lor Q\) is true only if \(P\) or \(Q\) is true (Definition: Or), so \(Q\) is true.
\(P \land Q\) is true only if both \(P\) and \(Q\) are true (Definition: And), so \(P\) is true.
\(P\) and \(Q\) are both true, so \(P \land Q\) is true (Definition: And).
\(P\) is true, so \(P \lor Q\) is true (Definition: Or).












Example 3 (Modus tollens on a slow page) “If the cache is warm, then the page loads in under a second” and “the page did not load in under a second” together give “the cache is not warm”, by modus tollens (Theorem 1).











Remark 2 (Two arguments that are not rules of inference). Argument 2 of Exercise 1, \[
\frac{P \Rightarrow Q, \quad Q}{P},
\] is called affirming the consequent, since it concludes \(P\) from the consequent \(Q\) of \(P \Rightarrow Q\) (Remark: Names for the parts, and other notation). It is not a rule of inference (Definition 3): \(P\) false and \(Q\) true make its premises true and its conclusion false.
Denying the antecedent, \[
\frac{P \Rightarrow Q, \quad \neg P}{\neg Q},
\] fails for the same values of \(P\) and \(Q\). Both read like modus ponens or modus tollens (Theorem 1), which is why they are common mistakes.






2 Even, odd and divisible







Exercise 2 (Two times something, plus maybe one) Write each of \(14\), \(15\), \(-7\) and \(0\) as \(2k\) or as \(2k + 1\), for an integer \(k\).










SolutionSolution






Solution 2. 

\(14 = 2 \cdot 7\).
\(15 = 2 \cdot 7 + 1\).
\(-7 = 2 \cdot (-4) + 1\).
\(0 = 2 \cdot 0\).












Definition 4 (Integers) The integers (Wikipedia contributors 2026a) are the whole numbers, together with their negatives and \(0\):
\[\mathbb{Z} \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\mathopen{}\left\{\ldots, -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, \ldots\right\}\mathclose{}\]
An integer is an element of \(\mathbb{Z}\).











Definition 5 (Positive integers) The integers (Definition 4) greater than \(0\) are the positive integers.











Definition 6 (Negative integers) The integers (Definition 4) less than \(0\) are the negative integers.











Example 4 (Integers and non-integers)  

\(-7\), \(0\), and \(12\) are integers.
\(\frac{1}{2}\) and \(-2.5\) are not integers.
\(\frac{6}{3}\) is an integer, because \(\frac{6}{3} = 2\).












Definition 7 (Even integer) An integer (Definition 4) \(n\) is even (Wikipedia contributors 2026d) if \(n = 2k\) for some integer \(k\).











Definition 8 (Odd integer) An integer (Definition 4) \(n\) is odd (Wikipedia contributors 2026d) if \(n = 2k + 1\) for some integer \(k\).











Example 5 (Even and odd integers)  

\(6\) is even, because \(6 = 2 \cdot 3\).
\(0\) is even, because \(0 = 2 \cdot 0\).
\(-3\) is odd, because \(-3 = 2 \cdot(-2) + 1\).
\(7\) is odd, because \(7 = 2 \cdot 3 + 1\).
\(2.5\) is neither even nor odd, because it is not an integer.












Remark 3 (Facts about integers used without proof). These notes use two facts about the integers (Definition 4) without proving them:

the sum, difference and product of two integers are integers;
every integer is even or odd (Definition 7, Definition 8), and none is both.












Remark 4 (A definition’s “if” means “if and only if”). Definition 7 says that \(n\) is even “if” \(n = 2k\) for some integer \(k\), but it means “if and only if” (Definition: If and only if): an integer is even exactly when it can be written as \(2k\). So a proof can use a definition in both directions: to show that \(n\) is even, write \(n\) as \(2k\); and from “\(n\) is even”, conclude that \(n = 2k\) for some integer \(k\).











Definition 9 (Divides) Let \(a\) and \(b\) be integers (Definition 4). We say that \(a\) divides \(b\), written \(a \mid b\), if \(b = a c\) for some integer \(c\). When \(a\) does not divide \(b\), we write \(a \nmid b\).











Example 6 (Divisors)  

\(3 \mid 12\), because \(12 = 3 \cdot 4\).
\(-2 \mid 6\), because \(6 = (-2) \cdot (-3)\).
\(3 \nmid 13\): \(3 c\) increases with \(c\), \(3 \cdot 4 = 12\) and \(3 \cdot 5 = 15\), and there is no integer between \(4\) and \(5\), so no integer \(c\) gives \(3 c = 13\).
Every integer \(a\) divides \(0\), because \(0 = a \cdot 0\).
\(0\) divides only \(0\), because \(0 \cdot c = 0\) for every integer \(c\).












Remark 5 (Divisibility in Racket). For a nonzero integer a, Racket’s (remainder b a) returns 0 exactly when \(a \mid b\) (Definition 9), so (zero? (remainder b a)) tests divisibility. (zero? (remainder 12 3)) returns #t and (zero? (remainder 13 3)) returns #f, as in Example 6. (remainder 12 0) raises an error, so a Racket test of \(a \mid b\) has to handle \(a = 0\) on its own.






3 Direct proof







Exercise 3 (An odd input) Show that if \(n\) is an odd integer, then \(3 n + 5\) is even.






TipHint



What does Definition 8 let you write in place of \(n\)?












SolutionSolution






Solution 3. Suppose \(n\) is an odd integer. By Definition 8, \(n = 2 k + 1\) for some integer \(k\). Then \[
3 n + 5 = 3 (2 k + 1) + 5 = 6 k + 3 + 5 = 6 k + 8 = 2 (3 k + 4).
\] Since \(3 k + 4\) is an integer (Remark 3), \(3 n + 5\) is even, by Definition 7.











Definition 10 (Proof) A proof (Wikipedia contributors 2026c) of a proposition (Definition: Proposition (statement)) is a finite list of statements that ends with that proposition, in which each statement is

an assumption,
a definition,
a previously proved result, or
a consequence of earlier statements in the list, by one rule of logic or algebra.












Example 7 (A proof, statement by statement) Solution 3 is a proof (Definition 10) of “\(3 n + 5\) is even” in which “\(n\) is an odd integer” is an assumption. Its statements are:

the assumption: \(n\) is an odd integer;
a definition: \(n = 2 k + 1\) for some integer \(k\), by Definition 8;
consequences by algebra: \(3 n + 5 = 6 k + 8 = 2 (3 k + 4)\);
a definition: \(3 n + 5\) is even, by Definition 7, since \(3 k + 4\) is an integer.












Definition 11 (Direct proof) A direct proof of a conditional \(P \Rightarrow Q\) (Definition: Implies) is a proof (Definition 10) of \(Q\) in which \(P\) is an assumption.











Example 8 (A direct proof) Solution 3 is a direct proof (Definition 11) of “if \(n\) is an odd integer, then \(3 n + 5\) is even”: it assumes \(P\), “\(n\) is an odd integer”, and ends with \(Q\), “\(3 n + 5\) is even”.











Remark 6 (The shape of a direct proof). A direct proof (Definition 11) of “if \(P\), then \(Q\)” has this shape:

Suppose \(P\).
\(\vdots\)
Therefore \(Q\).

Write the first and last lines first, then fill in the middle, usually by replacing each defined term with its definition (Remark 4).
A direct proof proves \(P \Rightarrow Q\): when \(P\) is true, the proof shows that \(Q\) is true, and when \(P\) is false, \(P \Rightarrow Q\) is true anyway (Definition: Implies).
When the statement is about every element of a set, as in “for every odd integer \(n\)” (Definition: Universal quantifier), the proof starts from an arbitrary element: “Suppose \(n\) is an odd integer.” Since the proof uses nothing about \(n\) except that \(n\) is odd, the same steps work for every odd integer.











Exercise 4 (Divisors of divisors) Let \(a\), \(b\) and \(c\) be integers. Prove that if \(a \mid b\) and \(b \mid c\), then \(a \mid c\).










SolutionSolution






Solution 4. Suppose \(a \mid b\) and \(b \mid c\). By Definition 9, \(b = a j\) and \(c = b k\) for some integers \(j\) and \(k\). Then \[
c = b k = (a j) k = a (j k).
\] Since \(j k\) is an integer (Remark 3), \(a \mid c\), by Definition 9.






4 Proof by cases







Exercise 5 (Even for every integer) Prove that \(n^2 + n\) is even for every integer \(n\).






TipHint



Every integer is even or odd (Remark 3). Handle the two kinds separately.












SolutionSolution






Solution 5. Let \(n\) be an integer. Every integer is even or odd (Remark 3), so one of these cases holds.
Case 1: \(n\) is even. By Definition 7, \(n = 2 k\) for some integer \(k\), and \[
n^2 + n = (2 k)^2 + 2 k = 4 k^2 + 2 k = 2 (2 k^2 + k).
\]
Case 2: \(n\) is odd. By Definition 8, \(n = 2 k + 1\) for some integer \(k\), and \[
n^2 + n = (2 k + 1)^2 + (2 k + 1) = (4 k^2 + 4 k + 1) + (2 k + 1) = 4 k^2 + 6 k + 2 = 2 (2 k^2 + 3 k + 1).
\]
In each case, \(n^2 + n\) is \(2\) times an integer (Remark 3), so \(n^2 + n\) is even, by Definition 7.











Definition 12 (Proof by cases) A proof by cases splits the situation into cases that together cover every possibility, and proves the conclusion separately in each case.











Example 9 (Two cases) Solution 5 is a proof by cases (Definition 12): every integer is even or odd (Remark 3), so its two cases cover every integer \(n\).











Exercise 6 (Larger plus smaller) For real numbers \(x\) and \(y\), let \(\max(x, y)\) be the larger of \(x\) and \(y\) and \(\min(x, y)\) the smaller (both equal \(x\) when \(x = y\)). Prove that \(\max(x, y) + \min(x, y) = x + y\).










SolutionSolution






Solution 6. Let \(x\) and \(y\) be real numbers. Either \(x \le y\) or \(y \le x\). Both sides of the equation stay the same when \(x\) and \(y\) are swapped, so without loss of generality, suppose \(x \le y\). Then \(\max(x, y) = y\) and \(\min(x, y) = x\), so \[
\max(x, y) + \min(x, y) = y + x = x + y.
\]











Remark 7 (Without loss of generality). Solution 6 is a proof by cases (Definition 12) with two cases, \(x \le y\) and \(y \le x\). The proof of the second case is the proof of the first with the names \(x\) and \(y\) swapped, which changes neither side of the equation. “Without loss of generality, suppose \(x \le y\)” says this, and writes out only the first case. Use it only when the other cases really are the same proof with names changed.

title: Contrapositive and Contradiction
text:
NoteSource





Adapted from Kameron Decker Harris’s Fall 2026 lecture notes “Contrapositive Proof” and “Proof by Contradiction”, which are typed transcriptions of Scott Wehrwein’s Spring 2025 handwritten lecture notes. These come from those notes:

the definition of congruence modulo \(n\), and the point that it is not the mod operator;
the human and mammal illustration of a contrapositive;
the example of a product not divisible by \(5\);
the truth table showing why a proof by contradiction works;
the outlines of a proof by contrapositive, a proof by contradiction, and a proof of a conditional by contradiction;
the definition and examples of a prime number, and the fact that every integer above one has a prime divisor;
the statement that \(\sqrt{2}\) is irrational (the proof here is different);
Euclid’s proof that there are infinitely many primes.

The exercises are new.
The definitions of the contrapositive, proof by contrapositive, proof by contradiction, and rational and irrational numbers, their examples of a proof by contradiction and of rational and irrational numbers, and the theorem that a conditional is equivalent to its contrapositive, are included from the mathematics prerequisites notes, so they read the same in both places.




1 Congruence modulo \(n\)







Exercise 1 (Differences divisible by five) For each integer \(a\) in the list \(23\), \(38\), \(50\), \(-7\), compute \(a - 8\), and decide whether \(5 \mid (a - 8)\) (Definition: Divides).










SolutionSolution






Solution 1. 

\(23 - 8 = 15 = 5 \cdot 3\), so \(5 \mid (23 - 8)\).
\(38 - 8 = 30 = 5 \cdot 6\), so \(5 \mid (38 - 8)\).
\(50 - 8 = 42\). Since \(5 \cdot 8 = 40 < 42 < 45 = 5 \cdot 9\), no integer \(c\) has \(5c = 42\), so \(5 \nmid (50 - 8)\).
\(-7 - 8 = -15 = 5 \cdot(-3)\), so \(5 \mid (-7 - 8)\).












Definition 1 (Congruence modulo \(n\)) Let \(a\) and \(b\) be integers (Definition: Integers), and let \(n\) be a positive integer. We say that \(a\) is congruent to \(b\) modulo \(n\), written \(a \equiv b \pmod{n}\), if \(n \mid (a - b)\) (Definition: Divides) (Wikipedia contributors 2026d). When \(a\) is not congruent to \(b\) modulo \(n\), we write \(a \not\equiv b \pmod{n}\).











Example 1 (Congruences)  

By Solution 1, \(23 \equiv 8 \pmod{5}\), \(38 \equiv 8 \pmod{5}\) and \(-7 \equiv 8 \pmod{5}\), but \(50 \not\equiv 8 \pmod{5}\).
A 24-hour clock that reads \(19\) shows the same hour as a 12-hour clock that reads \(7\), and \(19 \equiv 7 \pmod{12}\), because \(19 - 7 = 12 = 12 \cdot 1\).












Remark 1 (Two meanings of \(\equiv\), and the mod operator). The symbol \(\equiv\) also means logical equivalence (Definition: Logical equivalence). The “\((\operatorname{mod} n)\)” after it says which meaning is in use: \(23 \equiv 8 \pmod{5}\) is a statement about two integers, and \(P \equiv Q\) is a statement about two propositions.
Congruence is related to the mod operator of a programming language, but it is not the same thing. In Racket, (modulo 23 5) is the number \(3\), while \(23 \equiv 8 \pmod{5}\) is a proposition (Definition: Proposition (statement)), which is true or false.






2 Proof by contrapositive







Exercise 2 (An odd sum) Let \(x\) and \(y\) be integers. Prove: if \(x + y\) is odd, then \(x \ne y\).
First try a direct proof (Definition: Direct proof), starting from “Suppose \(x + y\) is odd.” Then try starting from “Suppose \(x = y\).”










SolutionSolution






Solution 2. The direct start gives \(x + y = 2k + 1\) for some integer \(k\) (Definition: Odd integer), which says little about whether \(x\) and \(y\) are equal.
The second start goes further. Suppose \(x = y\). Then \(x + y = x + x = 2x\), and \(x\) is an integer, so \(x + y\) is even (Definition: Even integer). No integer is both even and odd (Remark: Facts about integers used without proof), so \(x + y\) is not odd.
That proves “if \(x = y\), then \(x + y\) is not odd”. Why proving this proposition proves the one we were asked about is the subject of this section.











Definition 2 (Contrapositive) The contrapositive (Wikipedia contributors 2026a) of the proposition “if \(P\), then \(Q\)” is the proposition “if \(\neg Q\), then \(\neg P\)”.











Example 2 (Contrapositives)  

The contrapositive of “if \(x\) is a human, then \(x\) is a mammal” is “if \(x\) is not a mammal, then \(x\) is not a human”.
In Exercise 2, \(P\) is “\(x + y\) is odd” and \(Q\) is “\(x \ne y\)”. The negation of \(Q\) is “\(x = y\)” (Definition: Not), so the contrapositive is “if \(x = y\), then \(x + y\) is not odd”, which is what Solution 2 proved.












Theorem 1 (A conditional is equivalent to its contrapositive) For any propositions \(P\) and \(Q\),
\[
(P \Rightarrow Q) \equiv (\neg Q \Rightarrow \neg P).
\]










ProofProof






Proof. By the definition of implies, \(P \Rightarrow Q\) is false exactly when \(P\) is true and \(Q\) is false. By the same definition, \(\neg Q \Rightarrow \neg P\) is false exactly when \(\neg Q\) is true and \(\neg P\) is false, that is, exactly when \(Q\) is false and \(P\) is true. So the two propositions are false in the same row of a truth table and true in the other three, which is Definition: Logically equivalent.











Example 3 (A proposition and its contrapositive) Take “if today is Saturday, then today is a weekend day”, which is true.
Its contrapositive is “if today is not a weekend day, then today is not Saturday”. It is also true, as Theorem 1 says it must be: Monday through Friday are the days that are not weekend days, and none of them is Saturday.











Definition 3 (Proof by contrapositive) A proof by contrapositive (Wikipedia contributors 2026a) of a proposition “if \(P\), then \(Q\)” is a direct proof of its contrapositive, “if \(\neg Q\), then \(\neg P\)”: it assumes that \(Q\) is false and reaches the conclusion that \(P\) is false. By Theorem 1, proving the contrapositive proves the original proposition.











Example 4 (A product not divisible by \(5\)) Claim: let \(x\) and \(y\) be integers. If \(5 \nmid xy\), then \(5 \nmid x\) and \(5 \nmid y\).
A direct proof would start from \(5 \nmid xy\), which says only that \(xy\) is not \(5\) times an integer, and gives no equation to work with. By De Morgan’s laws (Theorem: De Morgan’s laws), the negation of “\(5 \nmid x\) and \(5 \nmid y\)” is “\(5 \mid x\) or \(5 \mid y\)”, so the contrapositive (Definition 2) is “if \(5 \mid x\) or \(5 \mid y\), then \(5 \mid xy\)”. We prove it by cases (Definition: Proof by cases).
Case 1: \(5 \mid x\). Then \(x = 5c\) for some integer \(c\) (Definition: Divides), so
\[
\begin{aligned}
xy
&= (5c) y
&& \text{(substitute } x = 5c \text{)}
\\&= 5 (c y),
&& \text{(regroup the product)}
\end{aligned}
\]
and \(c y\) is an integer (Remark: Facts about integers used without proof), so \(5 \mid xy\).
Case 2: \(5 \mid y\). Then \(y = 5d\) for some integer \(d\), so \(xy = x (5d) = 5 (x d)\), and \(x d\) is an integer, so \(5 \mid xy\).
In both cases \(5 \mid xy\), which proves the contrapositive and so the claim (Theorem 1). For example, \(x = 3\) and \(y = 7\) give \(xy = 21\), which \(5\) does not divide, and indeed \(5\) divides neither \(3\) nor \(7\).











Remark 2 (The shape of a proof by contrapositive). A proof by contrapositive (Definition 3) of “if \(P\), then \(Q\)” has this shape:

Suppose \(\neg Q\).
\(\vdots\)
Therefore \(\neg P\).

Use it when \(\neg Q\) gives you more to work with than \(P\) does. In Exercise 2, \(\neg Q\) was the equation \(x = y\), while \(P\) said only that \(x + y\) is odd.











Exercise 3 (A square not divisible by three) Let \(n\) be an integer. Prove: if \(3 \nmid n^2\), then \(3 \nmid n\).










SolutionSolution






Solution 3. We prove the contrapositive (Definition 3): if \(3 \mid n\), then \(3 \mid n^2\).
Suppose \(3 \mid n\). Then \(n = 3c\) for some integer \(c\) (Definition: Divides), so
\[
\begin{aligned}
n^2
&= (3c)^2
&& \text{(substitute } n = 3c \text{)}
\\&= 9 c^2
&& \text{(square each factor)}
\\&= 3 (3 c^2),
&& \text{(write } 9 = 3 \cdot 3 \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
and \(3 c^2\) is an integer (Remark: Facts about integers used without proof), so \(3 \mid n^2\). By Theorem 1, this proves the original proposition.






3 Proof by contradiction







Exercise 4 (No solution in integers) Show that there are no integers \(m\) and \(n\) with \(6m + 9n = 1\).
Hint: suppose there were. What would \(6m + 9n = 1\) say about \(3\) and \(1\)?










SolutionSolution






Solution 4. Suppose there are integers \(m\) and \(n\) with \(6m + 9n = 1\). Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
1
&= 6m + 9n
&& \text{(the assumption, read from right to left)}
\\&= 3 (2m + 3n),
&& \text{(distributive law, read from right to left)}
\end{aligned}
\]
and \(2m + 3n\) is an integer (Remark: Facts about integers used without proof), so \(3 \mid 1\) (Definition: Divides).
But \(3 \nmid 1\): since \(3 \cdot 0 = 0 < 1 < 3 = 3 \cdot 1\), no integer \(c\) has \(3c = 1\). So \(3 \mid 1\) and \(3 \nmid 1\), which is impossible. The assumption must be false, so there are no integers \(m\) and \(n\) with \(6m + 9n = 1\).











Definition 4 (Proof by contradiction) A proof by contradiction (Wikipedia contributors 2026f) of a proposition \(P\) assumes that \(P\) is false, and derives from that assumption a proposition that is known to be false.











Example 5 (No integer is both even and odd) Suppose, for contradiction, that some integer \(n\) is both even and odd (definition). Then \(n = 2j\) and \(n = 2k + 1\) for some integers \(j\) and \(k\), and
\[
\begin{aligned}
2j &= 2k + 1
&& \text{(both equal } n \text{)}
\\
2j - 2k &= 1
&& \text{(subtract } 2k \text{ from both sides)}
\\
2(j - k) &= 1
&& \text{(distributive law)}
\\
j - k &= \tfrac{1}{2}
&& \text{(divide both sides by } 2 \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
The third line uses the distributive law. But \(j - k\) is an integer, and \(\frac{1}{2}\) is not, so the last line is false. So no integer is both even and odd. For example, \(6 = 2 \cdot 3\) is even, and \(6 = 2k + 1\) would need \(k = 2.5\), which is not an integer.











Theorem 2 (Why a proof by contradiction works) For propositions \(P\) and \(C\),
\[
P \equiv \mathopen{}\left(\neg P \Rightarrow (C \land \neg C)\right)\mathclose{}.
\]










ProofProof






Proof. \(C \land \neg C\) is false in every row (Definition: And, Definition: Not), so it is a contradiction (Definition: Contradiction). So, by Definition: Implies, \(\neg P \Rightarrow (C \land \neg C)\) is true exactly in the rows where \(\neg P\) is false, which are the rows where \(P\) is true:

Example 6 (The six and nine proof, read through the theorem) In Solution 4, \(P\) is “there are no integers \(m\) and \(n\) with \(6m + 9n = 1\)”, and \(C\) is “\(3 \mid 1\)”. The solution assumed \(\neg P\), that such integers exist, and derived both \(C\) and \(\neg C\). That proves \(\neg P \Rightarrow (C \land \neg C)\), so, by Theorem 2, it proves \(P\).











Remark 3 (The shape of a proof by contradiction). A proof by contradiction (Definition 4) of a proposition \(P\) has this shape:

Suppose \(\neg P\).
\(\vdots\)
Therefore \(C\) and \(\neg C\).

Two things differ from a proof by contrapositive (Remark 2). \(P\) need not be a conditional. And the proof does not know \(C\) in advance: any proposition \(C\) for which the argument derives both \(C\) and \(\neg C\) will do.











Remark 4 (Proving a conditional by contradiction). To prove “if \(P\), then \(Q\)” by contradiction, suppose its negation, which is “\(P\) and \(\neg Q\)” (Theorem: Negating a conditional):

Suppose \(P\) and \(\neg Q\).
\(\vdots\)
Therefore \(C\) and \(\neg C\).

A proof by contrapositive (Remark 2) assumes only \(\neg Q\), and has the fixed goal \(\neg P\). A proof by contradiction assumes both \(P\) and \(\neg Q\), and any contradiction will do.











Example 7 (A number plus its reciprocal) Claim: let \(x\) be a real number. If \(x > 0\), then \(x + \frac{1}{x} \ge 2\).
Suppose, for contradiction, that \(x > 0\) and \(x + \frac{1}{x} < 2\). Since \(x > 0\), multiplying both sides by \(x\) keeps the inequality, so
\[
\begin{aligned}
x^2 + 1
&< 2x
&& \text{(multiply both sides by } x > 0 \text{)}
\\
x^2 - 2x + 1
&< 0
&& \text{(subtract } 2x \text{ from both sides)}
\\
(x - 1)^2
&< 0.
&& \text{(square of a difference)}
\end{aligned}
\]
Let \(C\) be “\((x - 1)^2 \ge 0\)”. \(C\) is true, because a square of a real number is never negative, and the last line says \(\neg C\). That is a contradiction, so the claim holds. The proof used \(x > 0\) in the first step, and the contradiction it reached is not \(x \le 0\). For example, \(x = 4\) gives \(4 + \frac{1}{4} = 4.25 \ge 2\).











Exercise 5 (Squares one apart) Prove that there are no positive integers \(x\) and \(y\) with \(x^2 - y^2 = 1\).










SolutionSolution






Solution 5. Suppose, for contradiction, that \(x\) and \(y\) are positive integers with \(x^2 - y^2 = 1\). Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
1
&= x^2 - y^2
&& \text{(the assumption, read from right to left)}
\\&= (x - y)(x + y).
&& \text{(difference of squares)}
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(x \ge 1\) and \(y \ge 1\), \(x + y \ge 2\). Dividing both sides by \(x + y\) gives \(x - y = \frac{1}{x + y}\), and \(0 < \frac{1}{x + y} \le \frac{1}{2}\), so \(x - y\) is strictly between \(0\) and \(1\) and is not an integer. But \(x - y\) is an integer (Remark: Facts about integers used without proof). That is a contradiction, so there are no such \(x\) and \(y\).






4 Irrational numbers







Exercise 6 (Bounds on a fraction for \(\sqrt{2}\)) Suppose \(a\) and \(b\) are positive integers with \(\frac{a}{b} = \sqrt{2}\). Use \(1 < 2 < 4\) to show that \(b < a < 2b\).










SolutionSolution






Solution 6. Square roots keep the order of positive numbers, so \(1 < 2 < 4\) gives \(1 < \sqrt{2} < 2\), that is, \(1 < \frac{a}{b} < 2\). Multiplying each part by \(b\), which is positive, keeps the order, and gives \(b < a < 2b\).











Definition 5 (Rational numbers) A rational number (Wikipedia contributors 2026h) is a number that can be written as a fraction \(\frac{a}{b}\), where \(a\) and \(b\) are integers (Definition: Integers) and \(b \ne 0\). The set of rational numbers is written \(\mathbb{Q}\):
\[\mathbb{Q} \stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\mathopen{}\left\{\frac{a}{b} : a \in \mathbb{Z},\ b \in \mathbb{Z},\ b \ne 0\right\}\mathclose{}\]











Example 8 (Rational numbers)  

\(\frac{3}{4}\) is rational, with \(a = 3\) and \(b = 4\).
\(0.75\) is rational, because \(0.75 = \frac{3}{4}\).
Every integer is rational: for example, \(-5 = \frac{-5}{1}\).
\(0.333\ldots\), with the \(3\)s repeating forever, is rational, because \(0.333\ldots = \frac{1}{3}\).












Definition 6 (Irrational numbers) An irrational number (Wikipedia contributors 2026c) is a real number (Definition: Real numbers) that is not rational (Definition 5).











Example 9 (Irrational numbers)  

\(\sqrt{2} = 1.41421\ldots\), the square root of \(2\), is irrational: no fraction of integers \(\frac{a}{b}\) squares to \(2\) (Wikipedia contributors 2026i).
\(\pi = 3.14159\ldots\) is irrational (Wikipedia contributors 2026g).
\(1.5\) is not irrational, because \(1.5 = \frac{3}{2}\) is rational.












Remark 5 (Smallest elements). These notes use one more fact about the integers without proving it (Wikipedia contributors 2026j):

every set of positive integers that has at least one element has a smallest element.

For example, the set of positive integers \(b\) for which \(\frac{3}{4} b\) is an integer has the elements \(4\), \(8\), \(12\) and so on, and its smallest element is \(4\).











Theorem 3 (\(\sqrt{2}\) is irrational) The square root of \(2\) is irrational (Definition 6) (Wikipedia contributors 2026i).










ProofProof






Proof. Suppose, for contradiction, that \(\sqrt{2}\) is rational (Definition 5). Then \(\sqrt{2} = \frac{a}{b}\) for some integers \(a\) and \(b\) with \(b \ne 0\). Since \(\sqrt{2} > 0\), we can take \(a\) and \(b\) positive (if \(b < 0\), replace \(a\) and \(b\) with \(-a\) and \(-b\)). So the set of positive integers \(b\) for which \(\sqrt{2}\, b\) is an integer has an element, and by Remark 5 it has a smallest element. Let \(b\) be that smallest element, and let \(a = \sqrt{2}\, b\), a positive integer.
By Solution 6, \(b < a < 2b\), so \(b' = a - b\) is an integer with \(0 < b' < b\). Let \(a' = 2b - a\), also an integer. Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sqrt{2}\, b'
&= \sqrt{2}\, (a - b)
&& \text{(definition of } b' \text{)}
\\&= \sqrt{2}\, a - \sqrt{2}\, b
&& \text{(distributive law)}
\\&= \sqrt{2}\, \sqrt{2}\, b - a
&& \text{(substitute } a = \sqrt{2}\, b \text{ in the first term, and } \sqrt{2}\, b = a \text{ in the second)}
\\&= 2b - a
&& \text{(} \sqrt{2}\, \sqrt{2} = 2 \text{)}
\\&= a'.
&& \text{(definition of } a' \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
So \(b'\) is a positive integer for which \(\sqrt{2}\, b'\) is an integer, and \(b' < b\). That contradicts the choice of \(b\) as the smallest such integer. So \(\sqrt{2}\) is not rational.











Example 10 (The step in the proof, on a fraction near \(\sqrt{2}\)) The proof of Theorem 3 turns a fraction \(\frac{a}{b}\) into \(\frac{2b - a}{a - b}\). Applied to \(\frac{7}{5} = 1.4\), whose square is \(\frac{49}{25} = 1.96\), it gives \(\frac{10 - 7}{7 - 5} = \frac{3}{2} = 1.5\), whose square is \(\frac{9}{4} = 2.25\). Neither fraction is exactly \(\sqrt{2}\), and the step moved from denominator \(5\) to the smaller denominator \(2\). If some fraction were exactly \(\sqrt{2}\), the step would give another fraction exactly equal to \(\sqrt{2}\), with a smaller positive denominator, and a smallest positive denominator could not exist.






5 Infinitely many primes







Exercise 7 (Which are prime?) Which of \(51\), \(53\) and \(57\) have no positive divisors other than \(1\) and themselves? Hint: try dividing by \(2\), \(3\), \(5\) and \(7\).










SolutionSolution






Solution 7. 

\(51 = 3 \cdot 17\), so \(3\) divides \(51\) (Definition: Divides).
\(57 = 3 \cdot 19\), so \(3\) divides \(57\).
\(53\) is not divisible by \(2\), \(3\), \(5\) or \(7\), because it lies strictly between two multiples of each: \(2 \cdot 26 = 52 < 53 < 54 = 2 \cdot 27\), \(3 \cdot 17 = 51 < 53 < 54 = 3 \cdot 18\), \(5 \cdot 10 = 50 < 53 < 55 = 5 \cdot 11\), and \(7 \cdot 7 = 49 < 53 < 56 = 7 \cdot 8\). A divisor \(d\) of \(53\) with \(1 < d < 53\) would pair with \(\frac{53}{d}\), and one of the two would be at most \(7\), because \(8 \cdot 8 = 64 > 53\). It would be one of \(2, \ldots, 7\), and \(4\) or \(6\) would make \(2\) a divisor too, since \(2\) divides both (Exercise: Divisors of divisors). So \(53\) has no positive divisors other than \(1\) and \(53\).












Definition 7 (Prime number) An integer \(n \ge 2\) is prime if its only positive divisors (Definition: Divides) are \(1\) and \(n\) (Wikipedia contributors 2026e).











Example 11 (Prime and not prime)  

\(2\), \(3\), \(5\), \(7\), \(11\) and \(13\) are prime.
\(9\) is not prime, because \(3 \mid 9\), and \(3\) is neither \(1\) nor \(9\).
\(1\) is not prime, because Definition 7 applies only to integers \(n \ge 2\).












Remark 6 (Every integer above one has a prime divisor). These notes use one more fact without proving it:

every integer \(n \ge 2\) is divisible by at least one prime (Definition 7).

For example, \(91\) is divisible by the primes \(7\) and \(13\), since \(91 = 7 \cdot 13\).











Theorem 4 (There are infinitely many primes) There are infinitely many prime numbers (Definition 7) (Wikipedia contributors 2026b).










ProofProof






Proof. Suppose, for contradiction, that there are only finitely many primes, and list them all as \(p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_k\). The list is not empty, because \(2\) is prime. Let
\[
N = p_1 p_2 \cdots p_k + 1.
\]
Each \(p_i \ge 2\), so \(N \ge 3\), and by Remark 6 some prime \(p\) divides \(N\): \(N = p s\) for some integer \(s\). The list holds every prime, so \(p\) is one of \(p_1, \ldots, p_k\), and so \(p\) also divides their product: \(p_1 p_2 \cdots p_k = p t\) for some integer \(t\). Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
1
&= N - p_1 p_2 \cdots p_k
&& \text{(definition of } N \text{)}
\\&= p s - p t
&& \text{(substitute both products)}
\\&= p (s - t).
&& \text{(distributive law, read from right to left)}
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(s - t\) is an integer (Remark: Facts about integers used without proof), \(p \mid 1\). But \(p \ge 2\), and \(p \cdot 0 = 0 < 1 < p = p \cdot 1\), so no integer \(c\) has \(p c = 1\), and \(p \nmid 1\). That is a contradiction, so there are infinitely many primes.











Example 12 (The number \(N\) in the proof) The proof of Theorem 4 does not claim that \(N\) is prime.

From the list \(2, 3, 5\), \(N = 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 + 1 = 31\), which is prime.
From the list \(2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13\), \(N = 30030 + 1 = 30031 = 59 \cdot 509\), which is not prime. Its prime divisors \(59\) and \(509\) are not in the list, which is what the proof needs: every list of primes misses some prime.







6 Choosing a method







Remark 7 (Which method to try). 

Try a direct proof (Definition: Direct proof) first.
Try the contrapositive (Definition 3) when \(\neg Q\) is the easier assumption (Remark 2).
Try contradiction (Definition 4) when the proposition says that something does not exist or is not true, as in “no integers satisfy”, “is irrational” or “infinitely many”: its negation hands you an object to work with.

Definition 1 (Logical equivalence) Two propositions \(A\) and \(B\), each built from some of the propositions \(P_1, \ldots, P_n\), are logically equivalent, written \(A \equiv B\), if they have the same truth value in every row of a truth table (Definition: Truth table), that is, for every combination of truth values of \(P_1, \ldots, P_n\).











Example 1 (An equivalence) By Exercise 1, \(P \lor (P \land Q) \equiv P\) (Definition 1): the truth table of \(P \lor (P \land Q)\) has the same column as \(P\), in a table with columns for both \(P\) and \(Q\).











Remark 1 (Notation for logical equivalence). \(A \equiv B\) (Definition 1) is a claim about \(A\) and \(B\), not a new proposition built from them with a logical connective (Definition: Logical connective). Some books write \(A \Leftrightarrow B\) or \(A \iff B\) for it instead, which is easy to confuse with the biconditional (Definition: If and only if); these notes use \(\equiv\).
Logical equivalence can be chained: if \(A \equiv B\) and \(B \equiv C\), then \(A \equiv C\), since in each row \(A\) has the value of \(B\), which has the value of \(C\).

Theorem 1 (Equivalence is a tautological biconditional) For propositions \(A\) and \(B\), \(A \equiv B\) (Definition 1) exactly when \(A \Leftrightarrow B\) is a tautology (Definition 2).










ProofProof






Proof. By Definition: If and only if, \(A \Leftrightarrow B\) is true in a row of the truth table exactly when \(A\) and \(B\) have the same truth value in that row. So \(A \Leftrightarrow B\) is true in every row exactly when \(A\) and \(B\) have the same truth value in every row, which is what \(A \equiv B\) means.











Example 4 (An equivalence as a tautology) Since \(P \lor (P \land Q) \equiv P\) (Example 1), Theorem 1 says that \((P \lor (P \land Q)) \Leftrightarrow P\) is a tautology.

Example 5 (Distributing “and”) For an integer \(x\), “\(x\) is even, and \(x > 0\) or \(x < 0\)” is logically equivalent, by law 1 of Theorem 2, to “\(x\) is even and \(x > 0\), or \(x\) is even and \(x < 0\)”.











Remark 3 (Checking an equivalence in Racket). A truth table is a loop over every combination of truth values, so a program can check an equivalence. In Racket, for*/and runs its body for every combination of p and q, and returns #f as soon as the body returns #f, and #t if it never does:
(for*/and ([p '(#t #f)]
           [q '(#t #f)])
  (equal? (or p (and p q)) p))
This returns #t, as Exercise 1 found. Replacing the body with (equal? (not (and p q)) (and (not p) (not q))) returns #f, as Exercise 2 found.

Exercise 4 (When is the door locked?) A door opens when the badge is valid, the PIN is correct, and it is a weekday. Let \(B\) be “the badge is valid”, \(N\) be “the PIN is correct” and \(W\) be “it is a weekday”, so the door stays locked when \(\neg (B \land N \land W)\) is true.
Describe when the door stays locked with a sentence that puts “not” only in front of \(B\), \(N\) or \(W\), never in front of a compound proposition.










SolutionSolution






Solution 4. The door stays locked when the badge is not valid, the PIN is not correct, or it is not a weekday: \(\neg B \lor \neg N \lor \neg W\). \(B \land N \land W\) is false exactly when at least one of \(B\), \(N\) and \(W\) is false.











Theorem 3 (Double negation) For a proposition \(P\), \(\neg \neg P \equiv P\) (Definition 1).










ProofProof

Example 6 (Not unreadable) “It is not the case that the file is not readable” means “the file is readable” (Theorem 3).











Theorem 4 (Replacing a part by an equivalent part) If \(A \equiv B\) (Definition 1), then replacing \(A\) by \(B\) inside a larger proposition gives a proposition logically equivalent to the larger one. In particular, \(\neg A \equiv \neg B\).










ProofProof






Proof. The truth value of the larger proposition in a row of its truth table depends on the truth value of \(A\) in that row, not on how \(A\) is written. \(A\) and \(B\) have the same truth value in every row, so the two larger propositions do too.











Example 7 (Replacing a part) Since \(P \lor (P \land Q) \equiv P\) (Example 1), Theorem 4 gives \(R \land (P \lor (P \land Q)) \equiv R \land P\) and \(\neg (P \lor (P \land Q)) \equiv \neg P\).

\(\neg (P \land Q) \equiv \neg P \lor \neg Q\);
\(\neg (P \lor Q) \equiv \neg P \land \neg Q\).

Law 2 follows from law 1. Law 1 holds for any two propositions, so it holds for \(\neg P\) and \(\neg Q\): \[
\neg (\neg P \land \neg Q) \equiv \neg \neg P \lor \neg \neg Q.
\] By double negation (Theorem 3) and Theorem 4, the right side is logically equivalent to \(P \lor Q\), so \[
\neg (\neg P \land \neg Q) \equiv P \lor Q.
\] Negating both sides (Theorem 4) gives \[
\neg \neg (\neg P \land \neg Q) \equiv \neg (P \lor Q),
\] and by double negation the left side is logically equivalent to \(\neg P \land \neg Q\). So \(\neg (P \lor Q) \equiv \neg P \land \neg Q\).











Example 8 (Neither coordinate positive) For real numbers \(x\) and \(y\), by law 2 of Theorem 5, “not (\(x > 0\) or \(y > 0\))” is logically equivalent to “\(x \le 0\) and \(y \le 0\)”.











Exercise 5 (A broken deployment rule) A team’s rule is “if the tests pass, then the build is deployed”. Let \(P\) be “the tests pass” and \(Q\) be “the build is deployed”. The rule is broken on the days when \(\neg (P \Rightarrow Q)\) is true.
Write \(\neg (P \Rightarrow Q)\) without \(\Rightarrow\), and in English.










SolutionSolution






Solution 5. The rule is broken on a day when the tests pass and the build is not deployed: \(P \land \neg Q\). On a day when the tests fail, the rule is not broken, whether or not the build is deployed.
“If the tests pass, then the build is not deployed”, \(P \Rightarrow \neg Q\), is not the negation: on a day when the tests fail, it is true, and so is the rule.











Theorem 6 (Negating a conditional) For propositions \(P\) and \(Q\), \(\neg (P \Rightarrow Q) \equiv P \land \neg Q\).










ProofProof






Proof. By Definition: Implies, \(P \Rightarrow Q\) is false exactly when \(P\) is true and \(Q\) is false, so \(\neg (P \Rightarrow Q)\) is true exactly in that row. \(P \land \neg Q\) is true exactly when \(P\) is true and \(\neg Q\) is true, which is the same row.











Example 9 (When a search claim fails) The negation of “if the list is sorted, then binary search finds the key” is “the list is sorted and binary search does not find the key” (Theorem 6).











Corollary 1 (A conditional without the arrow) For propositions \(P\) and \(Q\), \(P \Rightarrow Q \equiv \neg P \lor Q\).










ProofProof






Proof. By double negation (Theorem 3), \(P \Rightarrow Q \equiv \neg \neg (P \Rightarrow Q)\). By Theorem 6 and Theorem 4, \(\neg \neg (P \Rightarrow Q) \equiv \neg (P \land \neg Q)\). By De Morgan’s law 1 (Theorem 5), \(\neg (P \land \neg Q) \equiv \neg P \lor \neg \neg Q\), and by double negation again, that is logically equivalent to \(\neg P \lor Q\).











Example 10 (A rule as an “or”) By Corollary 1, “if the tests pass, then the build is deployed” is logically equivalent to “the tests fail or the build is deployed”.






3 Negating quantified propositions







Exercise 6 (Not every test passes) Let \(T\) be the set of tests in a test suite, and let \(P(t)\) be “test \(t\) passes”. The report “every test passes” is \(\forall t \in T, P(t)\).
Write the negation of this report in English and in symbols, without putting \(\neg\) in front of a quantifier.










SolutionSolution






Solution 6. “Some test fails”: \(\exists t \in T, \neg P(t)\). “Every test passes” is false exactly when at least one test does not pass.
“Every test fails”, \(\forall t \in T, \neg P(t)\), is not the negation: when some tests pass and some fail, both it and “every test passes” are false.











Theorem 7 (Negating a quantifier) For a set \(S\) and a predicate \(P(x)\) (Definition: Predicate) whose domain (Definition: Domain (domain of discourse, universe of discourse)) is \(S\):

\(\neg (\forall x \in S, P(x))\) and \(\exists x \in S, \neg P(x)\) have the same truth value;
\(\neg (\exists x \in S, P(x))\) and \(\forall x \in S, \neg P(x)\) have the same truth value.











ProofProof






Proof. 

By Definition: Universal quantifier, \(\forall x \in S, P(x)\) is false exactly when \(P(x)\) is false for at least one \(x\) in \(S\), which by Definition: Existential quantifier is when \(\exists x \in S, \neg P(x)\) is true.
By Definition: Existential quantifier, \(\exists x \in S, P(x)\) is false exactly when \(P(x)\) is false for every \(x\) in \(S\), which by Definition: Universal quantifier is when \(\forall x \in S, \neg P(x)\) is true.












Example 11 (No natural square root of 2) By part 2 of Theorem 7, \(\neg (\exists n \in \mathbb{N}, n^2 = 2)\) has the same truth value as \(\forall n \in \mathbb{N}, n^2 \ne 2\).











Remark 4 (De Morgan’s laws for quantifiers). Theorem 7 is often written \(\neg \forall x, P(x) \equiv \exists x, \neg P(x)\) and \(\neg \exists x, P(x) \equiv \forall x, \neg P(x)\). These notes say “has the same truth value” instead, because \(P(x)\) is a predicate, not a proposition, so Definition 1, which compares truth tables, does not apply.
On a finite set \(S = \{a, b\}\), \(\forall x \in S, P(x)\) has the same truth value as \(P(a) \land P(b)\), and \(\exists x \in S, P(x)\) has the same truth value as \(P(a) \lor P(b)\), so Theorem 7 is De Morgan’s laws (Theorem 5) applied to \(P(a)\) and \(P(b)\).
Racket shows the same pattern on a list: (not (andmap even? (list 2 4 5))) and (ormap odd? (list 2 4 5)) both return #t.











Remark 5 (Pushing a negation inward). To negate a proposition built with \(\neg\), \(\land\), \(\lor\), \(\Rightarrow\) and quantifiers, move the \(\neg\) inward one step at a time:

across a quantifier, with Theorem 7, which swaps \(\forall\) and \(\exists\);
across \(\land\) or \(\lor\), with De Morgan’s laws (Theorem 5);
across \(\Rightarrow\), with Theorem 6;
across another \(\neg\), with double negation (Theorem 3).

Stop when every \(\neg\) sits in front of a proposition with no connective or quantifier inside it. The result is easier to read and to check than a \(\neg\) in front of the whole proposition.











Exercise 7 (Completing a palindrome) Let \(W\) be the set of words made of the letters a and b, including the empty word, and write \(s t\) for word \(s\) followed by word \(t\). A palindrome is a word that reads the same forwards and backwards, such as abba.
Write the negation of \[
\forall s \in W,\ \exists t \in W,\ s t \text{ is a palindrome}
\] without putting \(\neg\) in front of a quantifier.










SolutionSolution






Solution 7. Apply Theorem 7 twice, from the outside in. First, the negation has the truth value of \[
\exists s \in W,\ \neg (\exists t \in W,\ s t \text{ is a palindrome}).
\] For each word \(s\), Theorem 7 says that \(\neg (\exists t \in W,\ s t \text{ is a palindrome})\) has the truth value of \(\forall t \in W,\ s t \text{ is not a palindrome}\). These have the same truth value for every \(s\), so the \(\exists s\) propositions built from them do too (Definition: Existential quantifier), and the negation has the truth value of \[
\exists s \in W,\ \forall t \in W,\ s t \text{ is not a palindrome}.
\] In English: some word cannot be made into a palindrome by adding letters at its end.











Exercise 8 (Which one is true?) Which is true: \(\forall s \in W,\ \exists t \in W,\ s t \text{ is a palindrome}\), from Exercise 7, or its negation?










SolutionSolution






Solution 8. The original is true, so its negation is false. For any word \(s\), let \(t\) be \(s\) written backwards; then \(s t\) reads the same backwards. For example, for \(s = \text{aab}\), \(t = \text{baa}\) and \(s t = \text{aabbaa}\).

Adapted from Kameron Decker Harris’s Fall 2026 lecture notes “Induction” and “More Induction!”, which are typed transcriptions of Scott Wehrwein’s Spring 2025 handwritten lecture notes. These come from those notes:

the names of the parts of a proof by induction: base case, induction hypothesis and inductive step;
the comparison of ordinary and strong induction;
the chocolate bar example of strong induction, with its proof;
the false claim that all horses are the same color, and where an induction proof of it fails.

The exercises, the other examples and the text of the false proof are new.




1 Proof by induction







Exercise 1 (Adding unit fractions of neighbors) Consider the claim that for every natural number (Definition: Natural numbers (our convention)) \(n\),
\[
\frac{1}{1 \cdot 2} + \frac{1}{2 \cdot 3} + \cdots + \frac{1}{n(n + 1)} = \frac{n}{n + 1}.
\]

Check the claim for \(n = 1\), \(n = 2\) and \(n = 3\).
Suppose the claim holds for some natural number \(k\). Add the next term, \(\frac{1}{(k + 1)(k + 2)}\), to both sides, and show that the claim then holds for \(k + 1\).











SolutionSolution






Solution 1. 

For \(n = 1\), the left side is \(\frac{1}{2}\) and the right side is \(\frac{1}{2}\). For \(n = 2\), the left side is \(\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{6} = \frac{2}{3}\) and the right side is \(\frac{2}{3}\). For \(n = 3\), the left side is \(\frac{2}{3} + \frac{1}{12} = \frac{3}{4}\) and the right side is \(\frac{3}{4}\).
Suppose \(\frac{1}{1 \cdot 2} + \cdots + \frac{1}{k(k + 1)} = \frac{k}{k + 1}\). Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{1}{1 \cdot 2} + \cdots + \frac{1}{k(k + 1)} + \frac{1}{(k + 1)(k + 2)}
\\&= \frac{k}{k + 1} + \frac{1}{(k + 1)(k + 2)}
&& \text{(the supposition)}
\\&= \frac{k(k + 2) + 1}{(k + 1)(k + 2)}
&& \text{(common denominator)}
\\&= \frac{k^2 + 2k + 1}{(k + 1)(k + 2)}
\\&= \frac{(k + 1)^2}{(k + 1)(k + 2)}
&& \text{(} k^2 + 2k + 1 = (k + 1)^2 \text{)}
\\&= \frac{k + 1}{k + 2},
&& \text{(cancel } k + 1 \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
which is the claim for \(k + 1\).

Part 1 shows the claim for \(n = 1\), and part 2 carries it from each natural number to the next, so it holds for \(n = 2, 3, 4, \ldots\) in turn.











Definition 1 (Proof by induction) Let \(n_0\) be an integer, and let \(P(n)\) be a predicate about the integers \(n \ge n_0\). A proof by induction (Wikipedia contributors 2026b) on \(n\) shows that \(P(n)\) holds for every integer \(n \ge n_0\) by showing two things:

Base case: \(P(n_0)\) holds.
Inductive step: for every integer \(n > n_0\), if \(P(n - 1)\) holds, then \(P(n)\) holds.

In the inductive step, the assumption that \(P(n - 1)\) holds is called the induction hypothesis.











Remark 1 (Stepping from \(k\) to \(k + 1\)). Definition 1 states the inductive step as “if \(P(n - 1)\), then \(P(n)\), for every \(n > n_0\)”. Many sources, and part 2 of Solution 1, state it as “if \(P(k)\), then \(P(k + 1)\), for every \(k \ge n_0\)”. The two say the same thing, with \(k = n - 1\), and the rest of this chapter uses the second form.
Writing the goal \(P(k + 1)\) correctly is a common place to go wrong: replace every \(n\) in \(P(n)\) with \(k + 1\), including in the last term of a sum and on the other side of the equation.











Remark 2 (The shape of a proof by induction). A proof by induction that \(P(n)\) holds for every integer \(n \ge n_0\) has two parts:

Base case. Show \(P(n_0)\).

Inductive step. Let \(k \ge n_0\) be an integer, and suppose \(P(k)\).
\(\vdots\)
Therefore \(P(k + 1)\).

So \(P(n)\) holds for every integer \(n \ge n_0\), by induction.

Write out the induction hypothesis \(P(k)\) and the goal \(P(k + 1)\) before starting the step, and mark the line where the step uses the hypothesis.











Example 1 (A sum of products of neighbors) Claim: for every natural number \(n\),
\[
1 \cdot 2 + 2 \cdot 3 + \cdots + n(n + 1) = \frac{n(n + 1)(n + 2)}{3}.
\]
Let \(P(n)\) be this equation, and follow Remark 2 with \(n_0 = 1\).
Base case. For \(n = 1\), the left side is \(1 \cdot 2 = 2\) and the right side is \(\frac{1 \cdot 2 \cdot 3}{3} = 2\).
Inductive step. Let \(k \ge 1\), and suppose \(P(k)\):
\[
1 \cdot 2 + \cdots + k(k + 1) = \frac{k(k + 1)(k + 2)}{3}.
\]
The goal \(P(k + 1)\) is
\[
1 \cdot 2 + \cdots + k(k + 1) + (k + 1)(k + 2) = \frac{(k + 1)(k + 2)(k + 3)}{3}.
\]
Starting from its left side,
\[
\begin{aligned}
& 1 \cdot 2 + \cdots + k(k + 1) + (k + 1)(k + 2)
\\&= \frac{k(k + 1)(k + 2)}{3} + (k + 1)(k + 2)
&& \text{(induction hypothesis)}
\\&= \frac{k(k + 1)(k + 2) + 3(k + 1)(k + 2)}{3}
&& \text{(common denominator)}
\\&= \frac{(k + 1)(k + 2)(k + 3)}{3}.
&& \text{(factor out } (k + 1)(k + 2) \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
So \(P(k + 1)\) holds, and by induction \(P(n)\) holds for every natural number \(n\).






2 Starting at another integer







Exercise 2 (When does \(2^n\) catch up with \(n^2\)?) Compare \(n^2\) with \(2^n\) for \(n = 1, 2, \ldots, 6\). Find the smallest natural number \(n_0\) such that \(n^2 \le 2^n\) holds for \(n_0\) and for every \(n\) you checked after it.

Example 2 (An induction that starts at 4) Claim: \(n^2 \le 2^n\) for every integer (Definition: Integers) \(n \ge 4\).
Let \(P(n)\) be the inequality \(n^2 \le 2^n\) (Definition: Inequality), and follow Remark 2 with \(n_0 = 4\). Solution 2 shows that \(n_0 = 1\) would not work, since \(P(3)\) is false.
Base case. \(4^2 = 16 \le 16 = 2^4\).
Inductive step. Let \(k \ge 4\), and suppose \(k^2 \le 2^k\). The goal is \((k + 1)^2 \le 2^{k + 1}\). Since \(k \ge 4\), we have \(k^2 \ge 4k = 2k + 2k \ge 2k + 8 > 2k + 1\). So
\[
\begin{aligned}
(k + 1)^2
&= k^2 + 2k + 1
\\&< k^2 + k^2
&& \text{(} 2k + 1 < k^2 \text{)}
\\&= 2k^2
\\&\le 2 \cdot 2^k
&& \text{(induction hypothesis)}
\\&= 2^{k + 1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
So \(P(k + 1)\) holds, and by induction \(n^2 \le 2^n\) for every integer \(n \ge 4\). The inductive step works for every \(k \ge 3\), since \(2k + 1 < k^2\) already holds at \(k = 3\). The induction starts at 4 because of the base case: \(P(3)\) is false.






3 Strong induction







Exercise 3 (Breaking a chocolate bar) A chocolate bar is a row of \(n\) squares. One break splits one piece into two pieces along a line between squares. How many breaks does it take to split a bar of 1, 2, 3 or 4 squares into single squares? Does the answer depend on where you break first?










SolutionSolution






Solution 3. A bar of 1 square takes 0 breaks, 2 squares take 1, 3 squares take 2, and 4 squares take 3. For 4 squares, breaking first in the middle gives two pieces of 2 squares, which take 1 break each, for \(1 + 1 + 1 = 3\) breaks; breaking first at one end gives pieces of 1 and 3 squares, which take 0 and 2 breaks, for \(1 + 0 + 2 = 3\) breaks. For these bars, the answer does not depend on where you break first.











Definition 2 (Proof by strong induction) Let \(n_0\) be an integer, and let \(P(n)\) be a predicate about the integers \(n \ge n_0\). A proof by strong induction (Wikipedia contributors 2026b) on \(n\) shows that \(P(n)\) holds for every integer \(n \ge n_0\) by showing one thing: for every integer \(n \ge n_0\), if \(P(k)\) holds for every integer \(k\) with \(n_0 \le k < n\), then \(P(n)\) holds.
The assumption that \(P(k)\) holds for every integer \(k\) with \(n_0 \le k < n\) is the strong induction hypothesis.
For \(n = n_0\) no integer \(k\) satisfies \(n_0 \le k < n\), so the strong induction hypothesis is vacuously true, and the proof for \(n = n_0\) is a base case. When the proof for \(n\) needs particular earlier cases that do not exist for the first few \(n\), those few cases are shown separately as further base cases.











Theorem 1 (Breaking a chocolate bar takes one break fewer than its squares) For every natural number (Definition: Natural numbers (our convention)) \(n\), splitting a bar of chocolate, a row of \(n\) squares, into single squares takes exactly \(n - 1\) breaks, however the breaks are made.










ProofProof






Proof. We use strong induction (Definition 2). Let \(P(n)\) be the claim for a bar of \(n\) squares, let \(n\) be a natural number, and suppose \(P(k)\) holds for every natural number \(k < n\).
If \(n = 1\), the bar is already a single square, so it takes \(0 = n - 1\) breaks.
If \(n \ge 2\), the first break splits the bar into two pieces of \(a\) and \(b\) squares, with \(a + b = n\), \(a \ge 1\) and \(b \ge 1\), so \(a < n\) and \(b < n\). Each later break splits a single piece, so it falls inside one of these two pieces, and the later breaks are the breaks of the \(a\)-square piece together with the breaks of the \(b\)-square piece. By the strong induction hypothesis, the piece of \(a\) squares takes \(a - 1\) breaks and the piece of \(b\) squares takes \(b - 1\) breaks. So the whole bar takes
\[
\begin{aligned}
1 + (a - 1) + (b - 1)
&= a + b - 1
\\&= n - 1
\end{aligned}
\]
breaks.











Remark 3 (Why the proof needs strong induction). The proof of Theorem 1 uses \(P(a)\) and \(P(b)\), where \(a\) and \(b\) can be any sizes smaller than \(n\), not only \(n - 1\). Ordinary induction gives only \(P(n - 1)\) in the step. Strong induction gives \(P(k)\) for every \(k < n\), which is what the proof needs.











Definition 3 (Recursively defined sequence) Let \(n_0\) be an integer and \(m\) a positive integer. A sequence \(a_{n_0}, a_{n_0 + 1}, \ldots\) is recursively defined (Wikipedia contributors 2026c) by two things:

Initial terms: specific values for \(a_{n_0}, \ldots, a_{n_0 + m - 1}\).
Recurrence: a rule that gives \(a_n\) from the \(m\) entries \(a_{n-1}, \ldots, a_{n-m}\) just before it, for every integer \(n \ge n_0 + m\).

The initial terms and the recurrence together fix every term: the first \(m\) entries are given, and each later entry follows from the \(m\) entries before it.











Example 3 (Powers of 3) The sequence \(a_0, a_1, \ldots\) with initial term \(a_0 = 1\) and recurrence \(a_n = 3 a_{n-1}\) for \(n \ge 1\) has \(m = 1\), and its terms are \(1, 3, 9, 27, \ldots\) A proof by induction shows \(a_n = 3^n\) for every integer \(n \ge 0\), using the recurrence in the inductive step: if \(a_{n-1} = 3^{n-1}\), then \(a_n = 3 \cdot 3^{n-1} = 3^n\).











Definition 4 (Fibonacci sequence) The Fibonacci sequence \(F_1, F_2, \ldots\) (Wikipedia contributors 2026a) is the recursively defined sequence with \(m = 2\), initial terms \(F_1 = 1\) and \(F_2 = 1\), and recurrence \(F_n = F_{n-1} + F_{n-2}\) for every integer \(n \ge 3\).











Example 4 (The first Fibonacci numbers) \(F_3 = F_2 + F_1 = 1 + 1 = 2\), \(F_4 = F_3 + F_2 = 2 + 1 = 3\), \(F_5 = F_4 + F_3 = 3 + 2 = 5\), and \(F_6 = F_5 + F_4 = 5 + 3 = 8\). So the sequence begins \(1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, \ldots\)











Example 5 (Every term of the Fibonacci sequence is less than a power of 2) Let \(F_1, F_2, \ldots\) be the Fibonacci sequence. To prove \(F_n < 2^n\) for every \(n \in \mathbb{N}\), let \(P(n)\) be the inequality \(F_n < 2^n\) and use Definition 2 with \(n_0 = 1\).
Base cases, \(n = 1\) and \(n = 2\). The step below uses the two entries \(F_{n-1}\) and \(F_{n-2}\) before \(F_n\), which do not exist for \(n = 1\) and \(n = 2\), so these two cases are shown directly:
\[
\begin{aligned}
F_1 &= 1 < 2 = 2^1
&& \text{(} 1 < 2 \text{)}
\\
F_2 &= 1 < 4 = 2^2.
&& \text{(} 1 < 4 \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
Step of the strong induction, \(n \ge 3\). Let \(n \ge 3\), and suppose \(P(k)\) holds for every integer \(k\) with \(1 \le k < n\). Then \(k = n - 1\) and \(k = n - 2\) both satisfy \(1 \le k < n\), so \(F_{n-1} < 2^{n-1}\) and \(F_{n-2} < 2^{n-2}\). Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
F_n
&= F_{n-1} + F_{n-2}
&& \text{(definition of } F_n \text{, since } n \ge 3 \text{)}
\\
&< 2^{n-1} + 2^{n-2}
&& \text{(strong induction hypothesis, twice)}
\\
&< 2^{n-1} + 2^{n-1}
&& \text{(} 2^{n-2} < 2^{n-1} \text{)}
\\
&= 2 \cdot 2^{n-1}
&& \text{(} a + a = 2a \text{)}
\\
&= 2^n,
&& \text{(} 2 \cdot 2^{n-1} = 2^n \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
which is \(P(n)\). By Definition 2, \(F_n < 2^n\) for every \(n \in \mathbb{N}\).






4 A proof by induction that fails







Example 6 (A proof by induction that fails) Claim (false): in every group of \(n \ge 1\) horses, all the horses are the same color.
“Proof”:

Base case. A group of 1 horse has only one color.
Inductive step. Suppose every group of \(k\) horses is all one color, and take a group of \(k + 1\) horses. Leaving out the first horse leaves \(k\) horses, which are all one color, and leaving out the last horse leaves \(k\) horses, which are all one color. The horses in the middle are in both groups, so the two colors are the same, and all \(k + 1\) horses are one color.

The inductive step fails for \(k = 1\): a group of 2 horses splits into two groups of 1 horse with no horse in both, so nothing links the two colors. So \(P(1)\) does not imply \(P(2)\), and the chain of implications breaks at its first link. An inductive step has to work for every \(k \ge n_0\), including the smallest.
