text:
NoteSource





Adapted from Kameron Decker Harris’s Fall 2026 lecture notes “Logic 2” and “Logic 3”, which are typed transcriptions of Scott Wehrwein’s Spring 2025 handwritten lecture notes. The convention that a conditional about a variable means “for all” comes from those notes; the exercises are new.
The definitions are included from the mathematics prerequisites notes, so they read the same in both places.




1 Predicates







Exercise 1 (Plug in a value) Let \(L(s)\) be the sentence “the string \(s\) has more than 3 characters”.

Is \(L(s)\) true or false?
What are the truth values of \(L(\texttt{"cat"})\), \(L(\texttt{"logic"})\) and \(L(\texttt{""})\)?











SolutionSolution






Solution 1. 

Neither: \(L(s)\) has no truth value until we know which string \(s\) is. It is a predicate (Definition: Predicate), not a proposition (Definition: Proposition (statement)).
Each value of \(s\) turns \(L(s)\) into a proposition:

\(L(\texttt{"cat"})\) is false, since "cat" has 3 characters.
\(L(\texttt{"logic"})\) is true, since "logic" has 5 characters.
\(L(\texttt{""})\) is false, since the empty string has 0 characters.













Definition 1 (Domain (domain of discourse, universe of discourse)) The domain of a predicate (Definition: Predicate), also called its domain of discourse or universe of discourse, is the set of values its variable may take.











Remark 1 (Predicates with more than one variable). A predicate can have more than one variable: “\(x < y\)” is a predicate \(P(x, y)\) in the two variables \(x\) and \(y\). Its domain (Definition 1) is a set of pairs, such as the pairs \((x, y)\) of real numbers.











Remark 2 (Predicates in Racket). A Racket procedure that returns #t or #f is also called a predicate, and by convention its name ends in ?, as in even? and string?. The predicate \(L(s)\) from Exercise 1 is
(define (long? s)
  (> (string-length s) 3))
and (long? "logic") returns #t.






2 Quantifiers







Exercise 2 (All or some) Let \(S = \{2, 3, 5, 7\}\). Which of these four sentences are true?

Every element of \(S\) is prime.
Every element of \(S\) is odd.
Some element of \(S\) is even.
Some element of \(S\) is greater than 10.











SolutionSolution






Solution 2. 

True: \(2\), \(3\), \(5\) and \(7\) are all prime.
False: \(2\) is not odd. One element that fails is enough.
True: \(2\) is even. One element that works is enough.
False: none of \(2\), \(3\), \(5\) and \(7\) is greater than \(10\).












Definition 2 (Quantifier) A quantifier (Wikipedia contributors 2026c) turns a predicate \(P(x)\) (Definition: Predicate) about the elements \(x\) of a set \(S\) into a proposition (Definition: Proposition (statement)). There are two, each defined next: the universal quantifier and the existential quantifier. 











Definition 3 (Universal quantifier) The universal quantifier (Wikipedia contributors 2026d) “for all” is a quantifier (Definition 2): \(\forall x \in S, P(x)\) (“for every \(x\) in \(S\), \(P(x)\)”) is true when \(P(x)\) is true for every element \(x\) of \(S\), and false otherwise.











Definition 4 (Existential quantifier) The existential quantifier (Wikipedia contributors 2026b) “there exists” is a quantifier (Definition 2): \(\exists x \in S, P(x)\) (“there is an \(x\) in \(S\) such that \(P(x)\)”) is true when \(P(x)\) is true for at least one element \(x\) of \(S\), and false otherwise.











Remark 3 (Reading and writing quantifiers). English has many phrasings of each quantifier:

\(\forall\): “for all”, “for every”, “for each”, “for any”, “every”, “all”.
\(\exists\): “there exists”, “there is”, “for some”, “some”, “at least one”.

Books also differ in punctuation: \(\forall x \in S, P(x)\) is also written \(\forall x \in S : P(x)\), \((\forall x \in S)\, P(x)\), or \(\forall x \in S .\, P(x)\). When the domain is clear, it is often left out, as in \(\forall x, P(x)\).











Remark 4 (Quantifiers in Racket). On a finite list, Racket computes the two quantifiers with andmap and ormap. (andmap odd? (list 2 3 5 7)) returns #f, as in part 2 of Exercise 2, and (ormap even? (list 2 3 5 7)) returns #t, as in part 3.











Exercise 3 (Nothing to check) Let \(\emptyset\) be the empty set, the set with no elements. What are the truth values of \(\forall x \in \emptyset, x > 5\) and \(\exists x \in \emptyset, x > 5\)?






TipHint



What would make each one false?












SolutionSolution






Solution 3. \(\forall x \in \emptyset, x > 5\) is true. It would be false only if some element of \(\emptyset\) were not greater than \(5\), and \(\emptyset\) has no elements.
\(\exists x \in \emptyset, x > 5\) is false, since \(\emptyset\) has no element at all, let alone one greater than \(5\).
Racket agrees: (andmap positive? '()) returns #t, and (ormap positive? '()) returns #f.











Definition 5 (Vacuous truth) A universally quantified proposition \(\forall x \in S, P(x)\) whose domain \(S\) is empty is vacuously true: it is true, because \(S\) has no element \(x\) for which \(P(x)\) could be false.






3 Counterexamples







Exercise 4 (A pattern that breaks) Consider the claim “for every integer \(n \ge 0\), \(n^2 + n + 41\) is prime”.

Check the claim for \(n = 0, 1, 2, 3\).
Find an integer \(n \ge 0\) for which the claim fails.







TipHint



Look for an \(n\) that makes every term of \(n^2 + n + 41\) a multiple of \(41\).












SolutionSolution






Solution 4. 

The values are \(41\), \(43\), \(47\) and \(53\), which are all prime.
Take \(n = 41\): \(41^2 + 41 + 41 = 41 \cdot (41 + 1 + 1) = 41 \cdot 43\), which is not prime. The value \(n = 40\) also fails: \(40^2 + 40 + 41 = 1681 = 41^2\).

The claim held for every value we checked in part 1, and it is still false: checking some cases cannot prove a universal claim.











Definition 6 (Counterexample) A counterexample (Wikipedia contributors 2026a) to a proposition of the form “for every \(x\) in \(A\), \(P(x)\)”, where \(P(x)\) is a predicate (Definition: Predicate), is an element \(x\) of \(A\) for which \(P(x)\) is false. A single counterexample shows that the proposition is false.











Remark 5 (One example, or every element). Settling a quantified proposition takes one element in two cases, and every element of the domain in the other two:

To show that \(\exists x \in S, P(x)\) is true, it is enough to find one \(x\) in \(S\) with \(P(x)\) true.
To show that \(\forall x \in S, P(x)\) is false, it is enough to find one \(x\) in \(S\) with \(P(x)\) false.
To show that \(\forall x \in S, P(x)\) is true, show \(P(x)\) for every \(x\) in \(S\).
To show that \(\exists x \in S, P(x)\) is false, show that \(P(x)\) is false for every \(x\) in \(S\).

When \(S\) is infinite, the last two need a proof rather than a check of each element.






4 Quantified conditionals







Exercise 5 (A hidden “for all”) Consider the sentence “if a string has more than 3 characters, then it is not empty”. Let \(L(s)\) be “\(s\) has more than 3 characters” and \(N(s)\) be “\(s\) is not empty”, for strings \(s\).

Write the sentence in symbols, with its quantifier.
Is it true?
Is its converse (Definition: Converse) true?











SolutionSolution






Solution 5. 

The sentence is about every string, so it is \(\forall s, (L(s) \Rightarrow N(s))\).
True: a string with more than 3 characters has at least 1 character, so it is not empty.
The converse is \(\forall s, (N(s) \Rightarrow L(s))\): “if a string is not empty, then it has more than 3 characters”. It is false. The string "ab" is a counterexample: it is not empty, but it has only 2 characters.












Remark 6 (A conditional about a variable means “for all”). By convention, a conditional whose parts are predicates, such as “if \(x > 3\), then \(x > 1\)”, means the universal statement \(\forall x, (x > 3 \Rightarrow x > 1)\), even though no quantifier is written. Mathematical statements leave out “for all” in this way all the time, so put it back before deciding whether the statement is true.






5 Nested quantifiers







Exercise 6 (Who takes what) Three students take courses as follows.



Student
Courses




Ana
201, 241


Ben
241


Cy
201, 247



Let \(E(s, c)\) be “student \(s\) takes course \(c\)”, where \(s\) ranges over the students and \(c\) over the courses 201, 241 and 247. Which of these are true?

\(\forall s, \exists c, E(s, c)\)
\(\exists c, \forall s, E(s, c)\)
\(\forall c, \exists s, E(s, c)\)
\(\exists s, \forall c, E(s, c)\)











SolutionSolution






Solution 6. 

True: “every student takes some course”. Ana takes 201, Ben takes 241, and Cy takes 201.
False: “some course is taken by every student”. Ben does not take 201, Cy does not take 241, and Ana does not take 247.
True: “every course has some student”. Ana takes 201 and 241, and Cy takes 247.
False: “some student takes every course”. Ana does not take 247, Ben does not take 201, and Cy does not take 241.

Parts 1 and 2 use the same quantifiers and the same predicate in a different order, and they have different truth values.











Remark 7 (Order of quantifiers). Read nested quantifiers from left to right. In \(\forall s, \exists c, E(s, c)\), the course \(c\) is chosen after the student \(s\), so it may depend on \(s\). In \(\exists c, \forall s, E(s, c)\), one course \(c\) must work for every student.
Swapping two quantifiers of the same kind does not change the meaning: \(\forall x, \forall y, P(x, y)\) means the same as \(\forall y, \forall x, P(x, y)\), and likewise for \(\exists\). Swapping a \(\forall\) and an \(\exists\) can change it, as parts 1 and 2 of Exercise 6 show.











Exercise 7 (English to symbols) Write each sentence in symbols, and say whether it is true.

Some integer \(n\) satisfies \(n^2 = 2n + 3\).
No integer is both positive and negative.
Every list of integers has a largest element.











SolutionSolution






Solution 7. 

\(\exists n \in \mathbb{Z}, n^2 = 2n + 3\). True: \(3^2 = 9 = 2 \cdot 3 + 3\).
\(\forall n \in \mathbb{Z}, \neg (n > 0 \land n < 0)\). True: an integer greater than \(0\) is not less than \(0\).
Let \(\mathcal{L}\) be the set of lists of integers. The sentence says that each list \(\ell\) has an element \(m\) that is at least as large as every element \(x\) of \(\ell\): \[
\forall \ell \in \mathcal{L},\
\exists m \in \ell,\
\forall x \in \ell,\
x \le m.
\] Here “\(m \in \ell\)” means “\(m\) is an element of the list \(\ell\)”. False: the empty list has no elements, so it has no largest element. The sentence is true for every nonempty list.

title: Recurrence Relations and Growth Rates
text:
NoteSource





The topics of this chapter follow the course calendar and Kameron Decker Harris’s Fall 2026 lecture notes, which name recurrence relations and order of growth as the topics after recursive algorithms. One idea comes from those notes: the running time of a recursive function is the running time of its recursive call plus the work outside it.
Everything else is new: the exercises, the examples, the algorithms pal_loop, table and pairs, the Racket functions, the theorems and their proofs. The algorithms pal and root come from earlier chapters of these notes.




1 Recurrence relations







Exercise 1 (Double and add a power of 2) A sequence (Definition: Sequence) starts with \(b_0 = 0\), and for every integer (Definition: Integers) \(n \ge 1\) the term \(b_n\) is twice the term before it, plus \(2^n\). Find \(b_1\), \(b_2\), \(b_3\), \(b_4\) and \(b_5\).










SolutionSolution






Solution 1. Each term comes from the one before it:
\[
\begin{aligned}
b_1 &= 2 \cdot 0 + 2^1 = 2,
\\ b_2 &= 2 \cdot 2 + 2^2 = 8,
\\ b_3 &= 2 \cdot 8 + 2^3 = 24,
\\ b_4 &= 2 \cdot 24 + 2^4 = 64,
\\ b_5 &= 2 \cdot 64 + 2^5 = 160.
\end{aligned}
\]











Definition 1 (Recurrence relation) A recurrence relation (Wikipedia contributors 2026e) is the recurrence of a recursively defined sequence (Definition: Recursively defined sequence), that is, its recursive rule (Definition: Recursive definition) written as an equation, which gives the term \(a_n\) in terms of the \(m\) terms \(a_{n-1}, \ldots, a_{n-m}\) just before it, for every integer \(n \ge n_0 + m\).











Example 1 (The sequence \(b_n\), defined recursively) The sequence of Exercise 1 is recursively defined (Definition: Recursively defined sequence) with \(n_0 = 0\) and \(m = 1\). Its initial term is \(b_0 = 0\), and its recurrence relation (Definition 1) is
\[
b_n = 2 b_{n-1} + 2^n
\quad\text{for every integer } n \ge 1.
\]
In Racket, where (expt 2 n) is \(2^n\), the recurrence relation becomes a recursive function:
(define (b n)
  (if (= n 0)
      0
      (+ (* 2 (b (- n 1))) (expt 2 n))))
(b 5) leads to calls of (b 4), (b 3), (b 2), (b 1) and (b 0) in turn, and returns 160, as in Solution 1.











Definition 2 (Closed form) A closed form (Wikipedia contributors 2026b) for a sequence \(a_{n_0}, a_{n_0 + 1}, \ldots\) (Definition: Sequence) is a formula for \(a_n\) that uses only \(n\) and fixed numbers, combined by a fixed number of operations such as addition, multiplication, powers and floors (Definition: Floor), and that uses no other term of the sequence.











Example 2 (Closed forms and recurrence relations) The double-minus-one sequence of Example: The double-minus-one sequence, defined recursively has the recurrence relation (Definition 1) \(a_n = 2 a_{n-1} - 1\), which is not a closed form (Definition 2), since it uses the term \(a_{n-1}\). By Theorem: A formula for the double-minus-one sequence, \(a_n = 2^n + 1\) is a closed form for the same sequence: it gives \(a_{50} = 2^{50} + 1\) without finding \(a_1\) through \(a_{49}\) first. Finding a closed form for a sequence from its recurrence relation is called solving the recurrence relation.






2 Solving recurrence relations by iteration







Exercise 2 (Using the recurrence relation three times) Let \(b_0, b_1, \ldots\) be the sequence of Example 1, and let \(n \ge 3\). Starting from \(b_n = 2 b_{n-1} + 2^n\), replace \(b_{n-1}\) by \(2 b_{n-2} + 2^{n-1}\), and then replace \(b_{n-2}\) by \(2 b_{n-3} + 2^{n-2}\), to write \(b_n\) in terms of \(b_{n-3}\).










SolutionSolution






Solution 2. Replacing \(b_{n-1}\) gives \(b_n\) in terms of \(b_{n-2}\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
b_n
&= 2 \mathopen{}\left(2 b_{n-2} + 2^{n-1}\right)\mathclose{} + 2^n
\\&= 4 b_{n-2} + 2^n + 2^n
\\&= 4 b_{n-2} + 2 \cdot 2^n.
\end{aligned}
\]
Replacing \(b_{n-2}\) then gives \(b_n\) in terms of \(b_{n-3}\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
b_n
&= 4 \mathopen{}\left(2 b_{n-3} + 2^{n-2}\right)\mathclose{} + 2 \cdot 2^n
\\&= 8 b_{n-3} + 2^n + 2 \cdot 2^n
\\&= 8 b_{n-3} + 3 \cdot 2^n.
\end{aligned}
\]











Definition 3 (Iteration (unrolling)) Solving a recurrence relation (Definition 1) by iteration, also called unrolling, finds a closed form (Definition 2) for its sequence in three steps:

use the recurrence relation again and again to write \(a_n\) in terms of \(a_{n-1}\), then \(a_{n-2}\), then \(a_{n-3}\), and so on;
guess, from the pattern, a formula for \(a_n\) in terms of \(a_{n-k}\) for every number \(k\) of steps;
choose \(k\) so that \(a_{n-k}\) is an initial term, and put in its value.












Example 3 (Unrolling \(b_n = 2 b_{n-1} + 2^n\)) The recurrence relation and Solution 2 give the first steps of iteration (Definition 3) for the sequence of Example 1:
\[
\begin{aligned}
b_n &= 2 b_{n-1} + 1 \cdot 2^n,
\\ b_n &= 4 b_{n-2} + 2 \cdot 2^n,
\\ b_n &= 8 b_{n-3} + 3 \cdot 2^n.
\end{aligned}
\]
After \(k\) steps the factor in front of \(b_{n-k}\) is \(2^k\), and the multiple of \(2^n\) is \(k\), so the pattern suggests
\[
b_n = 2^k b_{n-k} + k \cdot 2^n
\quad\text{for } k = 1, 2, \ldots, n.
\]
The initial term is \(b_0\), which is \(b_{n-k}\) when \(k = n\). With \(k = n\) and \(b_0 = 0\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
b_n
&= 2^n b_0 + n \cdot 2^n
\\&= n \cdot 2^n.
\end{aligned}
\]
This agrees with Solution 1: for example, \(5 \cdot 2^5 = 160 = b_5\).











Remark 1 (Iteration gives a guess). In Example 3, the formula for general \(k\) came from the three cases \(k = 1, 2, 3\). Nothing proved that the pattern continues, so the closed form \(b_n = n \cdot 2^n\) is still a guess. Induction (Definition: Proof by induction) turns such a guess into a theorem, with the recurrence relation in the inductive step.






3 Checking a closed form by induction







Exercise 3 (Checking a guess) A sequence starts with \(e_0 = 1\), and has the recurrence relation (Definition 1)
\[
e_n = 3 e_{n-1} + 2^n
\quad\text{for every integer } n \ge 1.
\]
Someone guesses the closed form (Definition 2) \(e_n = 3^{n+1} - 2^{n+1}\). Find \(e_1\), \(e_2\) and \(e_3\) from the recurrence relation, and check the guess for \(n = 0, 1, 2, 3\).










SolutionSolution






Solution 3. From the recurrence relation, \(e_1 = 3 \cdot 1 + 2 = 5\), \(e_2 = 3 \cdot 5 + 4 = 19\) and \(e_3 = 3 \cdot 19 + 8 = 65\).

The guess is right for \(n = 0, 1, 2, 3\). Four cases do not prove it for every \(n\).











Theorem 1 (A closed form for \(b_n = 2 b_{n-1} + 2^n\)) Let \(b_0, b_1, \ldots\) be the sequence with \(b_0 = 0\) and \(b_n = 2 b_{n-1} + 2^n\) for every integer \(n \ge 1\) (Example 1). Then \(b_n = n \cdot 2^n\) for every non-negative integer (Definition: Non-negative integers) \(n\).










ProofProof






Proof. We use induction (Definition: Proof by induction), following Remark: The shape of a proof by induction with \(n_0 = 0\). Let \(P(n)\) be the equation \(b_n = n \cdot 2^n\).
Base case. \(b_0 = 0 = 0 \cdot 2^0\).
Inductive step. Let \(k \ge 0\) be an integer, and suppose \(P(k)\): \(b_k = k \cdot 2^k\). The goal \(P(k + 1)\) is \(b_{k + 1} = (k + 1) \cdot 2^{k + 1}\). Since \(k + 1 \ge 1\), the recurrence relation gives \(b_{k + 1}\), and
\[
\begin{aligned}
b_{k + 1}
&= 2 b_k + 2^{k + 1}
&& \text{(recurrence relation)}
\\&= 2 \cdot k \cdot 2^k + 2^{k + 1}
&& \text{(induction hypothesis)}
\\&= k \cdot 2^{k + 1} + 2^{k + 1}
\\&= (k + 1) \cdot 2^{k + 1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
So \(P(k + 1)\) holds, and by induction \(b_n = n \cdot 2^n\) for every non-negative integer \(n\).











Theorem 2 (A closed form for \(e_n = 3 e_{n-1} + 2^n\)) Let \(e_0, e_1, \ldots\) be the sequence with \(e_0 = 1\) and \(e_n = 3 e_{n-1} + 2^n\) for every integer \(n \ge 1\). Then \(e_n = 3^{n+1} - 2^{n+1}\), as guessed in Exercise 3, for every non-negative integer (Definition: Non-negative integers) \(n\).










ProofProof






Proof. We use induction (Definition: Proof by induction), following Remark: The shape of a proof by induction with \(n_0 = 0\). Let \(P(n)\) be the equation \(e_n = 3^{n+1} - 2^{n+1}\).
Base case. \(e_0 = 1 = 3 - 2 = 3^1 - 2^1\).
Inductive step. Let \(k \ge 0\) be an integer, and suppose \(P(k)\): \(e_k = 3^{k+1} - 2^{k+1}\). The goal \(P(k + 1)\) is \(e_{k + 1} = 3^{k+2} - 2^{k+2}\). Since \(k + 1 \ge 1\), the recurrence relation gives \(e_{k + 1}\), and
\[
\begin{aligned}
e_{k + 1}
&= 3 e_k + 2^{k + 1}
&& \text{(recurrence relation)}
\\&= 3 \mathopen{}\left(3^{k+1} - 2^{k+1}\right)\mathclose{} + 2^{k + 1}
&& \text{(induction hypothesis)}
\\&= 3^{k+2} - 3 \cdot 2^{k+1} + 2^{k + 1}
\\&= 3^{k+2} - 2 \cdot 2^{k+1}
\\&= 3^{k+2} - 2^{k+2}.
\end{aligned}
\]
So \(P(k + 1)\) holds, and by induction \(e_n = 3^{n+1} - 2^{n+1}\) for every non-negative integer \(n\).











Example 4 (A guess that fails) The sequence of Exercise 3 starts \(e_0 = 1\), \(e_1 = 5\), which are \(5^0\) and \(5^1\). So one might guess \(e_n = 5^n\). The guess fails at \(n = 2\), since \(e_2 = 19\) and \(5^2 = 25\).
An attempt to prove the guess by induction (Definition: Proof by induction) shows where it goes wrong. Supposing \(e_k = 5^k\), the recurrence relation gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
e_{k + 1}
&= 3 e_k + 2^{k + 1}
\\&= 3 \cdot 5^k + 2^{k + 1},
\end{aligned}
\]
and the inductive step needs this to equal \(5^{k + 1} = 5 \cdot 5^k\), which happens only when \(2^{k + 1} = 2 \cdot 5^k\), that is, only when \(k = 0\).











Remark 2 (Finding a closed form, then proving it). Iteration (Definition 3) and checking small cases, as in Exercise 3, find a closed form (Definition 2) to try. Induction proves it, as in Theorem 1 and Theorem 2, or shows that it is wrong, as in Example 4. A proof by induction needs the closed form before it starts: it can check a formula, but it cannot find one.






4 Running times of recursive algorithms







Exercise 4 (How many calls does pal make?) Let pal be the algorithm of Exercise: Is it a palindrome?. How many calls of pal, including the first, does pal(abbaabba) make?










SolutionSolution






Solution 4. pal(abbaabba) calls pal(bbaabb), which calls pal(baab), which calls pal(aa), which calls pal on the empty string, which returns true. That is 5 calls, on strings of 8, 6, 4, 2 and 0 symbols: each call removes the first and last symbols.











Remark 3 (The size of an input and a step). To count the work an algorithm (Definition: Algorithm) does, we first fix two things:

the size of an input, such as the number of symbols in a string or the number of entries in an array;
what one step is, such as one comparison, one arithmetic operation or one call of a function.












Definition 4 (Running time) Fix, for an algorithm (Definition: Algorithm), the size of an input and what one step is (Remark 3). The running time (Wikipedia contributors 2026f) of the algorithm is the function \(T\) (Definition: Function (map, mapping, transformation)) whose value \(T(n)\) is the largest number of steps that the algorithm takes on any input of size \(n\).











Example 5 (The running time of pal) Take the size (Remark 3) of the input of pal (Exercise: Is it a palindrome?) to be the number \(n\) of symbols in the string, and count each call of pal as one step, since apart from its recursive call each call does at most two comparisons. This assumes that the call on s[2..n-1] passes the shorter string as a pair of positions in s, which takes a fixed number of operations; copying its \(n - 2\) symbols into a new string would add about \(n\) steps to every call. Let \(T(n)\) be the running time (Definition 4). The running time of a call is the running time of its recursive call plus the work outside it.

When \(n \le 1\), pal returns without calling itself, so \(T(0) = T(1) = 1\).
When \(n \ge 2\), the call that takes longest is one whose first and last symbols match, since otherwise pal returns at once. It calls pal on a string of \(n - 2\) symbols, which can be any such string, so \(T(n) = T(n - 2) + 1\).

Iteration (Definition 3) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
T(n)
&= T(n - 2) + 1
\\&= T(n - 4) + 2
\\&= T(n - 6) + 3,
\end{aligned}
\]
and in general \(T(n) = T(n - 2k) + k\), as long as \(n - 2k \ge 0\). To reach an initial term, take \(k = \mathopen{}\left\lfloor n / 2\right\rfloor\mathclose{}\) (Definition: Floor): then \(n - 2k\) is 0 when \(n\) is even and 1 when \(n\) is odd, and either way \(T(n - 2k) = 1\). So the guess is
\[
T(n) = \mathopen{}\left\lfloor n / 2\right\rfloor\mathclose{} + 1,
\]
which gives \(T(8) = 5\), as in Solution 4. Theorem 3 proves it.











Theorem 3 (A closed form for the running time of pal) Let \(T(0) = T(1) = 1\) and \(T(n) = T(n - 2) + 1\) for every integer \(n \ge 2\), as in Example 5. Then \(T(n) = \mathopen{}\left\lfloor n / 2\right\rfloor\mathclose{} + 1\) (Definition: Floor) for every non-negative integer (Definition: Non-negative integers) \(n\).










ProofProof






Proof. The recurrence relation uses \(T(n - 2)\), not \(T(n - 1)\), so we use strong induction (Definition: Proof by strong induction). Let \(n \ge 0\) be an integer, and suppose \(T(m) = \mathopen{}\left\lfloor m / 2\right\rfloor\mathclose{} + 1\) for every integer \(m\) with \(0 \le m < n\).
If \(n \le 1\), then \(T(n) = 1 = 0 + 1 = \mathopen{}\left\lfloor n / 2\right\rfloor\mathclose{} + 1\).
If \(n \ge 2\), then \(0 \le n - 2 < n\), and \(\mathopen{}\left\lfloor(n - 2) / 2\right\rfloor\mathclose{} = \mathopen{}\left\lfloor n / 2 - 1\right\rfloor\mathclose{} = \mathopen{}\left\lfloor n / 2\right\rfloor\mathclose{} - 1\), since subtracting the integer 1 from a real number subtracts 1 from its floor. So
\[
\begin{aligned}
T(n)
&= T(n - 2) + 1
&& \text{(recurrence relation)}
\\&= \mathopen{}\left\lfloor(n - 2) / 2\right\rfloor\mathclose{} + 1 + 1
&& \text{(strong induction hypothesis)}
\\&= \mathopen{}\left\lfloor n / 2\right\rfloor\mathclose{} - 1 + 2
\\&= \mathopen{}\left\lfloor n / 2\right\rfloor\mathclose{} + 1.
\end{aligned}
\]
So the formula holds for \(n\), and by strong induction it holds for every non-negative integer \(n\).

Theorem 4 (Two calls of size \(n - 1\) give \(2^n\) base cases) For every non-negative integer (Definition: Non-negative integers) \(n\), the calls that (dm n) of Exercise 5 makes include exactly \(2^n\) calls of (dm 0), counting (dm 0) itself when \(n = 0\). Definition 5 (Big-O) Let \(f\) and \(g\) be functions from the natural numbers to the real numbers. Then \(f(n)\) is big-O of \(g(n)\) (Wikipedia contributors 2026a), written \(f(n) = O(g(n))\), when there exist a real number \(c > 0\) and a natural number \(N\) such that, for every natural number \(n \ge N\), \[
|f(n)| \le c \, |g(n)|.
\] In words, from some point \(N\) on, the absolute value of \(f(n)\) is at most a fixed multiple \(c\) of the absolute value of \(g(n)\). The “there exist” is an existential quantifier, and the “for every” is a universal quantifier.











Definition 6 (Witnesses) A real number \(c > 0\) and a natural number \(N\) for which the inequality in Definition 5 holds for every natural number (Definition: Natural numbers (our convention)) \(n \ge N\) are a pair of witnesses for \(f(n) = O(g(n))\). Witnesses for \(f(n) = \Omega(g(n))\) are defined in the same way, from Definition 7. Some books write \(n_0\) for \(N\).











Example 6 (The running time of pal is \(O(n)\)) By Example 5, pal takes \(T(n) = \mathopen{}\left\lfloor n / 2\right\rfloor\mathclose{} + 1\) steps on a string of \(n\) symbols. For every natural number \(n \ge 2\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathopen{}\left|T(n)\right|\mathclose{}
&= \mathopen{}\left\lfloor n / 2\right\rfloor\mathclose{} + 1
&& \text{(} T(n) > 0 \text{)}
\\&\le n / 2 + 1
&& \text{(definition of the floor)}
\\&\le n / 2 + n / 2
&& \text{(} 1 \le n / 2 \text{, since } n \ge 2 \text{)}
\\&= n,
\end{aligned}
\]
so \(c = 1\) and \(N = 2\) are witnesses (Definition 6) for \(T(n) = O(n)\) (Definition 5). At \(n = 1\), also \(T(1) = 1 \le 1\), so \(c = 1\) and \(N = 1\) are witnesses too. Witnesses are not unique: any larger \(c\) or \(N\) works as well.











Example 7 (Finding witnesses for \(2 n^3 + 40 = O(n^3)\)) To prove \(2 n^3 + 40 = O(n^3)\) (Definition 5), we look for witnesses (Definition 6) \(c\) and \(N\). Since \(2 n^3 + 40 > 2 n^3\), the term \(2 n^3\) needs \(c > 2\). With \(c = 3\), the inequality \(2 n^3 + 40 \le 3 n^3\) is the same as \(40 \le n^3\), which holds when \(n \ge 4\), since \(4^3 = 64\), but not when \(n = 3\), since \(3^3 = 27\). So for every natural number \(n \ge 4\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathopen{}\left|2 n^3 + 40\right|\mathclose{}
&= 2 n^3 + 40
&& \text{(} 2 n^3 + 40 > 0 \text{)}
\\&\le 2 n^3 + n^3
&& \text{(} 40 \le 64 \le n^3 \text{, since } n \ge 4 \text{)}
\\&= 3 \mathopen{}\left|n^3\right|\mathclose{},
\end{aligned}
\]
and \(c = 3\), \(N = 4\) are witnesses. A larger \(c\) allows a smaller \(N\): since \(40 \le 40 n^3\) for every \(n \ge 1\), the pair \(c = 42\), \(N = 1\) also works.











Definition 7 (Big-Omega) Let \(f\) and \(g\) be functions from the natural numbers to the real numbers. Then \(f(n)\) is big-Omega of \(g(n)\) (Wikipedia contributors 2026a), written \(f(n) = \Omega(g(n))\), when there exist a real number \(c > 0\) and a natural number \(N\) such that, for every natural number \(n \ge N\), \[
|f(n)| \ge c \, |g(n)|.
\] In words, from some point \(N\) on, the absolute value of \(f(n)\) is at least a fixed positive multiple \(c\) of the absolute value of \(g(n)\). Dividing by \(c\) shows that \(f(n) = \Omega(g(n))\) exactly when \(g(n) = O(f(n))\) in the sense of Definition 5.











Example 8 (\(2 n^3 + 40 = \Omega(n^3)\)) For every natural number \(n \ge 1\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathopen{}\left|2 n^3 + 40\right|\mathclose{}
&= 2 n^3 + 40
&& \text{(} 2 n^3 + 40 > 0 \text{)}
\\&\ge 2 n^3
&& \text{(} 40 \ge 0 \text{)}
\\&= 2 \mathopen{}\left|n^3\right|\mathclose{},
\end{aligned}
\]
so \(c = 2\) and \(N = 1\) are witnesses (Definition 6) for \(2 n^3 + 40 = \Omega(n^3)\) (Definition 7).











Definition 8 (Big-Theta) Let \(f\) and \(g\) be functions from the natural numbers to the real numbers. Then \(f(n)\) is big-Theta of \(g(n)\) (Wikipedia contributors 2026a), written \(f(n) = \Theta(g(n))\), when both \(f(n) = O(g(n))\) (big-O) and \(f(n) = \Omega(g(n))\) (big-Omega). In words, \(f(n)\) and \(g(n)\) are within fixed multiples of each other, from some point on.











Example 9 (\(2 n^3 + 40 = \Theta(n^3)\)) By Example 7, \(2 n^3 + 40 = O(n^3)\), and by Example 8, \(2 n^3 + 40 = \Omega(n^3)\). So \(2 n^3 + 40 = \Theta(n^3)\) by Definition 8. The constant 40 and the factor 2 do not change how fast \(2 n^3 + 40\) grows.











Theorem 5 (Sums of big-O functions) Let \(f\), \(g\) and \(h\) be functions (Definition: Function (map, mapping, transformation)) from the natural numbers (Definition: Natural numbers (our convention)) to the real numbers (Definition: Real numbers). If \(f(n) = O(h(n))\) and \(g(n) = O(h(n))\) (Definition 5), then \(f(n) + g(n) = O(h(n))\).










ProofProof






Proof. Let \(c_1\), \(N_1\) be witnesses (Definition 6) for \(f(n) = O(h(n))\), and \(c_2\), \(N_2\) witnesses for \(g(n) = O(h(n))\). Let \(N\) be the larger of \(N_1\) and \(N_2\). The triangle inequality (Wikipedia contributors 2026g) says that \(\mathopen{}\left|x + y\right|\mathclose{} \le \mathopen{}\left|x\right|\mathclose{} + \mathopen{}\left|y\right|\mathclose{}\) for all real numbers \(x\) and \(y\). For every natural number \(n \ge N\), both \(n \ge N_1\) and \(n \ge N_2\) hold, so
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathopen{}\left|f(n) + g(n)\right|\mathclose{}
&\le \mathopen{}\left|f(n)\right|\mathclose{} + \mathopen{}\left|g(n)\right|\mathclose{}
&& \text{(triangle inequality)}
\\&\le c_1 \mathopen{}\left|h(n)\right|\mathclose{} + c_2 \mathopen{}\left|h(n)\right|\mathclose{}
&& \text{(} n \ge N_1 \text{ and } n \ge N_2 \text{)}
\\&= (c_1 + c_2) \mathopen{}\left|h(n)\right|\mathclose{}.
\end{aligned}
\]
So \(c_1 + c_2\) and \(N\) are witnesses for \(f(n) + g(n) = O(h(n))\).






7 Disproving a bound







Exercise 7 (Is \(n \cdot 2^n\) big-O of \(2^n\)?) By Theorem 1, the sequence of Example 1 has \(b_n = n \cdot 2^n\). Show that \(n \cdot 2^n = O(2^n)\) (Definition 5) is false.










SolutionSolution






Solution 7. We use proof by contradiction (Definition: Proof by contradiction). Suppose \(n \cdot 2^n = O(2^n)\), with witnesses (Definition 6) \(c > 0\) and \(N\). Then \(n \cdot 2^n \le c \cdot 2^n\) for every natural number \(n \ge N\), and dividing by \(2^n > 0\) gives \(n \le c\) for every natural number \(n \ge N\).
Let \(n = N + \mathopen{}\left\lfloor c\right\rfloor\mathclose{} + 1\), where \(\mathopen{}\left\lfloor c\right\rfloor\mathclose{}\) is the floor (Definition: Floor) of \(c\). Then \(n\) is a natural number with \(n \ge N\), so \(n \le c\). But \(\mathopen{}\left\lfloor c\right\rfloor\mathclose{} + 1 > c\) by the definition of the floor, and \(N \ge 1\), so \(n > c\). This is a contradiction, so \(n \cdot 2^n = O(2^n)\) is false.











Remark 5 (How to disprove a big-O bound). The statement \(f(n) = O(g(n))\) (Definition 5) says that there exist \(c > 0\) and \(N\) such that every \(n \ge N\) has \(\mathopen{}\left|f(n)\right|\mathclose{} \le c \mathopen{}\left|g(n)\right|\mathclose{}\). Its negation says that for every \(c > 0\) and every \(N\), some natural number \(n \ge N\) has \(\mathopen{}\left|f(n)\right|\mathclose{} > c \mathopen{}\left|g(n)\right|\mathclose{}\), by the rules for negating the existential (Definition: Existential quantifier) and universal (Definition: Universal quantifier) quantifiers. So a disproof cannot pick \(c\) and \(N\): like Solution 7, it takes any \(c\) and \(N\) and finds such an \(n\), which depends on \(c\) and \(N\). Checking that the inequality fails for a few chosen \(c\) and \(N\) is not a disproof.

Theorem 6 (A chain of growth rates) For every natural number (Definition: Natural numbers (our convention)) \(n \ge 4\),
\[
1 \le \log_2 n < n \le n \log_2 n < n^2 \le 2^n \le n!,
\]
where \(\log_2\) is the logarithm to the base 2 (Definition 9) and \(n!\) is the factorial (Definition 10).










ProofProof






Proof. We use that \(2^y < 2^z\) for real numbers \(y < z\). Let \(n \ge 4\) be a natural number, and let \(y = \log_2 n\), so that \(2^y = n\).
\(1 \le \log_2 n\). If \(y < 1\), then \(n = 2^y < 2^1 = 2\), which is false.
\(\log_2 n < n\). First, \(m < 2^m\) for every natural number \(m\), by induction (Definition: Proof by induction).
Base case. \(1 < 2 = 2^1\).
Inductive step. If \(k < 2^k\) for an integer \(k \ge 1\), then \(k + 1 \le 2^k < 2^k + 2^k = 2^{k + 1}\).
So \(n < 2^n\). If \(y \ge n\), then \(n = 2^y \ge 2^n\), which is false.
\(n \le n \log_2 n\) and \(n \log_2 n < n^2\). Multiply \(1 \le \log_2 n < n\) by \(n > 0\).
\(n^2 \le 2^n\). This is Example: An induction that starts at 4, since \(n \ge 4\).
\(2^n \le n!\). By induction, following Remark: The shape of a proof by induction with \(n_0 = 4\).
Base case. \(2^4 = 16 \le 24 = 4!\).
Inductive step. If \(2^k \le k!\) for an integer \(k \ge 4\), then
\[
\begin{aligned}
2^{k + 1}
&= 2 \cdot 2^k
\\&\le 2 \cdot k!
&& \text{(induction hypothesis)}
\\&< (k + 1) \cdot k!
&& \text{(} 2 < k + 1 \text{)}
\\&= (k + 1)!.
\end{aligned}
\]











Remark 7 (The common growth rates). By Theorem 6, each function in the chain
\[
1, \quad \log_2 n, \quad n, \quad n \log_2 n, \quad n^2, \quad 2^n, \quad n!
\]
is big-O (Definition 5) of the next, with witnesses (Definition 6) \(c = 1\) and \(N = 4\). In the other direction, none is big-O of the one before it. Solution 7 shows how to prove such a statement for \(n \cdot 2^n\) and \(2^n\), and the same argument, dividing by \(n\) instead of \(2^n\), shows that \(n^2 = O(n)\) is false. A running time that is \(\Theta\) (Definition 8) of one of these functions is called, in order,

constant, for \(1\);
logarithmic, for \(\log_2 n\);
linear, for \(n\);
\(n \log n\), for \(n \log_2 n\);
quadratic, for \(n^2\);
exponential, for \(2^n\);
factorial, for \(n!\).

Other powers of \(n\) fit between \(n\) and \(2^n\). For natural numbers \(a \le b\), \(n^a \le n^b\) for every natural number \(n\), so \(n^a = O(n^b)\). Every power \(n^a\) is also \(O(2^n)\), though the witness \(N\) grows with \(a\): for example, \(n^4 \le 2^n\) holds for every \(n \ge 16\), where \(16^4 = 65536 = 2^{16}\), but not for \(n = 15\), since \(15^4 = 50625 > 32768 = 2^{15}\). We do not prove the general statement here.

Exercise 9 (Printing a multiplication table) The algorithm table, in the pseudocode of Remark: How to read the pseudocode in this chapter, prints a multiplication table:

SolutionSolution






Solution 9. For each value of \(i\), the inner loop runs print i * j once for each of \(j = 1, 2, \ldots, n\), that is, \(n\) times. The outer loop makes \(n\) passes, one for each of \(i = 1, 2, \ldots, n\), so the line runs \(n + n + \cdots + n = n \cdot n = n^2\) times, once for each entry of an \(n\) by \(n\) table. Remark 8 (Counting the steps of loops). To find the running time (Definition 4) of an algorithm with loops:

a loop whose body takes the same number \(s\) of steps on each of \(p\) passes takes \(p \cdot s\) steps, so the steps of nested loops multiply, as in Solution 9;
parts of an algorithm that run one after the other take the sum of their steps, and Theorem 5 turns big-O bounds for the parts into a big-O bound for the sum.

Each test of a loop’s guard (Definition: Guard of a loop) and each line of setup is also a step, but counting them too changes the count by at most a fixed multiple plus a fixed number, which does not change a \(\Theta\) bound (Definition 8) on a count that is at least 1.











Example 12 (A loop, then a nested loop) The algorithm pairs takes an array A[1..n] of numbers, where \(n \ge 1\):
procedure pairs(A, n)    // A[1..n] is an array of numbers, n >= 1
    s := 0
    for i := 1 to n
        s := s + A[i]
    t := 0
    for i := 1 to n
        for j := 1 to n
            t := t + A[i] * A[j]
    return s + t
Count each run of an assignment inside a loop as one step. The first loop takes \(n\) steps, and the nested loops take \(n \cdot n = n^2\) steps, as in Solution 9, so the algorithm takes \(f(n) = n + n^2\) steps. Since \(n \le n^2\) and \(n^2 \le n^2\) for every natural number \(n\), both \(n = O(n^2)\) and \(n^2 = O(n^2)\) (Definition 5) with witnesses (Definition 6) \(c = 1\), \(N = 1\), so \(f(n) = O(n^2)\) by Theorem 5. Also \(f(n) \ge n^2\), so \(f(n) = \Omega(n^2)\) (Definition 7) with \(c = 1\), \(N = 1\). So \(f(n) = \Theta(n^2)\) (Definition 8): the nested loops decide the growth, and the first loop does not.











Example 13 (A loop with the same recurrence as pal) The algorithm pal_loop tests whether a string is a palindrome (Definition: Palindrome) with a loop instead of recursion:
procedure pal_loop(s)    // s is a string s[1] s[2] ... s[n] of n symbols
    i := 1
    j := n
    while i < j and s[i] = s[j]
        i := i + 1
        j := j - 1
    return i >= j
The test s[i] = s[j] is made only when i < j is true. Let \(L(n)\) be the largest number of passes through the body on a string of \(n\) symbols. When \(n \le 1\), the guard is false at once, so \(L(0) = L(1) = 0\). When \(n \ge 2\), the most passes come when the first and last symbols match; after the first pass, the loop then runs exactly as it would on the string \(s[2..n-1]\) of \(n - 2\) symbols, with every index one larger. So \(L(n) = L(n - 2) + 1\), the same recurrence relation (Definition 1) as for pal in Example 5, with initial terms one smaller.
So \(L(n) = \mathopen{}\left\lfloor n / 2\right\rfloor\mathclose{}\) (Definition: Floor), by strong induction (Definition: Proof by strong induction) as in the proof of Theorem 3: if \(n \le 1\), then \(L(n) = 0 = \mathopen{}\left\lfloor n / 2\right\rfloor\mathclose{}\), and if \(n \ge 2\) and the formula holds for \(n - 2\), then \(L(n) = \mathopen{}\left\lfloor(n - 2) / 2\right\rfloor\mathclose{} + 1 = \mathopen{}\left\lfloor n / 2\right\rfloor\mathclose{} - 1 + 1 = \mathopen{}\left\lfloor n / 2\right\rfloor\mathclose{}\). The guard is tested once more than the body runs, \(\mathopen{}\left\lfloor n / 2\right\rfloor\mathclose{} + 1\) times, which is the number of calls of pal by Theorem 3, and is \(O(n)\) by Example 6.











Example 14 (root takes \(\Theta(\sqrt{n})\) steps) The algorithm root of Exercise: Tracing a square-root loop returns \(r = \mathopen{}\left\lfloor\sqrt{n}\right\rfloor\mathclose{}\) (Definition: Square root), the largest integer whose square is at most \(n\), and its body adds 1 to r on each pass, starting from 0. So on input \(n\) the body runs exactly \(\mathopen{}\left\lfloor\sqrt{n}\right\rfloor\mathclose{}\) times. Let \(f(n) = \mathopen{}\left\lfloor\sqrt{n}\right\rfloor\mathclose{}\), for natural numbers \(n\).

\(f(n) \le \sqrt{n}\), so \(f(n) = O(\sqrt{n})\) (Definition 5) with witnesses (Definition 6) \(c = 1\), \(N = 1\).
\(f(n) \ge 1\) since \(n \ge 1\), and \(\sqrt{n} < f(n) + 1 \le 2 f(n)\) by the definition of the floor (Definition: Floor), so \(f(n) > \frac{1}{2} \sqrt{n}\), and \(f(n) = \Omega(\sqrt{n})\) (Definition 7) with \(c = \frac{1}{2}\), \(N = 1\).

So \(f(n) = \Theta(\sqrt{n})\) (Definition 8). Since \(\sqrt{n} \le n\) for \(n \ge 1\), the body of root runs no more times than the body of a loop with \(n\) passes: on \(n = 10^6\), its body runs \(1000\) times.

title: Proofs with Sets
text:
NoteSource





Adapted from Kameron Decker Harris’s Fall 2026 lecture notes “Proofs Involving Sets”, which are typed transcriptions of Scott Wehrwein’s Spring 2025 handwritten lecture notes. These come from those notes:

what to show to prove that an element is in a set given in set-builder notation;
the direct and contrapositive outlines of a subset proof;
proving set equality by proving that each set is a subset of the other;
the theorem that a nonempty factor cancels from both sides of an equation between Cartesian products, with the proof of its first half.

Everything else is new: the exercises, the other examples and theorems, the second half of that proof, the membership test for a set built with an expression, and the section on disproving a claim about sets.




1 Proving membership







Exercise 1 (In or out) Let \(T = {\mathopen{}\left\{3k + 2 : k \in \mathbb{Z}\right\}\mathclose{}}\) (Definition: Set-builder notation with an expression). Prove that \(17 \in T\) and that \(19 \notin T\).










SolutionSolution






Solution 1. \(17 \in T\). An element of \(T\) is a number of the form \(3k + 2\) with \(k\) an integer. Take \(k = 5\), which is an integer. Then \(3k + 2 = 3 \cdot 5 + 2 = 17\), so \(17 \in T\).
\(19 \notin T\). Suppose, for contradiction, that \(19 \in T\) (Definition: Proof by contradiction). Then \(19 = 3k + 2\) for some integer \(k\). Subtracting 2 from both sides gives \(3k = 17\), so \(k = 17/3\). But \(17/3\) is not an integer, since \(3 \cdot 5 = 15 < 17 < 18 = 3 \cdot 6\). This contradicts that \(k\) is an integer, so \(19 \notin T\).











Remark 1 (What to show for membership). To prove that \(a\) is an element of a set, show that \(a\) passes the set’s test:

for \(S = {\mathopen{}\left\{x \in A : P(x)\right\}\mathclose{}}\) (Definition: Set-builder notation), show that \(a \in A\) and that \(P(a)\) is true;
for \(S = {\mathopen{}\left\{x : P(x)\right\}\mathclose{}}\), the same notation with no set \(A\) named, show that \(P(a)\) is true;
for \(S = {\mathopen{}\left\{f(k) : k \in A\right\}\mathclose{}}\) (Definition: Set-builder notation with an expression), find some \(k \in A\) with \(f(k) = a\).

The last case is an existence proof, so it usually names the \(k\) (Definition: Constructive proof). To prove that \(a \notin S\), prove the negation of the test, often by contradiction, as in Solution 1.











Example 1 (A root of a polynomial) Let \(S = {\mathopen{}\left\{x \in \mathbb{R}: 2x^2 - x = 0\right\}\mathclose{}}\). Then \(\frac{1}{2} \in S\).
The set has the form \({\mathopen{}\left\{x \in A : P(x)\right\}\mathclose{}}\), so there are two things to show (Remark 1). First, \(\frac{1}{2}\) is a real number. Second,
\[
\begin{aligned}
2 \mathopen{}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\mathclose{}^2 - \frac{1}{2}
&= 2 \cdot \frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{2}
\\&= \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{2}
\\&= 0.
\end{aligned}
\]






2 Proving a subset







Exercise 2 (A disk inside a square) Let \(D = {\mathopen{}\left\{(x, y) \in \mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{R}: x^2 + y^2 \le 1\right\}\mathclose{}}\), the points of the plane at distance at most 1 from the origin. Prove that \(D \subseteq [-1, 1] \times [-1, 1]\), where \([-1, 1] = {\mathopen{}\left\{x \in \mathbb{R}: -1 \le x \le 1\right\}\mathclose{}}\) (Definition: Subset, Definition: Cartesian product, Definition: Closed interval).










SolutionSolution






Solution 2. Let \((a, b) \in D\), so \(a\) and \(b\) are real numbers with \(a^2 + b^2 \le 1\). Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
a^2
&\le a^2 + b^2
&& \text{(} b^2 \ge 0 \text{)}
\\&\le 1.
&& \text{(} (a, b) \in D \text{)}
\end{aligned}
\]
If \(a > 1\), then \(a^2 = a \cdot a > 1 \cdot 1 = 1\), and if \(a < -1\), then \(a^2 = (-a)^2 > 1\). Neither is possible, so \(-1 \le a \le 1\), that is, \(a \in [-1, 1]\). The same steps with \(a\) and \(b\) swapped give \(b \in [-1, 1]\). So \((a, b) \in [-1, 1] \times [-1, 1]\). Every element of \(D\) is in \([-1, 1] \times [-1, 1]\), so \(D \subseteq [-1, 1] \times [-1, 1]\).











Remark 2 (The shape of a subset proof). By Definition: Subset, \(A \subseteq B\) means the conditional “if \(a \in A\), then \(a \in B\)” is true for every \(a\). So a proof of \(A \subseteq B\) is a proof of that conditional, either directly (Definition: Direct proof):

Suppose \(a \in A\).
\(\vdots\)
Therefore \(a \in B\).
So \(A \subseteq B\).

or by contrapositive (Definition: Proof by contrapositive):

Suppose \(a \notin B\).
\(\vdots\)
Therefore \(a \notin A\).
So \(A \subseteq B\).

The element \(a\) is arbitrary: the proof may use only that \(a \in A\) (or that \(a \notin B\)), nothing else about it.











Example 2 (A subset proof by contrapositive) Claim: \({\mathopen{}\left\{(x, y) \in \mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{R}: x + y > 2\right\}\mathclose{}} \subseteq {\mathopen{}\left\{(x, y) \in \mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{R}: x > 1 \text{ or } y > 1\right\}\mathclose{}}\). If two numbers add up to more than 2, at least one of them is more than 1.
We use the contrapositive outline of Remark 2. Suppose \(p \notin {\mathopen{}\left\{(x, y) \in \mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{R}: x > 1 \text{ or } y > 1\right\}\mathclose{}}\). If \(p\) is not a pair of real numbers, then \(p\) is not in the left-hand set either, since every element of that set is a pair of real numbers. Otherwise \(p = (a, b)\) with \(a\) and \(b\) real, and “\(a > 1\) or \(b > 1\)” is false. By De Morgan’s laws (Theorem: De Morgan’s laws), \(a > 1\) is false and \(b > 1\) is false, that is, \(a \le 1\) and \(b \le 1\), so \(a + b \le 1 + 1 = 2\). So \(p \notin {\mathopen{}\left\{(x, y) \in \mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{R}: x + y > 2\right\}\mathclose{}}\). So the left-hand set is a subset of the right-hand set.
The contrapositive turns the conclusion “\(x > 1\) or \(y > 1\)”, which does not say which number is large, into the hypothesis “\(a \le 1\) and \(b \le 1\)”, which says something about both.











Theorem 1 (Subsets of subsets) Let \(A\), \(B\) and \(C\) be sets. If \(A \subseteq B\) and \(B \subseteq C\), then \(A \subseteq C\).










ProofProof






Proof. Suppose \(A \subseteq B\) and \(B \subseteq C\), and let \(a \in A\). Since \(A \subseteq B\), \(a \in B\) (Definition: Subset). Since \(B \subseteq C\), \(a \in C\). So every element of \(A\) is in \(C\), and \(A \subseteq C\).











Example 3 (A chain of subsets) Let \(D\) be the disk of Exercise 2, and let \(H = {\mathopen{}\left\{(x, y) \in \mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{R}: x + y \le 2\right\}\mathclose{}}\). Solution 2 shows that \(D \subseteq [-1, 1] \times [-1, 1]\). Every point \((x, y)\) of \([-1, 1] \times [-1, 1]\) has \(x \le 1\) and \(y \le 1\), so \(x + y \le 2\), and so \([-1, 1] \times [-1, 1] \subseteq H\). By Theorem 1, \(D \subseteq H\).






3 Proving set equality







Exercise 3 (Absorbing an intersection) Let \(A\) and \(B\) be sets. Prove that \(A \cup (A \cap B) = A\) (Definition: Union, Definition: Intersection).
Hint: prove that each side is a subset of the other.










SolutionSolution






Solution 3. \(A \cup (A \cap B) \subseteq A\). Let \(x \in A \cup (A \cap B)\). Then \(x \in A\) or \(x \in A \cap B\). In the first case, \(x \in A\). In the second case, \(x \in A\) and \(x \in B\), so again \(x \in A\). Either way, \(x \in A\) (Definition: Proof by cases).
\(A \subseteq A \cup (A \cap B)\). Let \(x \in A\). Then “\(x \in A\) or \(x \in A \cap B\)” is true, since its first part is true (Definition: Or), so \(x \in A \cup (A \cap B)\).
Each side is a subset of the other, so an element is in one side exactly when it is in the other, and the two sets are equal (Definition: Set).











Theorem 2 (Equal sets are subsets of each other) Let \(A\) and \(B\) be sets. Then \(A = B\) if and only if \(A \subseteq B\) and \(B \subseteq A\).










ProofProof






Proof. By Definition: Set, \(A = B\) means that every \(x\) has \(x \in A \Leftrightarrow x \in B\). By Theorem: A biconditional is two conditionals, that biconditional is the same as “\(x \in A \Rightarrow x \in B\), and \(x \in B \Rightarrow x \in A\)”. A conjunction is true for every \(x\) exactly when each of its two parts is true for every \(x\). The first conditional, for every \(x\), is \(A \subseteq B\) (Definition: Subset), and the second, for every \(x\), is \(B \subseteq A\).











Remark 3 (The shape of a set equality proof). By Theorem 2, a proof of \(A = B\) has two parts, each a subset proof (Remark 2):

(\(\subseteq\)) Suppose \(a \in A\).
\(\vdots\)
Therefore \(a \in B\).

(\(\supseteq\)) Suppose \(a \in B\).
\(\vdots\)
Therefore \(a \in A\).

So \(A = B\).

This is the “if and only if” outline of Remark: The shape of an “if and only if” proof, applied to \(a \in A\) and \(a \in B\).











Example 4 (Two kinds of odd number) Claim: \({\mathopen{}\left\{4k + 1 : k \in \mathbb{Z}\right\}\mathclose{}} \cup {\mathopen{}\left\{4k + 3 : k \in \mathbb{Z}\right\}\mathclose{}} = {\mathopen{}\left\{2m + 1 : m \in \mathbb{Z}\right\}\mathclose{}}\).
(\(\subseteq\)) Let \(x\) be in the left-hand side. If \(x = 4k + 1\) for some integer \(k\), then \(x = 2(2k) + 1\). If \(x = 4k + 3\) for some integer \(k\), then \(x = 2(2k + 1) + 1\). Both \(2k\) and \(2k + 1\) are integers (Remark: Facts about integers used without proof), so either way \(x\) is in the right-hand side.
(\(\supseteq\)) Let \(x = 2m + 1\) for some integer \(m\). The integer \(m\) is even or odd (Remark: Facts about integers used without proof).

If \(m\) is even, then \(m = 2j\) for some integer \(j\) (Definition: Even integer), so \(x = 2(2j) + 1 = 4j + 1\), and \(x \in {\mathopen{}\left\{4k + 1 : k \in \mathbb{Z}\right\}\mathclose{}}\).
If \(m\) is odd, then \(m = 2j + 1\) for some integer \(j\) (Definition: Odd integer), so \(x = 2(2j + 1) + 1 = 4j + 3\), and \(x \in {\mathopen{}\left\{4k + 3 : k \in \mathbb{Z}\right\}\mathclose{}}\).

Either way, \(x\) is in the left-hand side. So the two sets are equal (Theorem 2).











Theorem 3 (A subset is its own intersection) Let \(A\) and \(B\) be sets. Then \(A \subseteq B\) if and only if \(A \cap B = A\).










ProofProof






Proof. (\(\Rightarrow\)) Suppose \(A \subseteq B\). We show \(A \cap B = A\) with Theorem 2. If \(x \in A \cap B\), then \(x \in A\) (Definition: Intersection). If \(x \in A\), then \(x \in B\), since \(A \subseteq B\), so \(x \in A \cap B\).
(\(\Leftarrow\)) Suppose \(A \cap B = A\), and let \(x \in A\). Then \(x \in A \cap B\), since the two sets are equal, so \(x \in B\). So \(A \subseteq B\).











Example 5 (Intersecting with a larger set) Let \(B = {\mathopen{}\left\{1, 2, 3, 4\right\}\mathclose{}}\).

\({\mathopen{}\left\{2, 4\right\}\mathclose{}} \subseteq B\), and \({\mathopen{}\left\{2, 4\right\}\mathclose{}} \cap B = {\mathopen{}\left\{2, 4\right\}\mathclose{}}\), as Theorem 3 says.
\({\mathopen{}\left\{2, 5\right\}\mathclose{}} \not\subseteq B\), since \(5 \notin B\), and \({\mathopen{}\left\{2, 5\right\}\mathclose{}} \cap B = {\mathopen{}\left\{2\right\}\mathclose{}}\), which is not \({\mathopen{}\left\{2, 5\right\}\mathclose{}}\).












Theorem 4 (Cancelling a factor of a Cartesian product) Let \(A\), \(B\) and \(C\) be sets with \(C \ne \emptyset\). If \(A \times C = B \times C\), then \(A = B\) (Definition: Cartesian product).










ProofProof






Proof. Suppose \(A \times C = B \times C\). Since \(C \ne \emptyset\), there is some \(c \in C\) (Definition: Empty set).
(\(\subseteq\)) Let \(a \in A\). Then \((a, c) \in A \times C\). Since \(A \times C = B \times C\), also \((a, c) \in B \times C\), so \((a, c) = (b, c')\) for some \(b \in B\) and \(c' \in C\) (Definition: Cartesian product). Two ordered pairs are equal only when their first entries are equal (Definition: Ordered pair), so \(a = b\), and \(a \in B\).
(\(\supseteq\)) Let \(b \in B\). Then \((b, c) \in B \times C = A \times C\), so \(b \in A\), by the same steps with \(A\) and \(B\) swapped.
So \(A = B\) (Theorem 2).











Example 6 (Why \(C\) must not be empty) The condition \(C \ne \emptyset\) in Theorem 4 is needed. Let \(A = {\mathopen{}\left\{1\right\}\mathclose{}}\), \(B = {\mathopen{}\left\{2\right\}\mathclose{}}\) and \(C = \emptyset\). A pair in \(A \times C\) would need a second entry in \(C\), and \(C\) has none, so \(A \times C = \emptyset\), and likewise \(B \times C = \emptyset\). So \(A \times C = B \times C\), but \(A \ne B\).
The proof uses the condition in its first step, to find an element \(c \in C\).






4 Disproving a claim about sets







Exercise 4 (Regrouping differences) Show that the claim “for all sets \(A\), \(B\) and \(C\), \(A - (B - C) = (A - B) - C\)” is false (Definition: Set difference).










SolutionSolution






Solution 4. A counterexample (Definition: Counterexample) is one choice of \(A\), \(B\) and \(C\) for which the two sides differ. Let \(A = B = C = {\mathopen{}\left\{1\right\}\mathclose{}}\). Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
A - (B - C)
&= {\mathopen{}\left\{1\right\}\mathclose{}} - ({\mathopen{}\left\{1\right\}\mathclose{}} - {\mathopen{}\left\{1\right\}\mathclose{}})
\\&= {\mathopen{}\left\{1\right\}\mathclose{}} - \emptyset
\\&= {\mathopen{}\left\{1\right\}\mathclose{}},
\end{aligned}
\]
while
\[
\begin{aligned}
(A - B) - C
&= ({\mathopen{}\left\{1\right\}\mathclose{}} - {\mathopen{}\left\{1\right\}\mathclose{}}) - {\mathopen{}\left\{1\right\}\mathclose{}}
\\&= \emptyset - {\mathopen{}\left\{1\right\}\mathclose{}}
\\&= \emptyset.
\end{aligned}
\]
The two sides differ, so the claim is false.











Remark 4 (Disproving a claim about all sets). A claim of the form “for all sets \(A\), \(B\), …, some equation holds” is disproved by one choice of sets for which it fails (Definition: Disproof). Small sets, such as \(\emptyset\) and \({\mathopen{}\left\{1\right\}\mathclose{}}\), are a good place to look. A Venn diagram (Definition: Venn diagram) can suggest where to look: shade each side, find a region shaded on one side only, and put an element in that region.











Example 7 (A union does not cancel) Claim to disprove: for all sets \(A\), \(B\) and \(C\), if \(A \cup B = A \cup C\), then \(B = C\).
Let \(A = {\mathopen{}\left\{1\right\}\mathclose{}}\), \(B = {\mathopen{}\left\{1\right\}\mathclose{}}\) and \(C = \emptyset\). Then \(A \cup B = {\mathopen{}\left\{1\right\}\mathclose{}}\) and \(A \cup C = {\mathopen{}\left\{1\right\}\mathclose{}}\), so \(A \cup B = A \cup C\), but \(B \ne C\). So the claim is false.

title: WWU CSCI 201 Syllabus
text:
Course Description
This course is a rigorous introduction to the mathematical structures and reasoning techniques underlying computer science. Topics include sets, functions, relations, graphs, trees, and finite automata, with an emphasis on formal definitions and logical precision. You will learn to write mathematical proofs using direct proof, contrapositive, contradiction, and induction. Functional programming is introduced as a way to express computation and recursion within a mathematically grounded framework.

title: WWU CSCI 201 Syllabus
text:
Course Outcomes
Homework, labs, and exams test and measure the outcomes below. On completion of CSCI 201, students will demonstrate:

A thorough understanding of the mathematical definitions of concepts important to computer science, including sets, tuples, functions, and relations.
A basic understanding of graphs, trees, and their traversals.
A basic understanding of the mathematical definition of finite automata.
A basic understanding of asymptotic notation.
A basic understanding of recurrence relations and loop invariants.
The ability to prove basic theorems involving these concepts using direct proof, contradiction, contrapositive, and mathematical induction.
The ability to use functional style effectively in a functional programming language.

Questions and Corrections
If something in the course materials seems wrong, ask. The course materials include the notes, worksheets, assignments, and anything I say or show in class, including my slides. I will make mistakes, and so will the other authors of the materials.
Do not assume that you are the confused one when the material might be wrong. Ask your question first, in class or outside it, and we can talk through your reasoning together. If you are right, we all learn something and I fix the material. If you are not, we can jointly find out where the confusion started.

Health Precautions

Software
The labs and the programming parts of homework use Racket, a functional programming language. Racket is free, and it comes with the DrRacket editor. For any software that comes pre-installed in the department labs, please use the default installed version.

title: WWU CSCI 201 Syllabus
text:
Active Learning
Class time is for working on problems, not only for listening. You will be asked to think about questions on your own, write down answers, discuss them in small groups, and share your answers with the class. Sometimes you may be asked to write on the board. I will give you time to think things through before you are put on the spot. Please give me feedback about the structure of the class, the activities, or group dynamics.

ABCD Cards
On the first day of class, I will give each student an ABCD card, which you will use to vote on answers to questions in class. They work like electronic clickers, but they are free and need no batteries. They let both you and me quickly see how well you understand the material, so that I can adjust what I emphasize in class and you can adjust what you study outside it. Please bring this card to class each day. If you lose your card, print a new, landscape-mode color copy (PDF: TBD).


Worksheets
Most classes include a worksheet: guided practice that reinforces the day’s concepts and prepares you for the exams. Please keep your worksheets organized and bring them to later classes. You are encouraged to work on worksheet problems with classmates, but each student submits their own work and should be able to explain it. I will post selected worksheet solutions after the submission deadline, and review common mistakes at the start of the next class. Most midterm and final exam questions will be adapted from worksheet problems.

Thresholds for plus and minus grades are at my discretion. The overall grade Canvas displays may be inaccurate; the weights above are the ones that count.

Homework and Worksheets
Homework assignments combine written work and programming. Homework and worksheets are graded on completion, meaning whether you made a solid effort to solve each problem:

Complete: 100%
Substantial effort: 80%
Minimal effort: 40%
Missing: 0%

The lowest worksheet score is dropped.
Quiz 0 is a short quiz in the first week that checks the CSCI 145 and precalculus material this course assumes. It is graded on completion and counts as one worksheet, and its main purpose is to show you (and me) what to review.
When writing up your work:

Type all written work. You do not need to use LaTeX, but I recommend it.
Hand-drawn diagrams are welcome when they help illustrate a concept, as long as they are legible.
Format code and pseudocode in a fixed-width font. Do not submit screenshots of your editor or terminal.
Show your work. An answer alone will not get full credit, on homework or on exams.



Labs
Weekly labs give hands-on programming practice, with a TA available to answer questions during the lab period. To get full credit, you must both attend lab and submit the deliverable by its deadline, which will typically be 10pm on the Monday after the lab (or the next class day, when that Monday is a holiday).

If you do not attend lab but submit the deliverable on time, your score is multiplied by 0.5. This penalty is waived automatically for one lab; if you have a legitimate reason to miss more, contact me and the TA ahead of time.
Attending a lab section other than your own requires permission from both me and the TA(s).
Late lab submissions are not accepted.



Exams
The course has two in-class midterm exams, tentatively on Wednesday, January 27 (week 4) and Wednesday, February 17 (week 7), and a cumulative final exam during finals week, in our classroom at the time WWU’s finals schedule assigns, which is set by the lecture time: Tuesday, March 16 for the 11:00 sections (CRNs 13745 and 13746) and Thursday, March 18 for the 9:00 sections (CRNs 13747 and 13748), both 10:30am–12:30pm.

Each midterm lasts 50 minutes, and you may bring one page of notes (front and back).
The final exam lasts 120 minutes, and you may bring two pages of notes (front and back).

If you know in advance that you will be unable to take an exam at the scheduled time, let me know at least one week before the exam, and we may be able to reschedule it.


Grading Questions
If you have a question about a grade, send it to me in writing, as a Canvas message (see Communication), within 48 hours of the graded work being returned. You will never lose points for asking.

title: WWU CSCI 201 Syllabus
text:
Collaboration and AI Tools
Collaboration. You may work together on homework and worksheets unless an assignment or problem says it is individual. A group of about three works best, since it is hard for everyone to contribute in a large group. You may discuss the steps of an algorithm or proof on a whiteboard, but write your own math and code, and submit your own answers. Do not copy from classmates, the internet, a chatbot, or a forum.
AI tools. AI tools such as large language model chatbots are allowed on homework and worksheets only. Use them like a collaborator, not as a source of answers: you must still write your answer in your own words, and you are responsible for understanding it. Say whether you used an AI tool, and name it, on each assignment. Students who rely heavily on AI tools often struggle on exams, where the tools are not available. AI tools are not allowed on lab work, including lab work you finish after the lab period.
Exams are solo: work alone, without help from anyone else and without AI tools; the only aid allowed is your page(s) of notes, as described under Exams.

text:
Academic Honesty
As a future professional, your integrity is crucial. It is your responsibility to read and be familiar with the university’s academic honesty policy, found in Appendix D of the Western Washington University Course Catalog; Academic Honesty Resources for Students explains the procedures and the appeal process. Cheating on an exam will result in failing the course (grade of F), and I will file documentation of the incident with the university. All cases of academic dishonesty will be reported. When in doubt, ask me.

title: WWU CSCI 201 Syllabus
text:
Student Conduct
I am committed to maintaining an inclusive, supportive, and professional environment in all academic settings, including lectures, labs, and course-related online spaces. I expect students to live up to the Association for Computing Machinery (ACM) Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct, the ethical code adopted by nearly every software professional. A pattern of failing to follow the ACM Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct can negatively affect course grades, up to and including a failing grade for the course. Conduct is also considered when determining admission to the major.
